entries.answer: Tuberculous peritonitis diffuse thickened enhancing peritoneum partially loculated ascites mesenteric fat infiltration Peritonitis pattern with mesenteric infiltration and loculated fluid may represent TB as infectious etiology. Differential: Peritoneal carcinomatosis Pseudomyxoma peritonei Other infectious peritonitis

entries.clinicalContext: Child with acute abdominal pain and fever.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Peritonitis secondary to perforated appendicitis loculated ascites markedly thickened enhancing peritoneal lining MR shows smooth thickening and enhancement of peritoneum with loculated fluid consistent with florid peritonitis. Differential: Peritoneal carcinomatosis Benign ascites

entries.clinicalContext: Adult shortly after abdominal surgery with abdominal pain and fever.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Peritonitis due to small bowel anastomotic leak peritoneal thickening and enhancement adjacent ascites omental infiltration Postoperative leak listed as iatrogenic cause of peritonitis with inflammatory fat stranding. Differential: Reactive postoperative peritoneal enhancement Early carcinomatosis

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with chronic dialysis and bowel obstruction symptoms.3
entries.question: CT abdomen with contrast. Based on the image, name 3 key differentials and give ONE best discriminator for each.
entries.answer: Sclerosing encapsulating peritonitis; Peritoneal carcinomatosis; Adhesive small bowel obstruction (Model-inferred differentials (not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx; generated by ChatGPT from caption-described imaging pattern).)

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with chronic abdominal symptoms and systemic inflammatory signs.1
entries.question: CT abdomen with contrast. Based on the image, name 4 key differentials and give ONE best discriminator for each.
entries.answer: Peritonitis (infectious/inflammatory); Peritoneal carcinomatosis; Benign ascites; Pseudomyxoma peritonei

entries.question: In a cirrhotic patient with ascites and abdominal pain, what imaging or clinical finding pushes you away from spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) and toward secondary peritonitis?
entries.answer: Evidence of a surgically correctable source: • Free intraperitoneal air • Focal inflammatory source (e.g., perforated viscus) • Abscess • Anastomotic leak SBP occurs without a surgically correctable intra-abdominal source.

entries.question: On CT, what pattern of peritoneal thickening favors carcinomatosis over inflammatory peritonitis?
entries.answer: • Nodular or irregular peritoneal thickening • Omental caking • Discrete peritoneal implants Inflammatory peritonitis more commonly shows smooth, uniform enhancement.

entries.question: What condition is also known as the “abdominal cocoon”?
entries.answer: Sclerosing encapsulating peritonitis — fibrotic thickening of visceral and parietal peritoneum encasing bowel loops, often associated with chronic peritoneal dialysis.

entries.question: What imaging features increase suspicion for tuberculous peritonitis rather than uncomplicated SBP?
entries.answer: • Loculated or complex ascites • Diffuse smooth enhancing peritoneum • Mesenteric fat infiltration • Associated lymphadenopathy TB often produces more chronic inflammatory changes.

entries.question: What CT feature helps distinguish hemoperitoneum from simple inflammatory ascites?
entries.answer: High-attenuation fluid favors hemoperitoneum. Inflammatory ascites typically has lower attenuation unless complicated.

entries.question: What does ectopic gas within ascitic fluid suggest?
entries.answer: • Hollow viscus perforation • Gas-forming infection Strongly supports secondary bacterial peritonitis.

entries.question: Why are cirrhotic patients with ascites predisposed to spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
entries.answer: Impaired host defenses and bacterial translocation from the gut into ascitic fluid lead to infection without an identifiable perforation.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Define portal hypertension.
entries.answer: Source definition (Core IR): Portosystemic gradient > 5 mm Hg. Boundary: Hemodynamic state of elevated portal system pressure/gradient, not itself a single etiology; produces portosystemic collateralization. Synonyms/near-synonyms: Portosystemic hypertension (conceptual equivalent).

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: What type of entity is portal hypertension?
entries.answer: Pathophysiologic process (hemodynamic state) — defined by abnormal portal/systemic pressure gradient and drives collateral formation.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: What type of entity are varices?
entries.answer: Structural vascular lesion (collateral venous pathway) — dilated collateral veins formed in response to altered pressure gradients/flow.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Varices vs soft-tissue mass: what is the single fundamental discriminator?
entries.answer: They enhance/opacify like veins and connect to venous structures/shunts (tubular/serpiginous vascular channels), rather than forming a fixed solid enhancing tissue mass.

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with upper GI bleeding concern.1
entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Esophageal varices Keyword findings: esophagram | defects in esophageal wall | post endoscopic sclerosis | pliable/compressible Tight reasoning: Serpiginous intraluminal mural defects on esophagram in this context are consistent with varices; key functional clue is pliability/compressibility vs fixed lesion. Differential: Varicoid esophageal carcinoma Sclerosed/thrombosed varices

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with chronic liver disease stigmata.2
entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Splenorenal shunt (portosystemic shunt) with varices Keyword findings: coronal CECT | multiple LUQ varices | communicate with splenic vein | communicate with left renal vein | dilated left renal vein | splenorenal shunt Tight reasoning: Direct venous continuity between splenic vein territory varices and a dilated left renal vein supports a splenorenal portosystemic shunt due to portal hypertension. Differential: Perisplenic venous collaterals without established shunt Venous malformation

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Chronic portal vein thrombosis in portal hypertension Keyword findings: thrombus in main portal vein | calcification suggesting chronicity | markedly enlarged spleen | portal hypertension risk due to stasis/slow flow Tight reasoning: Calcified portal vein thrombus implies chronicity; portal hypertension/slow flow predisposes to thrombosis; associated splenomegaly supports portal HTN stigmata. Differential: Acute portal vein thrombosis Tumor thrombus

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with chronic liver disease stigmata.
entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Recanalized paraumbilical vein with caput medusae (portal hypertension) Keyword findings: axial CECT | recanalized paraumbilical vein | communicates with left portal vein | multiple periumbilical collaterals | caput medusae | virtually pathognomonic Tight reasoning: A recanalized paraumbilical vein arising from the left portal vein with radiating periumbilical collaterals is a classic/near-diagnostic portal HTN collateral pattern. Differential: Abdominal wall varices from other venous obstruction Dilated abdominal wall veins without portal venous communication

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with chronic liver disease and abdominal distention.
entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Portal gastropathy (with ascites in portal hypertension) Keyword findings: axial CECT | diffuse gastric submucosal edema | wall thickening | severe portal gastropathy on endoscopy | ascites Tight reasoning: Diffuse gastric submucosal edema/wall thickening in this setting, confirmed endoscopically as portal gastropathy, with concomitant ascites as portal HTN sequela. Differential: Gastritis Infiltrative gastric malignancy Hypoproteinemia-related edema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with chronic liver disease and lower GI bleeding concern.
entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Rectal varices (portal hypertension) Keyword findings: coronal CECT | extensive varices in/around rectum | cirrhotic patient | can bleed → GI hemorrhage Tight reasoning: Prominent rectal venous collaterals in cirrhosis represent rectal varices, a portosystemic collateral site that may cause bleeding. Differential: Hemorrhoids Rectal mass with prominent vessels

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Gastric varices (portal hypertension) Keyword findings: coronal CECT | multiple large gastric varices | venous-phase images | mimic intramural mass on NECT/arterial phase Tight reasoning: Venous-phase CT depiction of large serpiginous enhancing structures in typical perigastric distribution supports gastric varices; pitfall is mass mimic on noncontrast/arterial phase. Differential: Gastric carcinoma Adrenal carcinoma Pancreatic hypervascular tumor

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with chronic liver disease and prior abdominal surgery.
entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Peristomal varices (new portosystemic anastomosis site) Keyword findings: axial CECT | colostomy | varices around the stoma | new site of portosystemic anastomosis Tight reasoning: Surgical stoma creates an abnormal anastomotic territory for portosystemic collateralization; clustered enhancing veins around stoma are peristomal varices. Differential: Parastomal soft-tissue mass Inflammatory peristomal hyperemia/edema

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Paraesophageal varices (mass mimic on CXR/NECT) Keyword findings: axial CECT | large varices surrounding esophagus | paraesophageal varices | mistaken for mediastinal mass on CXR/NECT Tight reasoning: Enhancing serpiginous venous structures around the esophagus represent paraesophageal varices; key pitfall is mislabeling as mediastinal mass on noncontrast studies. Differential: Middle mediastinal mass Lymphadenopathy Aneurysm

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with upper GI bleeding concern.
entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Fluoroscopic esophagram. Based on the image, name 3 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
entries.answer: Esophageal varices Varicoid esophageal carcinoma Sclerosed/thrombosed varices

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: CT abdomen with contrast. Based on the image, name 3 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
entries.answer: Gastric varices Gastric carcinoma Adrenal carcinoma

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: CT chest/upper abdomen with contrast. Based on the image, name 3 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
entries.answer: Paraesophageal varices Lymphadenopathy Aneurysm

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: What is the classic pitfall confusing “downhill” vs “uphill” esophageal varices, and what’s the safety check?
entries.answer: Pitfall: assuming any esophageal varices implies portal hypertension. Safety check: localize varices (proximal vs distal) and consider SVC obstruction for proximal “downhill” varices; portal hypertension classically causes distal “uphill” varices.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: What vascular pitfall can mimic peritoneal/omental metastases, and what’s the safety check on CT?
entries.answer: Pitfall: mistaking numerous small omental varices for metastases or granulomas. Safety check: confirm tubular/serpiginous morphology and venous-phase enhancement matching veins with collateral continuity.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Portal vein Doppler: what’s the normal flow velocity range, and what velocity is “slow flow” (article)?
entries.answer: Normal portal vein flow 15–40 cm/s; slow flow < 15 cm/s.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: What portal vein diameter is commonly used as “dilated” in portal hypertension (article)?
entries.answer: Portal vein often > 13 mm.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: What coronary (left gastric) vein diameter is considered abnormal in portal hypertension (article)?

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: During TIPS creation, what pressure-gradient target is referenced in Core’s workflow?
entries.answer: Post-TIPS gradient < 12 mm Hg.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: What are the three hemodynamic classifications of portal hypertension?
entries.answer: Presinusoidal; Sinusoidal; Postsinusoidal.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Name 3 causes and one imaging clue.
entries.answer: Causes: portal vein thrombosis; splenic vein thrombosis; schistosomiasis. Imaging clue: portal vein occlusion or cavernous transformation with relatively preserved hepatic architecture early.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Why is venous-phase CT critical for detecting varices?
entries.answer: Varices enhance like adjacent veins; noncontrast or arterial phase may mimic soft-tissue mass or appear collapsed.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: How can collapsed varices create a diagnostic pitfall?
entries.answer: May appear as soft tissue or be occult on noncontrast imaging; venous-phase imaging clarifies enhancement pattern.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: Which varices most commonly cause life-threatening hemorrhage?
entries.answer: Distal esophageal varices.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: How do gastric varices differ clinically from esophageal varices?
entries.answer: Bleed less frequently but often more severely when bleeding occurs.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: CT shows splenomegaly, ascites, dilated portal vein, and varices. Unifying diagnosis?
entries.answer: Portal hypertension.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: What does hepatofugal portal vein flow indicate?
entries.answer: Reversal of portal flow consistent with advanced portal hypertension.

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: What is cavernous transformation of the portal vein?
entries.answer: Network of collateral venous channels replacing chronically thrombosed portal vein. example of case Cavernous transformation of portal vein | Radiology Case | Radiopaedia.org

entries.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
entries.question: What is portal hypertensive colopathy?
entries.answer: Mucosal vascular congestion and edema of the colon due to portal hypertension; may cause bleeding.

entries.question: What type of entity is pneumoperitoneum?
entries.answer: Imaging-defined entity (radiologic finding/state). Entity classification inferred from source description.

entries.question: Pneumoperitoneum vs Chilaiditi syndrome: what is the single fundamental discriminator?
entries.answer: Free peritoneal gas vs colonic interposition (colon between liver and diaphragm) that mimics free air on radiographs.

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Bowel anastomotic leak (rectal anastomosis) Caption-keyword findings: greater than expected pneumoperitoneum; immediately after surgery; focal collection of ectopic gas; near the rectal anastomosis Tight reasoning: Postoperative free air can be normal, but large/greater-than-expected pneumoperitoneum plus a focal ectopic gas collection near the anastomosis supports an anastomotic leak rather than routine postoperative air. Differential: Normal postoperative pneumoperitoneum Iatrogenic injuries or complications Hollow viscus perforation

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Normal postoperative pneumoperitoneum Caption-keyword findings: after abdominal surgery; thin crescent of pneumoperitoneum; nondependent upper abdomen; normal finding in the postoperative period Tight reasoning: A thin crescent of free air in the nondependent upper abdomen shortly after surgery matches expected postoperative pneumoperitoneum. Differential: Bowel anastomotic leak Hollow viscus perforation Iatrogenic injuries or complications

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Barotrauma-related pneumoperitoneum Caption-keyword findings: positive-pressure ventilation; large bilateral pneumothoraces; gas dissecting downward; retroperitoneum; intraperitoneal space; classic findings for barotrauma Tight reasoning: In a ventilated patient with pneumothoraces, gas dissecting into retroperitoneal + intraperitoneal spaces is the classic pattern for barotrauma. Differential: Iatrogenic injuries or complications Perforated ulcer Hollow viscus perforation

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Duodenal perforation after ERCP Caption-keyword findings: after ERCP; gas tracking from the duodenum; peritoneal; retroperitoneal; subcutaneous soft tissues; sequelae of duodenal perforation Tight reasoning: Post-ERCP with gas tracking from the duodenum into both peritoneal and retroperitoneal spaces (plus subcutaneous emphysema) supports duodenal perforation as an iatrogenic complication. Differential: Perforated duodenal ulcer Other iatrogenic injuries or complications Barotrauma

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Perforated duodenal ulcer Caption-keyword findings: extravasation of enteric contrast; from the duodenum; free intraperitoneal air; large ascites; contain oral contrast material; perforated duodenal ulcer Tight reasoning: Enteric contrast extravasation from the duodenum with free air and ascites containing oral contrast indicates an active duodenal perforation consistent with perforated duodenal ulcer. Differential: Iatrogenic injuries or complications (duodenal perforation) Hollow viscus perforation Other causes of bowel perforation

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Perforated gastric ulcer Caption-keyword findings: marked wall edema and thickening; lesser curvature of the stomach; free intraperitoneal air; perforated gastric ulcer Tight reasoning: Gastric wall edema/thickening along the lesser curvature plus free air supports perforated gastric ulcer. Differential: Perforated duodenal ulcer Iatrogenic injuries or complications (endoscopy) Other causes of bowel perforation

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Perforated sigmoid diverticulitis Caption-keyword findings: gas and enteric contrast; tracking upward; inflamed sigmoid colon; perforated sigmoid diverticulitis Tight reasoning: Gas + enteric contrast tracking upward from an inflamed sigmoid colon supports perforated sigmoid diverticulitis. Differential: Other causes of bowel perforation Colonic ischemia with perforation Intestinal trauma

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Colonic injury with perforation (trauma) Caption-keyword findings: multiple stab wounds; multiple foci of free air; gas and ectopic enteric contrast; immediately along the outer margin of the colon; discovered at surgery Tight reasoning: Penetrating trauma with free air plus ectopic enteric contrast adjacent to the colon margin supports colonic injury/perforation. Differential: Intestinal trauma (other site) Other causes of bowel perforation Diverticulitis with perforation

entries.clinicalContext: Asymptomatic adult with incidental imaging finding.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Benign pneumatosis with small adjacent free air Caption-keyword findings: asymptomatic; bubbly pneumatosis; right colon; several foci of adjacent free air; clinically doing well; thought to represent benign pneumatosis Tight reasoning: Bubbly pneumatosis with small adjacent free air in a clinically well, asymptomatic patient supports benign pneumatosis in this context. Differential: Colonic ischemia with perforation Other causes of bowel perforation Peritonitis (gas-forming organisms)

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Benign pneumatosis with small adjacent free air (steroid-treated, asymptomatic) Caption-keyword findings: asymptomatic; chronic steroid treatment; extensive benign pneumatosis; throughout the right colon; resultant perforation; small adjacent free air Tight reasoning: The caption frames extensive pneumatosis as benign in an asymptomatic steroid-treated patient, with small adjacent free air despite concerning CT appearance. Differential: Colonic ischemia with perforation Other causes of bowel perforation Peritonitis/abscess

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Small bowel diverticulitis with tiny adjacent ectopic gas Caption-keyword findings: abdominal pain; inflamed contrast-filled diverticulum; arising from a small bowel loop; tiny focus of adjacent ectopic gas; compatible with small bowel diverticulitis Tight reasoning: Inflamed small-bowel diverticulum with tiny adjacent ectopic gas supports small bowel diverticulitis with microperforation. Differential: Foreign body perforation Other causes of bowel perforation Severe infection/inflammatory bowel disease with perforation

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with psychiatric history and abdominal pain.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Foreign body perforation of small bowel Caption-keyword findings: psychiatric patient; intentionally ingested pin; perforating through the small bowel; into the adjacent abdominal wall; required surgical intervention Tight reasoning: Direct visualization of an ingested pin traversing bowel into the abdominal wall is diagnostic of foreign body perforation. Differential: Other causes of bowel perforation Penetrating trauma Small bowel diverticulitis with perforation

entries.question: CT chest/abdomen context. Based on the image, name 3 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
entries.answer: Barotrauma-related pneumoperitoneum Iatrogenic injuries or complications Perforated ulcer

entries.question: Contrast-enhanced CT. Based on the image, name 3 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
entries.answer: Perforated duodenal ulcer Iatrogenic injuries or complications (duodenal perforation) Bowel anastomotic leak

entries.question: CT abdomen. Based on the image, name 3 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
entries.answer: Colonic ischemia with perforation Benign pneumatosis (pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis) with small adjacent free air Other causes of bowel perforation

entries.question: Define pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis.
entries.answer: Source definition: Described as an uncommon, benign form of pneumatosis with cystic collections of gas in the bowel wall. Refined definition based on medical consensus: Benign condition characterized by multiple gas-filled cysts within the bowel wall that may rupture and produce pneumoperitoneum. Boundary condition: A bowel-wall gas cyst entity (not merely any pneumatosis); may look worrisome on CT but can be clinically benign. Synonyms: Benign pneumatosis (as used in source context).

entries.question: What type of entity is pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis?
entries.answer: Pathologic entity / pathophysiologic process characterized by cystic intramural gas in the bowel wall (benign).

entries.question: Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis vs ischemic pneumatosis: what is the single fundamental discriminator?
entries.answer: Benign intramural gas cysts that can exist in clinically stable/asymptomatic patients vs pneumatosis as a manifestation of bowel wall injury/ischemia in a clinically ill patient (distinction is context-dependent).

entries.question: How can positive-pressure ventilation produce pneumoperitoneum?
entries.answer: Positive-pressure ventilation can lead to alveolar rupture with thoracic air (e.g., pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum); gas can dissect along tissue planes into the retroperitoneum and/or peritoneal cavity, producing pneumoperitoneum.

entries.question: Why can pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis cause pneumoperitoneum in an asymptomatic patient?
entries.answer: Cystic intramural gas collections can rupture, releasing gas into the peritoneal cavity; despite a concerning CT appearance, the underlying process can be benign and patients may be asymptomatic.

entries.question: Why do duodenal vs gastric ulcer perforations tend to show different gas/fluid distributions?
entries.answer: Duodenal bulb perforation tends to produce ectopic gas/fluid/stranding adjacent to the bulb and may involve both intraperitoneal and extraperitoneal compartments (e.g., anterior pararenal space). Gastric ulcer perforation can occur into the lesser sac, with gas/fluid posterior to the stomach and extension into the peritoneal cavity via the epiploic foramen.

entries.question: Post-op free air pitfall: what is the common mistake, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Assuming any postoperative pneumoperitoneum is normal. Safety check: Evaluate whether free air is greater than expected and look for focal ectopic gas near an anastomosis; large/massive postoperative free air should raise concern for anastomotic leak or perforation.

entries.question: Pneumoperitoneum mimic pitfall: what entity can be mistaken for free air, and what safety check prevents the error?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking interposed colon between the diaphragm and liver for free intraperitoneal air. Safety check: Identify bowel configuration/haustral markings and a continuous colon loop beneath the right hemidiaphragm (colonic interposition).

entries.question: Radiograph pitfall: what thoracic process can simulate pneumoperitoneum, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: A thin crescent of pleural air (pneumothorax) near the diaphragm may simulate free intraperitoneal air. Safety check: Look for a pleural line and absence of lung markings peripheral to it; correlate with other thoracic air signs.

entries.question: Radiograph pitfall: how can basal atelectasis mimic pneumoperitoneum, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: Plate-like basal atelectasis can create a curvilinear density paralleling the diaphragm with aerated lung below, mimicking free air. Safety check: Identify lung markings/volume loss and ensure the lucency corresponds to aerated lung rather than free peritoneal gas.

entries.question: Radiograph pitfall: how can cystic lung disease near the diaphragm mimic pneumoperitoneum, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: Bullae or cysts near the diaphragm can simulate free air on radiographs due to proximity to the diaphragm. Safety check: Trace lung parenchyma continuity and look for internal lung markings/contours consistent with cystic lung disease.

entries.question: Radiograph pitfall: how can subphrenic fat be mistaken for free air, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: Radiolucent subxiphoid/perihepatic fat collections may be misinterpreted as free intraperitoneal air. Safety check: Confirm fat density pattern and anatomic location; correlate with CT when uncertain.

entries.question: Radiograph pitfall: how can a gas-containing subphrenic abscess simulate free air, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: A gas-containing subphrenic abscess can simulate free abdominal gas on an upright radiograph. Safety check: Look for a localized collection (often with fluid component/air-fluid level) and correlate with CT for confirmation.

entries.question: Suspected hollow viscus perforation: what imaging test is most sensitive for pneumoperitoneum?
entries.answer: CT is significantly more sensitive than plain radiographs for detection of pneumoperitoneum and should be the test of choice in suspected hollow viscus perforation.

entries.question: For detecting free intraperitoneal air on radiographs, which views are most sensitive vs least sensitive?
entries.answer: Upright or decubitus radiographs are much more sensitive than supine films for detection of free air.

entries.question: Pneumoperitoneum localization: how does free-air location relative to the transverse mesocolon help localize the perforation?
entries.answer: Gastric/duodenal perforations typically result in free air in the upper abdomen (above the transverse mesocolon); jejunal, ileal, and colonic perforations tend to result in free air below the transverse mesocolon.

entries.question: Pneumoperitoneum amount rule: which sites tend to produce small vs massive free air?
entries.answer: Small bowel perforation usually results in only small amounts of pneumoperitoneum, while gastric and colonic perforations can result in massive free air (per source framing).

entries.question: After surgery, how common is free air on CT early, and when does it usually resolve?
entries.answer: Free air is seen on CT in ~90% of patients at 3 days and ~50% at 6 days after surgery; it typically resolves in 7–10 days but may rarely persist longer in some patients.

entries.question: Post-op pneumoperitoneum: what finding should raise concern for anastomotic leak or perforation?
entries.answer: Large or massive postoperative pneumoperitoneum is abnormal and should raise concern for anastomotic leak or perforation.

entries.question: Supine Upright Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Adhesive small bowel obstruction (SBO) Keyword findings (from caption): - no obvious dilation of the SB - string-of-pearls sign - gas within fluid-distended, obstructed segments of the SB - collapsed distal SB - massive dilation of proximal SB segments Tight reasoning: Supine radiograph can miss fluid-distended SBO (“no obvious dilation”), while the upright view shows the string-of-pearls sign, and CT confirms a transition pattern with collapsed distal bowel and markedly dilated proximal segments consistent with SBO from an adhesive transition (no other cause described). Differential: Adynamic or paralytic ileus Colonic obstruction Internal hernia

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Adhesive small bowel obstruction (SBO) Keyword findings (from caption): - prior surgical history - dilated proximal SB - decompressed bowel distal to the transition site - transition from dilated to collapsed SB - No mass, hernia, or other specific cause was identified Tight reasoning: CT shows a clear transition from dilated proximal to decompressed distal bowel, and explicitly notes no mass or hernia—supporting adhesive SBO as the cause (diagnosis of exclusion when a transition exists without another etiology). Differential: Internal hernia Small-bowel tumor causing obstruction Colonic obstruction

entries.clinicalContext: Older adult with abdominal pain, distention, vomiting.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Small bowel obstruction due to right femoral hernia Keyword findings (from caption): - markedly dilated proximal SB segments - distal SB and colon are decompressed - dilated SB entering a right femoral hernia - "knuckle" of SB trapped within the femoral hernia - transition point as the dilated SB enters the right femoral hernia Tight reasoning: Multiple CT planes directly show bowel entering and becoming trapped within a femoral hernia at the transition point, with proximal dilation and distal decompression—defining both SBO and its etiology. Differential: Inguinal hernia causing SBO Obturator hernia causing SBO Adhesive SBO

entries.clinicalContext: Prior bowel surgery; recurrent obstructive symptoms.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Small bowel obstruction due to peritoneal carcinomatosis (serosal implants) Keyword findings (from caption): - metastatic ovarian carcinoma - ileostomy - SB segments that are matted together - without definable mesenteric fat between SB segments - SB loops that are encased and angulated - due to serosal implants Tight reasoning: CT explicitly describes matted, encased, angulated bowel loops without normal intervening mesenteric fat, attributed to serosal implants—an extrinsic malignant cause of SBO. Differential: Adhesive SBO Internal hernia Closed loop obstruction

entries.clinicalContext: Older adult with abdominal distention and pain.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Closed-loop small bowel obstruction with volvulus Keyword findings (from caption): - moderate gas dilation of proximal SB segments - minimal gas in the distal SB and colon - suggestion of a lower abdominal mass - dilated mid-SB segments that are almost entirely fluid-filled with little gas - mesenteric vessels … engorged and crowded with blurred margins - Ascites is present - whirl sign - twisting of the SB mesenteric vessels Tight reasoning: Radiograph suggests a “mass,” but CT shows fluid-filled dilated small bowel with crowded/engorged mesenteric vessels and a whirl sign indicating twisting of mesenteric vessels—supporting a closed-loop obstruction/volvulus pattern with associated edema/ascites. Differential: Internal hernia with closed-loop obstruction Adhesive closed-loop obstruction Strangulating SBO from hernia

entries.clinicalContext: Postoperative patient with acute abdominal pain/distention.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?

entries.clinicalContext: Chronic inflammatory bowel symptoms with progressive distention and pain.12
entries.question: How does active Crohn inflammation create an obstructing transition segment on contrast CT?
entries.answer: Active inflammatory injury in distal small bowel → mucosal hyperemia and hyperenhancement → increased permeability → submucosal edema and wall thickening → luminal narrowing at involved segment → mechanical bottleneck → proximal dilation with transition at inflamed segment.

entries.clinicalContext: Young adult with recurrent abdominal pain and distention.0
entries.question: Why does DIOS produce distal ileal obstruction with feculent material and proximal small-bowel dilation?
entries.answer: Cystic fibrosis → dehydrated and viscous intestinal contents → inspissated feculent material accumulates in distal ileum → intraluminal obstruction at distal small bowel → proximal accumulation of fluid and gas → proximal small-bowel dilation and possible small-bowel feces sign near transition.

entries.question: What mechanism allows a gallstone to obstruct the small bowel in gallstone ileus?
entries.answer: Chronic gallstone disease → inflammation and erosion between gallbladder and adjacent bowel → biliary-enteric fistula formation → large gallstone enters gastrointestinal tract → stone migrates until it lodges in small bowel lumen → intraluminal mechanical obstruction → proximal small-bowel dilation.

entries.clinicalContext: Patient with abdominal pain; supine abdominal radiograph appears nondiagnostic.
entries.question: Why can a supine abdominal radiograph miss small bowel obstruction, and what breaks the trap?
entries.answer: Fluid-filled small bowel segments may not demonstrate obvious gas dilation on supine imaging → obstruction is present but gas does not outline distended loops → false reassurance if relying on supine film alone → upright or decubitus imaging may reveal multiple air-fluid levels or the string-of-pearls sign → CT definitively establishes dilation and transition zone.

entries.clinicalContext: CT shows transition from dilated to collapsed small bowel with no visible mass or hernia.
entries.question: Why is adhesive SBO considered a diagnosis of exclusion on CT, and what is the cognitive trap?
entries.answer: Adhesions are fibrous bands not directly visualized on CT → imaging may show a clear transition but no structural lesion → cognitive trap is assuming no cause is present and under-calling obstruction → correct reasoning is that absence of mass or hernia in a postoperative patient strongly supports adhesive SBO.

entries.clinicalContext: Supine radiograph suggests a lower abdominal mass in a patient with pain and distention.
entries.question: How can closed-loop obstruction mimic a mass on radiograph, and what imaging finding breaks the trap?
entries.answer: Closed-loop obstruction may produce a markedly fluid-filled dilated loop with little intraluminal gas → on supine radiograph this may appear as a soft-tissue mass → cognitive trap is mislabeling as tumor → CT demonstrates fluid-filled dilated loops with whirl sign or vessel crowding confirming closed-loop obstruction.

entries.clinicalContext: Post–gastric bypass patient with CT transition zone and no obvious mass.
entries.question: Why is internal hernia after gastric bypass a high-risk mimic of adhesive SBO?
entries.answer: Both may show transition from dilated to collapsed bowel without obvious mass → cognitive trap is labeling as simple adhesive obstruction → internal hernia involves mesenteric defect with twisted vessels and clustered loops → carries high risk of strangulation → presence of twisted SMV or displaced anastomosis breaks the trap.

entries.clinicalContext: CT shows small-bowel feces sign near distal ileum.
entries.question: Why does the small-bowel feces sign not automatically equal DIOS?
entries.answer: Small-bowel feces sign represents particulate intraluminal material proximal to obstruction → can occur in mechanical SBO of various causes → cognitive trap is equating feces sign exclusively with DIOS → DIOS requires clinical context such as cystic fibrosis and distal ileal impaction pattern.

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with imaging-confirmed small bowel obstruction.
entries.question: In SBO, what imaging diagnosis is crucial because it directs prompt surgical intervention?
entries.answer: CT diagnosis of closed-loop obstruction or strangulating (ischemic) SBO is crucial because these represent complicated obstruction with vascular compromise risk and require prompt surgical intervention rather than conservative management.

entries.clinicalContext: Patient with suspected small bowel obstruction on CT.
entries.question: In suspected SBO, what is the single most important anatomic imaging target to identify and why?
entries.answer: The transition zone between dilated and collapsed bowel is the key imaging target because it confirms obstruction, localizes the level, and helps determine the cause; CT is superior to plain radiographs for defining this transition.

entries.clinicalContext: CT demonstrates dilated small bowel with possible torsion pattern.
entries.question: What constellation of CT findings should make you diagnose closed-loop SBO?
entries.answer: Closed-loop SBO is suggested by obstruction at two points with markedly fluid-distended loops often greater than 4 cm, little gas, converging or twisted mesenteric vessels, and morphologic signs such as the whirl sign or beak sign, reflecting torsion of mesentery.

entries.clinicalContext: CT abdomen with contrast in SBO patient.
entries.question: On contrast CT in SBO, what bowel wall enhancement finding indicates strangulation or ischemia?
entries.answer: Absent, decreased, or delayed bowel wall enhancement in the obstructed segment indicates vascular compromise and supports the diagnosis of strangulating or ischemic SBO requiring urgent management.

entries.question: Besides enhancement abnormality, what additional CT findings support strangulating SBO?
entries.answer: Supporting findings include bowel wall thickening from edema or hemorrhage, mesenteric and interloop edema with ascites, congested or obscured mesenteric vessels, obscured loop margins, and high attenuation bowel wall on noncontrast CT reflecting hemorrhagic ischemia.

entries.clinicalContext: Post–gastric bypass patient with SBO pattern on CT.
entries.question: What CT constellation suggests internal hernia causing SBO in postoperative patients?
entries.answer: A cluster of dilated small-bowel loops with crowding or twisting of mesenteric vessels, a transition through a mesenteric defect, twisted SMV, infiltrated mesentery, displaced anastomosis, and possible decreased bowel wall enhancement suggests internal hernia with high risk of strangulation.

entries.question: Epidemiology pivot for SBO: what is the single exam-relevant etiology frequency breakdown?
entries.answer: • Most common causes: adhesions (~60%), hernias (15%), tumors (~15%; metastases > primary tumor). Exam pivot: If no mass or hernia is seen at the transition zone, adhesive SBO becomes the leading diagnosis (diagnosis of exclusion).

entries.question: What percentage of acute abdominal presentations is sbo
entries.answer: • SBO accounts for ~20% of acute abdomen presentations. Exam pivot: SBO is a high-probability diagnosis in acute abdomen—prioritize finding a transition zone and complications on CT.

entries.question: What is the sensitivity and specificity of multiplanar CECT for high-grade SBO (as stated in source)?
entries.answer: • Sensitivity: 95% • Specificity: 96% Exam pivot: In suspected high-grade SBO, CT is a high-confidence test—use it to define the transition zone and look for complications.

entries.question: For high-grade SBO, what does the source state about CT vs plain film performance?
entries.answer: • Transition zone and cause are all better determined on CT than on plain films with accuracy near 100% for high-grade SBO. Exam pivot: If the question is high-grade SBO, default to CT for definitive presence/site/cause (plain films can miss fluid-filled SBO).

entries.question: What are the size cutoffs for dilated small bowel (radiograph vs CT), and what size supports a fluid-distended closed-loop SBO?
entries.answer: • Radiographs: SB > 3 cm • CT: SB > 2.5 cm • Closed loop: affected SB segments markedly distended > 4 cm (fluid, little gas). Exam pivot: Use the correct modality cutoff, and >4 cm fluid-distended segments should raise concern for closed-loop.

entries.question: What does the source recommend about positive oral contrast for CT in SBO, and why?
entries.answer: • Positive oral contrast is rarely useful and may impede CT detection of complications such as ischemia. Exam pivot: In suspected complicated SBO, avoid routine positive oral contrast—prioritize evaluation for ischemia/strangulation.

entries.question: What CT findings in SBO suggest strangulation/ischemia (as stated in source)?
entries.answer: • Absent, decreased, or delayed bowel wall enhancement. • Bowel wall thickening (edema or hemorrhage); high density wall on NECT = hemorrhage = ischemia. • Mesenteric and interloop edema ± ascites. • Mesenteric vessels: congested, thrombosed, or obscured. • Obscured margins among affected SB segments. Exam pivot: These findings should push you toward complicated SBO and prompt surgical escalation.

entries.question: What are the key CT signs of closed-loop SBO (as stated in source)?
entries.answer: • Markedly distended fluid-filled SB segments (> 4 cm) with little gas. • Relatively little dilatation proximal to the closed loop. • Stretched mesenteric vessels converging toward torsion. • Beak sign (fusiform tapering at torsion/obstruction point). • Whirl sign (tightly twisted mesenteric vessels). • Balloons-on-strings appearance. Exam pivot: Closed-loop pattern is a complication class—actively search for ischemia/strangulation signs and communicate urgency.

entries.question: How is SBO classified into simple vs complicated (and what defines complicated)?
entries.answer: Simple SBO: intermittent, incomplete, or partial low-grade obstruction; prolonged complete or high-grade obstruction without vascular compromise. Complicated SBO: closed loop or incarcerated obstruction; strangulation indicating vascular compromise. Exam pivot: Complicated SBO = vascular compromise risk → surgical urgency.

entries.question: On imaging, how do you distinguish partial (low-grade) from complete (high-grade) SBO?
entries.answer: Partial/low-grade: some distal gas or contrast beyond transition. Complete/high-grade: no distal gas; complete obstruction at transition. Passage of enteric contrast into colon excludes complete SBO. Exam pivot: Distal gas or contrast beyond transition argues against complete obstruction.

entries.question: What imaging findings distinguish adynamic/paralytic ileus from mechanical SBO?
entries.answer: Ileus: dilated small bowel AND colon with no discrete transition point. SBO: transition zone between dilated proximal and collapsed distal bowel. Ileus: gas in nondependent SB and transverse colon; minimal gas in dependent colon/rectum. Exam pivot: Presence of a discrete transition zone defines mechanical SBO.

entries.question: When is enteroclysis preferred over CT in suspected SBO?
entries.answer: Enteroclysis: most sensitive test for intermittent, low-grade SBO. CT: best tool for acute high-grade SBO and evaluation of ischemia, sepsis, or cancer. Exam pivot: Intermittent/low-grade → enteroclysis; acute/complicated → CT.

entries.question: What does passage of enteric contrast into the colon indicate in suspected SBO?
entries.answer: Passage of contrast into colon excludes complete SBO. Exam pivot: If contrast reaches colon, obstruction is partial or resolving—not complete.

entries.question: Why can plain radiographs miss SBO, and what subtle sign may still suggest it?
entries.answer: Fluid-distended bowel may not be evident on plain films. String-of-pearls sign: small air bubbles within fluid-distended bowel on supine view. Exam pivot: Supine radiographs may underestimate obstruction—look for subtle intraluminal air bubbles.

entries.question: What is the small bowel feces sign and where is it located relative to the obstruction?
entries.answer: Gas bubbles mixed with particulate matter in dilated loops. Located just proximal to the site of obstruction. Exam pivot: SB feces sign helps localize the transition zone.

entries.question: What CT pattern suggests internal hernia as a cause of SBO?
entries.answer: Cluster of dilated small bowel segments. Crowding, twisting, displacement of mesenteric vessels. Dilated segment entering hernia; collapsed segment leaving hernia. Exam pivot: Mesenteric vessel crowding + clustered loops strongly suggests internal hernia rather than adhesive SBO.

entries.question: What is the pathophysiologic cascade from obstruction to bowel necrosis in SBO?
entries.answer: Obstruction → proximal dilation → accumulation of GI secretions and swallowed air. Luminal distention occludes small vessels in bowel wall. Mesenteric vessel twisting/occlusion (closed loop) → ischemia. Ischemia → infarction → gangrene → perforation → peritonitis → sepsis. Exam pivot: Closed-loop obstruction carries highest ischemia risk due to mesenteric vessel compromise.

entries.question: What defines a closed-loop SBO?
entries.answer: Obstruction at two points involving the mesentery. Affected SB segments markedly distended (>4 cm) by fluid with little gas. Relatively little proximal dilatation. Exam pivot: Closed loop configuration carries high strangulation risk.

entries.question: Define ileus.
entries.answer: Source definition: Proportional gaseous dilatation of large and small bowel (SB) due to lack of intestinal peristalsis, not mechanical obstruction. Boundary: Functional motility failure with no obstructing lesion/transition point (NOT a mechanical obstruction). Synonyms: Paralytic ileus; functional ileus.

entries.question: What diagnostic pitfall is demonstrated here, and what imaging safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking ileus with ascites (or recent bowel surgery) for small bowel obstruction (SBO) on plain films. Why it happens: Gas may collect only in nondependent bowel, while dependent small bowel and colon are fluid-filled and less dilated, creating an apparent segmental gas pattern. Safety check: Look for a true transition point or obstructing lesion. If unclear, obtain CT to confirm generalized dilation of small and large bowel without a transition zone. Key discriminator: Mechanical obstruction shows a discrete transition point with upstream dilation; ileus shows proportional dilation without a focal obstructing site.

entries.answer: • Plain radiograph: SB > 3 cm • CT: SB > 2.5 cm Exam pivot: Use modality-appropriate thresholds; ileus is suggested when SB and colon are proportionally dilated without a transition point.

entries.question: For postoperative ileus, what is the typical natural history time course (as stated in source)?
entries.answer: Usually resolves spontaneously in 3–7 days. Exam pivot: Persistent or worsening distention beyond the expected window should prompt evaluation for mechanical obstruction.

entries.question: Define Crohn disease.
entries.answer: 1) Source definition: Disease of unknown etiology characterized by transmural inflammation of GI tract. 2) Refined definition based on medical consensus: A chronic relapsing inflammatory bowel disease with segmental (skip) transmural inflammation that can involve any part of the GI tract. 3) Boundary condition (IS vs IS NOT): IS transmural, segmental inflammatory bowel disease; IS NOT a purely mucosal, continuously distributed colitis pattern (classically ulcerative colitis). 4) Synonyms: Terminal ileitis; regional enteritis; ileocolitis

entries.question: Why does Crohn disease commonly produce fistulas, sinus tracts, and abscesses?
entries.answer: Crohn disease causes transmural inflammation extending through the full thickness of the bowel wall. Persistent deep ulceration penetrates the serosa and adjacent structures, producing sinus tracts, enteric fistulas, and abscesses. This penetrating behavior reflects transmural disease and distinguishes Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis, which is primarily mucosal.

entries.question: What causes the engorged vasa recta (comb sign) seen in active Crohn disease?
entries.answer: Active Crohn inflammation produces hyperemia of the mesenteric circulation supplying the affected bowel segment. Inflammatory mediators increase mesenteric blood flow and dilate the vasa recta, producing parallel vascular structures extending toward the bowel wall, known as the CT comb sign.

entries.question: What causes mesenteric fibrofatty proliferation (creeping fat) in Crohn disease?
entries.answer: Chronic Crohn inflammation stimulates mesenteric adipocyte hypertrophy and inflammatory fat proliferation adjacent to the diseased bowel. This results in fat wrapping around the inflamed bowel and mesenteric thickening, referred to as creeping fat, reflecting chronic transmural inflammation.

entries.question: What causes the string sign in Crohn disease?
entries.answer: Repeated cycles of inflammation and healing lead to submucosal fibrosis and muscular hypertrophy, producing progressive luminal narrowing. When severe, contrast passes through a thin stream on fluoroscopic studies, producing the string sign associated with chronic stricturing Crohn disease.

entries.question: Why can diffusion restriction be seen in active Crohn disease on MRI?
entries.answer: Active inflammation leads to dense cellular infiltration and edema that reduce extracellular space, restricting Brownian motion of water molecules. This produces high signal on diffusion-weighted imaging with low ADC values, although this finding is not specific and must be interpreted with other imaging features.

entries.question: What is the typical age distribution of Crohn disease?
entries.answer: Crohn disease has a bimodal age distribution: Peak 1 at 15–35 years (most common) and Peak 2 at 50–70 years. Most patients are diagnosed in young adulthood.

entries.question: What is the most common anatomic location of Crohn disease?
entries.answer: The terminal ileum and ileocecal region are the most commonly involved sites. Ileocolic disease is the most common distribution pattern.

entries.question: What is the relationship between smoking and Crohn disease?
entries.answer: Smoking increases both the risk and severity of Crohn disease and is associated with increased disease activity and postoperative recurrence.

entries.question: What malignancies are associated with Crohn disease?
entries.answer: Crohn disease increases risk of small bowel adenocarcinoma, colorectal carcinoma in long-standing colonic disease, and lymphoma particularly in patients receiving immunomodulator therapy.

entries.question: What is the comb sign in Crohn disease?
entries.answer: The comb sign refers to engorged mesenteric vasa recta supplying inflamed bowel segments, appearing as parallel vascular structures projecting toward the bowel on contrast-enhanced CT or MR enterography and indicating active inflammation.

entries.question: What are skip lesions in Crohn disease?
entries.answer: Skip lesions are segments of inflamed bowel separated by normal bowel, producing a discontinuous distribution characteristic of Crohn disease and contrasting with the continuous colonic involvement of ulcerative colitis.

entries.question: What is the string sign in Crohn disease?
entries.answer: The string sign represents severe luminal narrowing from chronic stricturing inflammation, where contrast passes through a thin linear channel of bowel on fluoroscopic studies.

entries.question: What is creeping fat in Crohn disease?
entries.answer: Creeping fat refers to mesenteric fibrofatty proliferation that wraps around inflamed bowel loops and reflects chronic Crohn inflammation.

entries.question: On imaging, what key feature helps distinguish Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis?
entries.answer: Crohn disease shows segmental involvement with skip lesions and often involves the terminal ileum, whereas ulcerative colitis demonstrates continuous colonic disease beginning in the rectum and extending proximally without skip areas.

entries.question: What imaging finding favors Crohn disease over infectious ileitis?
entries.answer: Crohn disease is favored when there are skip lesions, mesenteric fibrofatty proliferation (creeping fat), and engorged vasa recta (comb sign). Infectious ileitis usually produces short-segment inflammation without chronic mesenteric changes.

entries.question: Why should diffusion restriction on MR enterography not be used alone to diagnose Crohn disease activity?
entries.answer: Diffusion restriction reflects inflammation and cellularity but is not specific. It can occur in infection, ischemia, or neoplasm, so Crohn activity must be assessed with additional findings such as bowel wall enhancement and distribution.

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Perianal fistula Caption-derived KEYWORD FINDINGS: - Fistula caudally from anal sphincter - Perineum to scrotum course - Hardly visible on axial T2-weighted image - Easier to see on axial fat-saturated T2-weighted image - Brightness of fluid-filled fistula stands out against suppressed fat Tight reasoning: Perianal fistulous tract arising from the anal sphincter and coursing through the perineum is directly described, and improved conspicuity on fat-saturated T2 supports a fluid-containing tract against suppressed fat. Differential (Model-inferred; not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx): Perianal abscess Hidradenitis suppurativa with sinus tracts Anal fissure with inflammatory change

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Horseshoe perianal abscess Caption-derived KEYWORD FINDINGS: - Large horseshoe-shaped structure - Extends on both sides of anal midline - Extends superiorly and inferiorly relative to levator ani muscle - Infralevatoric location described - Partial rim enhancement with fluid center on post-contrast fat-saturated T1-weighted image - Fat-suppressed T2 makes size/location more conspicuous Tight reasoning: A horseshoe-shaped perianal collection crossing the midline with a fluid center and rim enhancement is described, consistent with a horseshoe abscess; the captions explicitly localize extension relative to the levator ani and highlight fat-suppressed sequences improving conspicuity. Differential (Model-inferred; not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx): Perianal phlegmon / inflammatory mass Complex fistulizing disease without abscess Postoperative or traumatic perineal collection

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Perianal abscess Caption-derived KEYWORD FINDINGS: - Hyperintense collection on axial T2-weighted image - Hyperintense structure on axial fat-saturated T2-weighted image - Rim enhancement with non-enhancing core on post-contrast fat-saturated T1-weighted image - Fluid center with rim of inflammatory tissue described Tight reasoning: A fluid-containing collection with peripheral rim enhancement and a nonenhancing core on post-contrast imaging is classic for abscess; the captions explicitly state fluid center with inflammatory rim. Differential (Model-inferred; not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx): Granulation tissue / inflammatory mass without abscess Postoperative collection / seroma Necrotic tumor (rare)

entries.question: What are the three classic Crohn disease phenotypes?
entries.answer: Inflammatory, stricturing, and penetrating. Exam pivot: phenotype predicts imaging complications (obstruction vs fistula/abscess) and guides interpretation.

entries.question: What is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating perianal Crohn disease?
entries.answer: MRI pelvis. Exam pivot: best for delineating fistula tracts, abscesses, and relationship to sphincter/levator ani.

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Acute mesenteric ischemia (occlusive arterial ischemia) Caption-derived keyword findings: - luminal narrowing - loss of normal SB fold pattern in the ileum - dilation of the more proximal segments - cutoff of some of the ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) - lack of blood flow to the ileum Tight reasoning: Small-bowel follow-through shows ileal narrowing with loss of fold pattern plus proximal dilation, and angiography shows branch cutoff with absent ileal perfusion—together supporting acute occlusive arterial ischemia affecting the ileum. Differential: Small intestine vasculitis Crohn disease Shock bowel

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Mesenteric venous thrombosis with small-bowel ischemia Caption-derived keyword findings: - thrombus within the lumen of the superior mesenteric and portal veins - SB markedly dilated and fluid filled - wall is thickened - ascites is present - engorged mesenteric veins - mesenteric edema Tight reasoning: Direct visualization of venous thrombus (SMV/portal) plus marked fluid-filled dilation, wall thickening, ascites, engorged mesenteric veins, and mesenteric edema supports venous-side occlusion with ischemic injury. Differential: Intestinal (angioneurotic) angioedema Small intestine vasculitis Shock bowel

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Advanced small-bowel ischemia with infarction Caption-derived keyword findings: - dilated SB - pneumatosis - portal venous gas was also present on other sections (not shown) Tight reasoning: Dilated small bowel with pneumatosis, plus associated portal venous gas, is a classic advanced ischemia pattern and matches infarcted bowel confirmed at surgery in this case. Differential: Shock bowel Small intestine vasculitis Intestinal (angioneurotic) angioedema

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Small-bowel ischemia (with congenital malrotation context) Caption-derived keyword findings: - mural thickening of the jejunum - lies on the right side of the abdomen due to congenital malrotation - aberrant position of the superior mesenteric vessels - focal ascites Tight reasoning: Jejunal mural thickening with focal ascites in the setting of congenital malrotation and aberrant SMA/SMV position supports ischemic small bowel in an anatomic predisposition setting, consistent with ischemic bowel found at surgery. Differential: Crohn disease Small intestine vasculitis Shock bowel

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Closed-loop obstruction with resulting ischemia Caption-derived keyword findings: - marked dilation of a long segment of midsmall intestine - edema of the mesentery near dilated loops - normal caliber of the SB is upstream and downstream from this segment - classic findings of closed-loop obstruction with resulting ischemia Tight reasoning: A long, isolated dilated mid–small-bowel segment with adjacent mesenteric edema and normal caliber upstream/downstream is the key localization pattern for a closed-loop, which is high-risk for ischemia. Differential: Simple small-bowel obstruction Shock bowel Small intestine vasculitis

entries.question: Define mesenteric ischemia.
entries.answer: Source definition: Mesenteric arterial or venous narrowing or occlusion, leading to inadequate supply of nutrients and oxygen to small bowel (SB). Refined definition based on medical consensus: Insufficient mesenteric perfusion causing bowel injury, potentially reversible or progressing to infarction. Boundary: It is a bowel perfusion disorder, not merely nonspecific bowel wall thickening. Synonyms: acute mesenteric ischemia (article synonym context).

entries.question: Define nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMI).
entries.answer: Source definition: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features. Refined definition based on medical consensus: Intestinal ischemia caused by severe reduction in mesenteric perfusion without an identifiable arterial or venous occlusion. Boundary: It is low-flow ischemia with patent proximal vessels, not thromboembolic occlusion. Synonyms: NOMI.

entries.question: Mesenteric ischemia is what percentage of acute abdomen cases?
entries.answer: Accounts for 1% of acute abdomen cases. Exam pivot: uncommon overall, so recognition depends on pattern + high suspicion rather than prevalence.

entries.question: What type of occlusive mesenteric ischemia is more common? What is the incidence?
entries.answer: Arterial > venous occlusive ischemia (9:1). Also, 60-70% of acute ischemia is due to arterial occlusion and 5-10% is due to venous occlusion. Exam pivot: if imaging shows vascular occlusion in acute disease, arterial causes are more likely than venous causes.

entries.question: What percentage of acute ischemia is non-occlusive? What is its mortality?
entries.answer: 25% of acute ischemia is nonocclusive (NOMI); mortality: 70%. Exam pivot: low-flow ischemia is common enough and deadly enough that distal vascular pruning in shock/heart failure should not be dismissed.

entries.question: Chronic mesenteric ischemia diagnostic requirement: what vascular pattern is required?
entries.answer: Diagnosis requires occlusion of ≥ 2 major mesenteric arteries and narrowing of the 3rd artery.

entries.question: What is the earliest CT sign of acute mesenteric ischemia?
entries.answer: Lack of bowel mucosal enhancement due to compromised arterial flow.

entries.question: What CT finding is most specific for bowel infarction in this topic framework?
entries.answer: Pneumatosis intestinalis with mesenteric or portal venous gas in the appropriate clinical setting.

entries.question: What imaging features distinguish arterial from venous mesenteric ischemia?
entries.answer: Arterial ischemia: SMA occlusion or branch cutoff; lack of bowel mucosal enhancement is more emphasized. Venous ischemia: SMV thrombus, more impressive bowel wall thickening, mesenteric infiltration, ascites, and engorged mesenteric veins. Exam pivot: venous ischemia tends to produce more dramatic wall/mesenteric edema findings.

entries.question: How do you distinguish NOMI from arterial occlusive mesenteric ischemia?
entries.answer: Occlusive ischemia shows clot/stenosis of the SMA or its branches. NOMI shows patent proximal vessels with poor visualization and pruning of distal vasculature; angiography shows slow flow in the SMA. Exam pivot: thrombus/cutoff favors occlusion; distal pruning with low-flow physiology favors NOMI.

entries.question: What imaging feature helps distinguish shock bowel from mesenteric ischemia?
entries.answer: Shock bowel shows intense mucosal enhancement with submucosal and mesenteric edema, usually in hypotension/trauma, and may reverse with resuscitation. Exam pivot: hyperenhancing bowel favors shock bowel; poor enhancement/occlusion pattern favors ischemia.

entries.question: Does pneumatosis intestinalis always indicate bowel infarction?
entries.answer: No. Within this topic, late-phase ischemia can lead to diffuse or localized pneumatosis intestinalis, and the combination with mesenteric or portal venous gas is especially worrisome. Exam pivot: interpret pneumatosis in full clinical/imaging context rather than in isolation.

entries.question: Diagnostic performance of CT/CTA for acute mesenteric ischemia: what are the pooled sensitivity and specificity?
entries.answer: External literature source (not stated in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx/Radiopaedia). Pooled CT sensitivity: 94% (95% CI 90%-97%). Pooled CT specificity: 95% (95% CI 93%-97%). Exam pivot: a negative high-quality contrast-enhanced CT/CTA substantially lowers the probability of AMI, but clinical suspicion still matters.

entries.question: Lab test pivot for suspected acute mesenteric ischemia: can laboratory markers conclusively rule in or rule out the diagnosis?
entries.answer: No. No laboratory parameter is sufficiently accurate to conclusively identify the presence or absence of ischemic or necrotic bowel; elevated lactate, leukocytosis, and D-dimer may assist but do not replace CTA.

entries.question: How does mesenteric venous thrombosis lead to bowel ischemia?
entries.answer: Venous outflow obstruction causes venous congestion, bowel wall edema, mesenteric edema, and impaired capillary perfusion, which eventually leads to ischemia. Imaging pivot: venous ischemia often shows more impressive wall thickening, mesenteric infiltration, and ascites than arterial occlusion.

entries.question: What is the mechanism of nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMI)?
entries.answer: Low-flow states and mesenteric vasoconstriction reduce intestinal perfusion despite patent proximal vessels. Imaging pivot: distal vascular pruning/poor distal visualization with bowel wall thickening favors NOMI over thromboembolic occlusion.

entries.question: Why does closed-loop obstruction lead to bowel ischemia?
entries.answer: Two-point obstruction traps a bowel segment, causing rising intraluminal pressure that first blocks venous drainage and eventually compromises arterial inflow. Imaging pivot: an isolated dilated segment with nearby mesenteric edema and normal-caliber bowel upstream/downstream suggests the mechanism.

entries.clinicalContext: Older adult with lower abdominal pain, fever, and tenderness.

entries.answer: Perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with free intraperitoneal air and diverticular abscesses Keyword findings: extensive free intraperitoneal gas; fluid that has loculated into abscesses; extensive sigmoid diverticulosis; free air; abscesses Reasoning: The case shows a complicated perforating colonic process with free intraperitoneal gas and loculated abscesses, and the caption directly identifies extensive sigmoid diverticulosis as the source. This is the classic appearance of complicated perforated diverticulitis rather than uncomplicated inflammatory thickening alone. Differential (Model-inferred; not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx): Perforated colon carcinoma Perforated ischemic colitis Postoperative bowel perforation

entries.clinicalContext: Older adult with left lower quadrant pain and fever.1
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis Keyword findings: mural thickening; a diverticulum; fluid collecting at the base of the sigmoid mesentery; engorged pericolonic vessels; hyperemia of the inflamed pericolonic fat; characteristic feature of acute diverticulitis Reasoning: This is the classic CT constellation of uncomplicated diverticulitis: focal diverticulum, adjacent mural thickening, inflammatory change at the sigmoid mesenteric base, and engorged hyperemic pericolonic vessels without a frank large abscess or free intraperitoneal contamination. Differential: Colon carcinoma Radiation colitis Ischemic colitis Pseudomembranous colitis

entries.clinicalContext: Young adult with left lower quadrant pain and fever.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Acute descending colonic diverticulitis Keyword findings: extensive inflammation surrounding the descending colon; long segmental thickening of the wall of the descending colon; pericolonic inflammation; numerous diverticula Reasoning: Long-segment descending colonic wall thickening plus numerous diverticula and marked adjacent inflammatory change is the prototypical pattern of diverticulitis. The long-segment inflammatory process favors diverticulitis over a short annular malignant lesion. Differential: Colon carcinoma Ischemic colitis Radiation colitis

entries.clinicalContext: Older adult with abdominal pain and pneumaturia.22
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Colovesical fistula secondary to diverticulitis Keyword findings: extensive sigmoid diverticulosis; inflammation of the surrounding tissues; collection of gas and fluid bridging the inflamed colon and the thick-walled bladder; bladder contains gas; colovesical fistula Reasoning: Pneumaturia plus a gas/fluid-containing bridge between inflamed sigmoid colon and gas-containing thick-walled bladder is classic for a colovesical fistula from complicated diverticulitis. Differential (Model-inferred; not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx): Colovesical fistula from colon carcinoma Crohn disease with enterovesical fistula Radiation fistula

entries.clinicalContext: Adult woman with foul-smelling vaginal discharge after prior pelvic surgery.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Colovaginal fistula secondary to diverticulitis Keyword findings: sigmoid colonic wall thickening; rectally administered contrast material; some of which has entered the vagina along with gas; contrast material distending the lumen of the vagina; colovaginal fistula; contrast medium within the vagina Reasoning: Rectal contrast traversing from diseased sigmoid colon into and distending the vagina directly demonstrates a colovaginal fistula. The associated sigmoid inflammatory changes and operative correlation support diverticulitis as the cause. Differential (Model-inferred; not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx): Postoperative fistula Colon carcinoma with fistula Crohn disease with fistula

entries.clinicalContext: Middle-aged adult with recent hepatic mass on CT.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Septic thrombophlebitis (pylephlebitis) from diverticulitis with secondary pyogenic hepatic abscess Keyword findings: segmental transient hepatic attenuation difference (THAD); encapsulated, multiseptate lesion surrounded by enhancing septa and peripheral walls; characteristic of a pyogenic abscess; occlusion of the posterior branch of the right portal vein; filling defect within the lumen of the inferior mesenteric vein; diverticula; mild pericolonic infiltration; source of the septic phlebitis and hepatic abscess Reasoning: The hepatic lesion is explicitly described as a pyogenic abscess, while the associated portal venous branch occlusion and IMV filling defect establish septic thrombophlebitis. The source is low-grade but persistent diverticulitis in the colon. Differential (Model-inferred; not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx): Pyogenic abscess from another intraabdominal source Metastatic liver lesion with bland venous thrombosis Infected portal venous thrombosis from appendicitis

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with acute lower abdominal pain.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis Keyword findings: irregular luminal narrowing and wall thickening; numerous gas-filled diverticula; relatively mild infiltration of the pericolonic fat Reasoning: Numerous sigmoid diverticula with adjacent wall thickening and mild pericolonic inflammatory change is a classic uncomplicated diverticulitis pattern. The presence of diverticula and inflammatory change favors diverticulitis over an isolated neoplastic stricture. Differential: Colon carcinoma Ischemic colitis Radiation colitis

entries.clinicalContext: Adult with acute right lower quadrant pain and fever.
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Acute right-sided diverticulitis Keyword findings: inflamed fat and thickened fascial planes adjacent to the cecum and ascending colon; several diverticula; consistent with acute diverticulitis Reasoning: The combination of right-sided pericolonic inflammatory change adjacent to the cecum/ascending colon plus visible diverticula supports right-sided diverticulitis, an important mimic of appendicitis clinically. Differential (Model-inferred; not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx): Appendicitis Cecal carcinoma Epiploic appendagitis

entries.clinicalContext: Older adult with pain and fever.45

entries.answer: Diverticular abscess complicating sigmoid diverticulitis Keyword findings: rim-enhancing abscess in the left hemipelvis; surrounding an inflamed diverticulum of the sigmoid colon; pain and fever due to diverticulitis Reasoning: A rim-enhancing pelvic abscess centered on an inflamed sigmoid diverticulum is a classic CT appearance of complicated diverticulitis with abscess formation. Differential (Model-inferred; not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx): Tubo-ovarian abscess Perforated colon carcinoma with abscess Contained perforation from ischemic colitis

entries.question: How does diverticulitis lead to portal venous thrombophlebitis and hepatic abscess formation?
entries.answer: Infected pericolonic veins draining an inflamed diverticular segment become contaminated with enteric bacteria → septic thrombophlebitis develops in mesenteric veins (e.g., inferior mesenteric vein). The infected thrombus propagates through the portal venous system → septic emboli reach the liver → bacteria seed hepatic parenchyma, producing pyogenic liver abscesses visible on CT.

entries.question: Epidemiology pivot for diverticular disease of the colon: what is the prevalence of diverticulosis in patients older than 50 years in the United States?
entries.answer: Fact: > 50% of patients > 50 years of age have diverticulosis in the United States. Exam pivot: Because diverticulosis is extremely common in older adults, CT findings of diverticula with focal inflammatory change in this age group strongly support diverticulitis as the cause of acute left lower quadrant pain.

entries.question: Imaging discriminator pivot: what CT features favor diverticulitis over colon carcinoma?
entries.answer: Diverticulitis typically shows: • Long-segment colonic involvement (> ~10 cm) • Prominent pericolonic inflammatory change and fat stranding • Visible diverticula in the affected segment • Absence of lymphadenopathy or distant metastases Exam pivot: Short-segment asymmetric thickening with nodal disease favors colon carcinoma, while long inflammatory segments with diverticula favor diverticulitis.

entries.question: CT prognostic pivot for diverticulitis: what imaging findings predict unfavorable outcome with nonoperative treatment?
entries.answer: Abscess or pockets of extraintestinal gas ≥ 5 mm. Exam pivot: These CT findings indicate complicated diverticulitis and predict a higher likelihood of failure of conservative therapy.

entries.question: Outcome pivot for diverticulitis: which form carries the highest mortality?
entries.answer: External literature source (not stated in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx/Radiopaedia). Freely perforated diverticulitis with generalized peritonitis (Hinchey III–IV) carries the highest mortality; mortality is driven primarily by perforation/peritonitis rather than uncomplicated disease. Exam pivot: Do not memorize a single mortality for all diverticulitis—advanced perforated disease is the mortality-driving phenotype.

entries.question: What is the most common fistula complication of diverticulitis?
entries.answer: Colovesical fistula. Exam pivot: In an older patient with diverticulitis, pneumaturia or gas within the bladder should immediately raise concern for a colovesical fistula.

entries.question: Which CT entity commonly mimics diverticulitis but arises from inflammation of an epiploic appendage?
entries.answer: Epiploic appendagitis. Exam pivot: Look for a small oval fat-attenuation lesion with a hyperattenuating rim and only minimal adjacent bowel wall thickening; diverticulitis instead centers on an inflamed diverticulum and colonic wall inflammation.
