entries.question: Why does choledocholithiasis produce biliary ductal dilatation and potentially cholangitis or pancreatitis?
entries.answer: A stone lodged within the extrahepatic biliary duct mechanically obstructs antegrade bile flow. As bile drainage is impeded, pressure rises proximal to the obstruction and the common bile duct and/or intrahepatic ducts dilate; the degree of dilatation varies with stone size and the degree and duration of obstruction. Ongoing stasis also promotes superimposed infection, which explains why obstructed stone disease may present as ascending cholangitis. When the obstructing stone is periampullary/distal, it can also affect the pancreatic outflow region and present with acute pancreatitis. The imaging pivot is that a shadowing intraductal stone plus upstream ductal dilatation supports obstructive choledocholithiasis rather than a nonobstructing mimic.

entries.question: Which is more common: primary choledocholithiasis or secondary choledocholithiasis?
entries.answer: Secondary choledocholithiasis is more common; it reflects migration of gallstones from the gallbladder into the bile ducts, whereas primary choledocholithiasis forms de novo within the ducts. Exam pivot: If you see CBD stones, gallbladder stone disease/migration should be your default etiologic assumption unless the case specifically suggests primary intraductal stone formation.

entries.question: What proportion of patients with gallstones have choledocholithiasis at the time of cholecystectomy?
entries.answer: 5-20% of patients with gallstones will have choledocholithiasis at the time of cholecystectomy. Exam pivot: Gallstones meaningfully raise the pretest probability of concomitant CBD stones, so biliary obstruction or jaundice in a gallstone patient should prompt active evaluation of the ductal system.

entries.question: MRI appearance pivot for choledocholithiasis: what is the key MRCP signal pattern?
entries.answer: - Bile: T2-hyperintense signal - Ductal stones: T2-hypointense foci - Calculi appear as low-intensity filling defects within increased-signal bile ducts - Exam pivot: On MRCP, a dark intraductal filling defect within bright bile strongly supports choledocholithiasis rather than simple ductal dilatation alone.

entries.question: What common bile duct caliber is generally considered normal, equivocal, and dilated on ultrasound in the article?
entries.answer: - CBD: 4-6 mm = normal - CBD: 6-7 mm = equivocal - CBD: > 8 mm = dilatation - Exam pivot: In suspected choledocholithiasis, upstream ductal enlargement strengthens the case for obstructive stone disease.

entries.question: What is Core's rule of thumb for normal common bile duct diameter by age?
entries.answer: - CBD should be 6 mm or less before age 60 - It may still be normal if about 1 mm larger per decade after age 60 - Example: an 8 mm duct in an 80-year-old patient may be normal - Exam pivot: Mild CBD enlargement is not automatically pathologic in older adults, so duct size must be interpreted in age context.

entries.question: What are the reported sensitivity ranges of transabdominal US, endoscopic US, CT, MRCP, and ERCP for choledocholithiasis?
entries.answer: - Transabdominal US: 20-78% - Endoscopic US: 94-98% - CT: 67-88% - MRCP: 81-100% - ERCP: 90-95% - Exam pivot: Negative transabdominal US does not exclude choledocholithiasis, especially for distal CBD stones; MRCP/EUS are much more sensitive, while ERCP is both highly sensitive and potentially therapeutic.

entries.question: What are the best imaging tools for choledocholithiasis according to the article?
entries.answer: - Best imaging tools: US and MRCP - ERCP is the gold standard and is potentially therapeutic - Exam pivot: Start with ultrasound in typical practice, but escalate to MRCP or ERCP when clinical suspicion persists or therapeutic intervention is needed.

entries.question: What practical sonographic maneuvers improve detection of common bile duct stones when the distal CBD is obscured?
entries.answer: - Examine in different positions: supine, left lateral oblique, sitting upright - Use multiple scanning sites/windows - Apply firm probe pressure to collapse superficial bowel and its contents - Assess the pancreatic head region carefully - If gas obscures the CBD, have the patient drink 6-12 oz of water, keep them in right decubitus for 2-3 minutes, then rescan in semierect position - Exam pivot: Distal/periampullary stones are commonly missed because of bowel gas, so a technically negative scan may need active optimization rather than premature exclusion.

entries.question: What color Doppler finding can support choledocholithiasis on ultrasound?
entries.answer: - The echogenic focus is avascular and may show twinkling artifact - Color Doppler also helps distinguish biliary ducts from adjacent intrahepatic/parahilar vessels - Exam pivot: Doppler can both support a stone and reduce the common anatomic pitfall of mistaking vessels for the ductal target.

entries.question: On this ultrasound appearance, what is the key pitfall, and what check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Mistaking dilated biliary ducts for adjacent vascular structures in the porta hepatis or liver parenchyma. Safety check: Use color Doppler or power Doppler to test for flow. Key discriminator: Dilated ducts are fluid-filled nonvascular channels and therefore do not show color flow, whereas hepatic arterial, portal venous, cavernomatous, or collateral vessels demonstrate flow. Why the error occurs: Both ducts and vessels can appear as tubular anechoic structures accompanying portal triads on grayscale ultrasound, creating a strong visual mimic.

entries.question: What sonographic threshold defines extrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation?
entries.answer: Extrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation is defined as common hepatic/common bile duct > 6-7 mm or > 40% of the diameter of the adjacent portal vein. Exam pivot: These are the article’s explicit size criteria for abnormal extrahepatic duct dilatation and help separate a truly enlarged duct from a normal-caliber extrahepatic bile duct.

entries.question: On grayscale ultrasound, what is the best diagnostic clue for biliary ductal dilatation?
entries.answer: Tubular, anechoic, fluid-filled structures accompanying portal veins in the extrahepatic and intrahepatic segments. Exam pivot: The key recognition pattern is a periportal branching or tubular fluid-filled structure that follows the biliary tree.

The article specifically identifies twinkling as a useful sign for otherwise occult stones, and the caption localizes the stones to dilated calyces within the kidney. entries.question: Define urinary tract stone (urolithiasis).
entries.answer: Source definition: Macroscopic concretions of crystals in the urinary system, sometimes mixed with proteins. Boundary condition: This is a formed urinary calculus within the collecting system/urinary tract, not diffuse parenchymal calcification such as nephrocalcinosis and not vascular calcification. Synonyms: urinary tract stone; urinary calculous disease; nephrolithiasis; ureterolithiasis; vesicolithiasis

entries.question: What pitfall can this appearance cause, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Mistaking echogenic renal sinus fat for a renal stone on ultrasound. Safety check: Confirm sharp posterior acoustic shadowing; use color Doppler twinkling as an additional aid when needed. Key discriminator: A true stone is an echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing, whereas sinus fat may have similar echogenicity but lacks the same confirming stone features. Why the error occurs: Small stones can blend with central renal sinus fat on grayscale, so echogenicity alone can falsely suggest or falsely exclude a stone.

entries.question: On CT in this topic, what common mimic-related pitfall occurs, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Mistaking a phlebolith for a distal ureteral stone. Safety check: Look for the comet-tail sign of an adjacent vein, assess for central lucency versus central density, and use the soft-tissue rim sign to support a true ureteral stone when present. Key discriminator: A stone is centrally dense and may have a soft-tissue rim sign from ureteral wall edema; a phlebolith is often centrally lucent and may show a comet-tail sign with eccentric tapering soft tissue from the vein. Why the error occurs: Pelvic calcifications can lie close to the ureteral course and mimic a distal ureteral calculus on noncontrast CT.

entries.question: What important interpretation pitfall should be remembered when the expected direct culprit is not seen, and what safety check helps?
entries.answer: Incorrectly excluding stone disease because no calculus is directly seen on CT. Safety check: If secondary signs of obstruction are present, consider a recently passed stone; in the correct clinical setting also consider a radiolucent drug stone such as a protease inhibitor stone in an HIV-positive patient. Key discriminator: The article specifically states that secondary signs without a visible stone should prompt consideration of recent passage, while certain radiolucent calculi may also explain the mismatch. Why the error occurs: Readers may overvalue direct stone visualization and under-recognize that obstruction can persist briefly after passage or that rare radiolucent stones may not be conspicuous on CT.

entries.question: What proportion of men and women develop urinary tract stones?
entries.answer: Up to 14% of men and 6% of women develop stones. Exam pivot: Stone disease is common and more prevalent in men, which raises the baseline diagnostic prior in the appropriate flank-pain setting.

entries.question: What is the most common cause of urinary tract stone formation?
entries.answer: Dehydration / low urine volume is the most common cause. Exam pivot: When thinking etiologically, low urine volume is the default board answer unless a more specific metabolic, infectious, drug-related, or anatomic cause is clearly established.

entries.question: What proportion of urinary tract stone disease has a metabolic etiology?
entries.answer: A metabolic etiology is found in > 95% of cases. Exam pivot: Stone disease should not be framed as random; metabolic contributors are overwhelmingly common and should remain high on the causal differential.

entries.question: What are the approximate proportions of the major urinary stone types?
entries.answer: Calcium oxalate/calcium phosphate stones: 70-80% Struvite: 5-15% Uric acid: 5-10% Cystine: 1-2.5% Other: Exam pivot: Calcium-based stones are by far the dominant default category; uncommon stone types matter mainly when the imaging pattern, attenuation, or clinical setting points away from the calcium majority.

entries.question: In an adult with acute flank pain, what is the preferred imaging test to confirm urinary tract stone, and what is its diagnostic performance?
entries.answer: NECT is the preferred imaging modality in adults with acute flank pain. Sensitivity: 95-98% Specificity: 96-100% Exam pivot: Noncontrast CT is the default confirmatory test because it is the highest-performance study for acute urolithiasis.

entries.question: What is the ultrasound performance for renal stones larger than 5 mm?
entries.answer: Sensitivity: 96% Specificity: nearly 100% Exam pivot: Ultrasound performs very well for larger renal stones and is especially useful for follow-up when radiation avoidance matters.

entries.question: What is the role of color Doppler twinkling artifact in urinary stone detection?
entries.answer: Twinkling artifact is more sensitive than acoustic shadowing for identifying otherwise occult stones, but it has a higher false-positive rate, up to 51%. Exam pivot: Twinkling is a helpful adjunct sign, not a standalone proof of stone.

entries.question: Which urinary stones are efficiently treated with oral chemolysis, and what attenuation cutoff supports that?
entries.answer: Urate stones are the only stones efficiently treated with oral chemolysis (alkalinization). Supporting attenuation clue: Exam pivot: A low-HU stone should immediately raise uric acid stone and possible dissolution therapy.

entries.question: What are the spontaneous passage rates for ureteral stones by size?
entries.answer: ≤ 5 mm: ~ 68% pass spontaneously > 5 mm and ≤ 10 mm: 47% pass spontaneously > 8 mm: rarely passes without intervention 95% of stones up to 4 mm pass within 40 days Exam pivot: Small stones usually pass; larger stones increasingly shift the balance toward intervention.

entries.question: How should follow-up imaging be chosen after CT based on stone visibility on the CT scout image?
entries.answer: If visible on CT scout: use KUB for follow-up, with CT scout as baseline If not visible and stone If not visible and stone 5-9 mm: obtaining a baseline KUB at the time of CT is reasonable If not visible and stone > 10 mm: likely uric acid or xanthine; follow-up with CT if conservative management is chosen Exam pivot: Scout visibility helps decide whether KUB follow-up is worthwhile.

entries.question: When is low-dose or ultra-low-dose CT appropriate for urinary stone imaging?
entries.answer: Low-dose and ultra-low-dose CT have stone detection accuracy comparable to standard-dose CT in patients with BMI Exam pivot: In appropriately sized patients, low-dose CT is a high-yield surveillance and posttreatment follow-up option.

entries.question: Which urinary stones are typically radiolucent on radiography?
entries.answer: Urate, xanthine, pure matrix, and drug stones are radiolucent. Exam pivot: A nonopaque stone burden on KUB raises noncalcium composition and limits radiographic follow-up.

entries.question: Which urinary stones may be missed on CT even though virtually all stones are usually visible?
entries.answer: Pure matrix stones and protease inhibitor stones such as indinavir may be missed on CT. Exam pivot: A negative CT does not absolutely exclude stone disease in the right clinical setting, especially with protease inhibitor exposure.

entries.question: How should ureteral jets be interpreted on Doppler ultrasound in obstruction? Difference in presence between high grade and low grade
entries.answer: Ureteral jets are usually absent in high-grade obstruction. In low-grade obstruction, only about one-third have an absent ureteral jet. The affected side may instead show an asymmetric decrease or a continuous low-amplitude jet. Exam pivot: A preserved jet does not exclude low-grade obstruction.

entries.question: What bladder/UVJ protocol pearl should always be remembered on urinary stone ultrasound?
entries.answer: Always include the bladder with special attention to the UVJ. Rolling the patient can show mobility of a bladder calculus. Exam pivot: Distal ureteral and bladder stones are easy to miss if the bladder/UVJ is omitted.

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Hepatic cirrhosis with portal hypertension Keyword findings: diffusely heterogeneous echotexture of liver; mildly dilated portal vein Reasoning: Diffuse hepatic heterogeneity together with portal venous dilatation matches chronic cirrhotic change with portal-hypertension sequelae rather than a focal hepatic process. Differential: Budd-Chiari syndrome Infiltrative hepatocellular carcinoma Treated metastatic disease

entries.clinicalContext: 57-year-old man with progressive abdominal swelling and early satiety P4D8J1W6T9KY

entries.answer: Decompensated hepatic cirrhosis Keyword findings: markedly shrunken liver; heterogeneous liver; nodular, irregular contour; large-volume ascites Reasoning: Advanced shrunken nodular liver morphology with associated large-volume ascites supports severe cirrhosis with decompensation rather than only mild chronic liver disease. Differential: Budd-Chiari syndrome Infiltrative hepatocellular carcinoma Treated metastatic disease

entries.clinicalContext: 55-year-old man with abdominal swelling and fatigue V6N1K8P3T4HD
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Severe portal hypertension due to cirrhosis Keyword findings: recannalized paraumbilical vein; arises from the left portal vein; left lobe of the liver; collateral pathway Reasoning: A paraumbilical collateral arising from the left portal vein on Doppler is a classic portosystemic shunt pattern of advanced portal hypertension in cirrhosis. entries.question: Define hypoalbuminemia-related gallbladder wall edema in cirrhosis.
entries.answer: Source definition: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from the article statement that gallbladder wall thickening in cirrhosis, especially with ascites, is due to hypoalbuminemia and hypoproteinemia leading to edema of the gallbladder wall. Refined definition based on medical consensus: Secondary edematous gallbladder wall thickening caused by low oncotic pressure in advanced cirrhosis rather than primary gallbladder inflammation. Boundary condition: It is systemic edema-related wall thickening in cirrhosis, not acute cholecystitis by default. Synonyms: gallbladder wall edema in cirrhosis; hypoalbuminemic gallbladder wall thickening

entries.question: Why can cirrhosis cause gallbladder wall thickening without primary cholecystitis?
entries.answer: Advanced cirrhosis impairs hepatic synthetic function, leading to hypoalbuminemia and hypoproteinemia. When plasma oncotic pressure falls, fluid more easily leaves the intravascular space and accumulates in dependent or loose soft tissues, including the gallbladder wall and bowel wall, often alongside ascites. The resulting sonographic wall thickening is therefore edema from low oncotic pressure rather than primary gallbladder inflammation. This mechanism matters because in a cirrhotic patient with ascites, a thick gallbladder wall can be a secondary systemic manifestation of liver failure and portal-hypertensive decompensation, not automatic evidence of acute cholecystitis.

entries.clinicalContext: 61-year-old woman with abdominal distention and edema R2Z7M4Q8L1XC [BT1]
entries.question: What is the key pitfall here, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking gallbladder wall thickening in a cirrhotic patient with ascites for acute cholecystitis by default. Safety check / maneuver: Ask whether the wall thickening is a primary gallbladder process or part of a systemic edema state; specifically look for cirrhosis, ascites, and the source-stated hypoalbuminemic/hypoproteinemic setting. Key discriminator: In this source, the thickened wall is explicitly attributed to edema from hypoalbuminemia/hypoproteinemia, especially with ascites, rather than primary inflammatory gallbladder disease. Why the error occurs: Thickened gallbladder wall is visually nonspecific, so readers may jump straight to cholecystitis without recognizing the cirrhotic decompensation context.

entries.clinicalContext: 55-year-old man with abdominal swelling and fatigue V6N1K8P3T4HD [BT2]
entries.question: What is the key pitfall here, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: Seeing an unusual vessel in the left lobe/falciform region and failing to recognize it as a recanalized paraumbilical collateral, thereby missing severe portal hypertension. Safety check / maneuver: On Doppler, trace the vessel to the left portal vein and assess whether it courses toward the anterior abdominal wall, which is the classic collateral pathway described in the source. Key discriminator: Continuity with the left portal vein identifies a portal-systemic collateral rather than a nonspecific superficial abdominal wall vessel. Why the error occurs: The vessel can look unfamiliar in location/course, so it is easy to dismiss it as incidental vascular anatomy instead of a major portal-hypertension sign.

entries.question: How much higher is the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhotic hepatitis B-positive patients according to the source?
entries.answer: 2.5× higher. Exam pivot: Hepatitis B positivity meaningfully raises HCC risk within cirrhosis, so surveillance-level concern should be especially high in this subgroup.

entries.question: According to the source, how much does alcohol or primary biliary cirrhosis increase the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma?
entries.answer: Alcohol and primary biliary cirrhosis are associated with a 2–5× increased risk of HCC. Exam pivot: These etiologic backgrounds are not just causes of cirrhosis; they also materially increase malignant transformation risk.

entries.question: What classic lobar remodeling pattern on imaging favors cirrhosis?
entries.answer: Atrophy of the right lobe and medial segment of the left lobe, with relative enlargement of the caudate lobe and lateral segment of the left lobe. Exam pivot: Cirrhosis is a dysmorphic remodeling process, not just a small liver.

entries.question: What caudate:right lobe ratio strongly suggests cirrhosis on imaging?
entries.answer: Greater than 0.65. Exam pivot: A disproportionately enlarged caudate lobe is a classic morphologic clue to cirrhosis.

entries.question: What Core morphologic sign reflects shrinkage of the medial left lobe in cirrhosis?
entries.answer: Expanded gallbladder fossa sign. Exam pivot: This is an early morphologic clue that helps you recognize cirrhotic remodeling before focusing only on global liver size.

entries.question: In a patient with cirrhosis, how often should surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma be performed according to the source?
entries.answer: Every 6 months. Exam pivot: Cirrhosis is an HCC-surveillance disease state, so the follow-up interval itself is testable.

entries.question: On surveillance ultrasound in cirrhosis, what lesion threshold requires characterization with contrast-enhanced US, CT, or MR?
entries.answer: Any solid lesion greater than 1 cm, of any echogenicity. Exam pivot: On surveillance US, the key next-step trigger is size threshold, not whether the lesion looks hypo-, iso-, or hyperechoic.

entries.question: How are dysplastic nodules greater than 1 cm regarded in cirrhosis, and what key imaging problem do they pose?
entries.answer: They are considered premalignant and are difficult to differentiate from small hepatocellular carcinoma. Exam pivot: A nodule over 1 cm in a cirrhotic liver is not automatically benign regenerative change.

entries.question: MRI appearance pivot for siderotic regenerative nodules: what is the key MRI signal pattern as stated in the source?
entries.answer: T1WI: Hypointense. T2WI: Increased conspicuity of low signal intensity. T2 GRE or FLASH: Markedly hypointense. Exam pivot: Iron-containing regenerative nodules become especially conspicuous on susceptibility-sensitive sequences.

entries.question: MRI appearance pivot for dysplastic regenerative nodules: what is the key MRI signal pattern as stated in the source?
entries.answer: T1WI: Hyperintense compared with liver parenchyma. T2WI: Hypointense relative to liver parenchyma. Exam pivot: This signal combination is a source-stated clue for dysplastic regenerative nodules in cirrhosis.

entries.question: What is the current reference standard for liver fibrosis staging according to the source?
entries.answer: Liver biopsy. Exam pivot: Noninvasive elastography is increasingly used, but biopsy remains the reference standard in the source.

entries.question: In the Metavir staging system, which fibrosis stage corresponds to cirrhosis?
entries.answer: F4. Exam pivot: Metavir stage tracks fibrosis severity, and F4 is the cirrhotic endpoint.

entries.question: What transient elastography thresholds in the source correspond to significant fibrosis and cirrhosis?
entries.answer: Significant fibrosis: ≥ 7.71 kPa (Metavir F2). Cirrhosis: ≥ 15.08 kPa (Metavir F4). Exam pivot: The cirrhosis threshold is much higher than the significant-fibrosis threshold, so do not collapse these stages into one number.

entries.question: What shear wave elastography ranges in the SRU 2020 update correspond to high probability of normal liver and to ruling out cACLD in the absence of other clinical signs?
entries.answer: Less than 5 kPa (1.3 m/s): High probability of being normal. 5-9 kPa (1.3-1.7 m/s): In the absence of other known clinical signs, rules out compensated advanced chronic liver disease. Exam pivot: These low-end thresholds are most useful as exclusion pivots, not as confirmation of cirrhosis.

entries.question: Define acute pancreatitis.
entries.answer: Source definition (formal): Acute pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas due to a variety of etiologies that share a final common pathway of premature activation of pancreatic enzymes with resultant autodigestion of pancreatic parenchyma. Boundary condition: This is the acute inflammatory pancreatic process itself, not one of its morphologic subtypes or one of its associated fluid/necrotic collections. Synonyms: AP.

entries.question: Define interstitial edematous pancreatitis.
entries.answer: Source definition: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features. Refined definition based on medical consensus: Interstitial edematous pancreatitis is the non-necrotizing morphologic subtype of acute pancreatitis characterized by pancreatic interstitial edema/inflammation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma rather than necrosis. Boundary condition: It is acute pancreatitis without pancreatic or peripancreatic necrosis; once necrosis is present, the entity is necrotizing pancreatitis instead. Synonyms: IEP.

entries.question: Define necrotizing pancreatitis.
entries.answer: Source definition: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features. Refined definition based on medical consensus: Necrotizing pancreatitis is the morphologic subtype of acute pancreatitis in which pancreatic parenchyma and/or peripancreatic tissues undergo necrosis. Boundary condition: It is not merely edematous inflammatory enlargement; the defining boundary is the presence of necrotic tissue. Synonyms: None explicitly stated in source.

entries.question: Define acute peripancreatic fluid collection.
entries.answer: Source definition (formal): Acute peripancreatic fluid collection is a non-encapsulated fluid collection. Boundary condition: It is an early fluid-only collection; it is not a mature encapsulated pseudocyst and not a heterogeneous necrotic collection. Synonyms: APFC.

entries.question: Define acute necrotic collection.
entries.answer: Source definition (formal): Acute necrotic collection is a non-encapsulated collection containing heterogeneous material. Boundary condition: It is an early non-encapsulated necrotic collection; it is not a simple fluid-only APFC and not the later encapsulated form of walled-off necrosis. Synonyms: ANC.

entries.question: Define pancreatic pseudocyst.
entries.answer: Source definition (formal): A pancreatic pseudocyst is a collection of pancreatic enzymes and fluid enclosed by a fibrous wall lacking an epithelial lining; the fibrous wall usually takes about 4–6 weeks to mature. Boundary condition: It is an encapsulated mature fluid collection, not an early non-encapsulated APFC and not a heterogeneous necrotic collection such as walled-off necrosis. Synonyms: Pseudocyst.

entries.question: Define walled-off necrosis.
entries.answer: Source definition (formal): Walled-off necrosis is an encapsulated heterogeneous, non-liquified collection with thick walls. Boundary condition: It is the mature encapsulated form of necrotic collection; it is not a simple fluid-only pseudocyst and not an early non-encapsulated ANC. Synonyms: WON.

entries.question: Define autoimmune pancreatitis.
entries.answer: Source definition: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features. Refined definition based on medical consensus: Autoimmune pancreatitis is an immune-mediated fibroinflammatory form of pancreatitis. Boundary condition: It is an inflammatory pancreatic disorder, not infiltrating pancreatic carcinoma and not the typical acute pancreatitis pattern with peripancreatic fluid collections emphasized elsewhere in this build. Synonyms: None explicitly stated in source.

entries.question: Define shock pancreas.
entries.answer: Source definition: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features. Refined definition based on medical consensus: Shock pancreas is a pancreatic and peripancreatic manifestation of systemic hypotension/hypoperfusion rather than a primary inflammatory pancreatitis process. Boundary condition: It is a hemodynamic mimic of pancreatitis, not true acute enzymatic pancreatic inflammation. Synonyms: None explicitly stated in source.

entries.question: Why does necrotizing pancreatitis show nonenhancing pancreatic tissue on contrast-enhanced CT?
entries.answer: Starting point: In uncomplicated interstitial edematous pancreatitis, the pancreatic parenchyma is inflamed but still perfused, so it enhances more uniformly. Primary pathologic escalation: When pancreatitis is severe, the inflammatory process progresses beyond edema to tissue devitalization. The article and Core distinguish this from interstitial edematous pancreatitis by the presence of necrosis/nonenhancement. Tissue consequence: Severe inflammation, microvascular injury, and impaired pancreatic perfusion lead to ischemic destruction of pancreatic parenchyma and/or adjacent tissues. Once a region is devitalized, it no longer receives contrast like viable parenchyma. Imaging manifestation: On contrast-enhanced CT, viable edematous pancreas enhances, but necrotic pancreas remains relatively nonenhancing because perfusion has failed in that tissue. This is why pancreatic-phase CT is the key study for detecting necrosis. Board discriminator / interpretation pivot: Enlargement alone does not establish necrosis. The discriminator is enhancement behavior: preserved enhancement favors interstitial edematous pancreatitis, while nonenhancing parenchyma indicates necrotizing pancreatitis. External literature source (not stated in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx/Radiopaedia). Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4133524/

entries.question: Why does a pancreatic pseudocyst become a mature encapsulated fluid collection after pancreatitis, and why does it lack an epithelial lining?
entries.answer: Initial event: After pancreatitis, pancreatic juice and inflammatory fluid can leak outside the normal ductal/parenchymal confines into the peripancreatic region. Early phase: At first this is an acute peripancreatic fluid collection, meaning fluid without a mature wall. Maturation step: If the leaked enzyme-rich fluid persists rather than resolving, the surrounding tissues respond by organizing it with granulation/fibrous tissue over several weeks, creating a defined capsule. Why it is a “pseudo”-cyst: The wall is not a true epithelial-lined cyst wall formed by native cyst epithelium; it is a reactive fibrous/granulation tissue boundary produced by inflammation and healing. Imaging manifestation: Once this organizing wall matures, the collection appears encapsulated and fluid-dominant, which is why a pseudocyst belongs in the > 4 week mature-collection category rather than the early nonencapsulated category. Board discriminator / interpretation pivot: The key mechanistic separator is organized enzyme-rich fluid without epithelial lining. That is why pseudocyst is distinguished from early APFC on one side and from necrotic collections/WON on the other, which contain nonliquefied necrotic material rather than a simple mature fluid collection. External literature source (not stated in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx/Radiopaedia). Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2653285/

entries.question: On pancreatic ultrasound, what common pitfall can falsely lower diagnostic confidence, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Falsely excluding acute pancreatitis because the pancreas looks normal or only subtly abnormal on ultrasound. Safety check: Remember that in mild acute pancreatitis, sonographic findings may be subtle or even absent; use ultrasound primarily to search for gallstones or biliary calculi, and escalate to contrast-enhanced CT or MR when diagnosis, severity, or complications remain uncertain. Key discriminator: A near-normal or nondiagnostic ultrasound does not rule out pancreatitis; ultrasound is best for etiology, not for confidently excluding the disease or assessing necrosis. Why it happens: Mild interstitial edema may create only subtle sonographic change, and bowel gas or limited acoustic windows can further obscure the pancreas.

entries.question: When a focal hypoechoic pancreatic abnormality is seen, what pitfall can occur, and what safety check prevents misclassification?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking infiltrating pancreatic carcinoma for pancreatitis. Safety check: Search specifically for a discrete hypoechoic mass, pancreatic or biliary duct dilation, and lymphadenopathy rather than assuming focal enlargement is inflammatory. Key discriminator: Infiltrating pancreatic carcinoma is more likely when there is a hypoechoic mass with duct dilation and LAD, whereas acute pancreatitis favors inflammatory enlargement with peripancreatic edema or fluid collections. Why it happens: Both can appear as hypoechoic pancreatic enlargement, especially when only limited sonographic views are available.

entries.question: What are the most common causes of acute pancreatitis?
entries.answer: Alcohol use and an obstructing gallstone are the most common causes of acute pancreatitis. Exam pivot: These are the default top etiologies to rank first, so early imaging/workup should actively assess the biliary branch rather than treating all pancreatitis as idiopathic.

entries.question: How is acute pancreatitis diagnosed clinically?
entries.answer: Diagnosis is made when 2 of 3 are present: • Abdominal pain consistent with pancreatitis • Lipase or amylase level > 3x upper limit of normal • Imaging consistent with acute pancreatitis Exam pivot: Imaging is not mandatory when the clinical/laboratory picture already establishes the diagnosis.

entries.question: In acute pancreatitis, which imaging test is best for cholelithiasis, which is best for choledocholithiasis, and which is best for detecting necrosis?
entries.answer: • Ultrasound: Best to evaluate for cholelithiasis / biliary calculi • MRCP: Best to detect choledocholithiasis • Contrast-enhanced CT in the pancreatic phase / late arterial phase: Best to detect necrosis Exam pivot: Choose the study based on the question - biliary cause vs duct stone vs necrosis/severity.

entries.question: In acute pancreatitis, what are the two collection terms used at more than 4 weeks?
entries.answer: • Pseudocyst • Walled-off necrosis Exam pivot: After 4 weeks, think mature encapsulated collections, then separate fluid-dominant pseudocyst from necrotic walled-off necrosis.

entries.clinicalContext: 58-year-old patient with abdominal pain and distention N4K8Q2M7T1ZX
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Portal venous thrombosis Keyword findings: intrahepatic portal veins; main PV; superior mesenteric vein; inferior mesenteric vein; splenic vein Tight reasoning: This case depicts thrombotic occlusion within the portal venous system and its major tributaries. The article explicitly frames portal vein occlusion as obstruction of the portal vein, most commonly due to thrombosis, and this graphic emphasizes that thrombus may involve the main portal vein, intrahepatic portal veins, or extend into the mesenteric and splenic venous system. Differential: Nonocclusive thrombosis Splenic vein occlusion Hepatic vein/inferior vena cava occlusion

entries.question: Color Doppler US of the porta hepatis. Based on the image, name 3 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
entries.answer: Splenic vein occlusion Hepatic vein/inferior vena cava occlusion Portal venous stasis without thrombosis

entries.question: Define tumor in vein (tumor thrombus).
entries.answer: Source definition: Tumor in vein (tumor thrombus) is tumor growing within the vein lumen with the portal vein wall intact. Refined definition based on medical consensus: Tumor thrombus is intraluminal neoplastic tissue extending within a vein rather than bland coagulated blood. Boundary condition: It is intraluminal tumor with preserved vessel wall, not direct transwall tumor invasion destroying the portal vein wall. Synonyms: tumor thrombus

entries.question: Why does occlusive portal vein thrombosis produce absent Doppler flow and faint intraluminal echoes on ultrasound?
entries.answer: When thrombus fills the portal-vein lumen, normal moving blood is replaced by relatively static clot material, so there is little or no detectable forward venous signal on color or spectral Doppler. Because the lumen is occupied by thrombus rather than freely flowing blood, the vein may also contain visible internal echoes on grayscale US. In acute thrombosis the vein may be enlarged as thrombus fills the lumen; with more chronic occlusion the vein may become small, echogenic, or difficult to see. The imaging pivot is that true luminal thrombus explains the combination of absent flow plus intraluminal material, whereas very slow flow can mimic the first feature but does not create a truly thrombosed lumen.

entries.question: What is the major sonographic pitfall that can falsely suggest portal vein thrombosis, and what maneuver/check helps prevent the error?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking very slow or stagnant portal venous flow for true portal vein thrombosis. Safety check / maneuver: Optimize Doppler aggressively before calling thrombosis: decrease scale/PRF, increase gain, narrow the color box, position the color focus appropriately, lower the wall filter, consider B-flow, use grayscale cine without moving the transducer, or gently push on the belly to propel venous blood. Key discriminator: True thrombosis produces an occluded lumen with absent flow and often visible intraluminal thrombus; slow flow may be hard to detect at first, but some flow can often be recovered with technique optimization. Why the error occurs: Portal venous flow in portal hypertension or stasis states may be so sluggish that color/spectral Doppler initially appears empty, mimicking occlusion.

entries.clinicalContext: 52-year-old patient with abdominal pain and fever Q4M7N2R8K5LX [BT1]
entries.question: What visual pitfall does this image create, and what single check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking a dilated bile duct for a thrombosed portal vein, or letting the adjacent bile duct distract from the actual portal-vein abnormality. Safety check / maneuver: Use color Doppler to confirm which tubular structure is vascular and which is biliary. Key discriminator: A patent portal vein demonstrates flow; a bile duct does not. In this case, the portal vein itself is the abnormal structure because it shows no detectable internal flow with intraluminal echoes, while the dilated common bile duct is only an associated adjacent finding. Why the error occurs: In the porta hepatis, adjacent tubular structures can mimic one another on grayscale alone, especially when one is dilated and the other is thrombosed.

entries.question: What is the key pitfall in interpreting intraluminal portal-vein material here, and what check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: Calling all portal-vein thrombus bland, or missing tumor thrombus by ignoring enhancement/vascularity within the intraluminal material. Safety check / maneuver: Assess whether the portal-vein material enhances or shows internal arterial flow; compare it with adjacent tumor when present. Key discriminator: Bland thrombus does not enhance on CEUS, whereas tumor thrombus enhances similarly to adjacent tumor and may show internal arterial vascularity. Why the error occurs: Both bland and tumoral material occupy the portal-vein lumen, so they can look similar unless enhancement behavior or internal vascularity is deliberately assessed.

entries.question: According to the source, what underlying conditions account for most cases of portal vein occlusion?
entries.answer: Most cases of portal vein occlusion are related to cirrhosis or pancreatitis. Exam pivot: In an adult with suspected portal vein occlusion, first anchor your causal search to cirrhosis, pancreatitis, and their hemodynamic/inflammatory consequences before reaching for less common etiologies.

entries.question: What is the most common tumor associated with portal-vein tumor thrombus?
entries.answer: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common tumor associated with portal-vein tumor thrombus. Exam pivot: If intraluminal portal-vein material shows enhancement or internal arterial flow, HCC should be the first malignant cause you consider.

entries.question: What is the typical age distribution of portal vein occlusion?
entries.answer: Portal vein occlusion occurs usually in adults, occasionally in children. Exam pivot: Adult cases should push you toward common acquired causes such as cirrhosis, pancreatitis, neoplasm, surgery, or hypercoagulability, while pediatric cases remain possible and should not be dismissed.

entries.question: What is the best initial imaging tool for surveillance and diagnosis of portal vein occlusion?
entries.answer: Color/spectral Doppler sonography is the best imaging tool for surveillance and initial diagnosis. Exam pivot: Start with Doppler US to decide whether portal venous flow is absent, slow, reversed, or replaced by collaterals.

entries.question: After portal vein occlusion is identified on ultrasound, what imaging is best for comprehensive evaluation of extent, collateralization, and cause?
entries.answer: Contrast-enhanced CT or MR is best for comprehensive evaluation of the extent of occlusion, collateralization, and the underlying cause/associated condition. Exam pivot: Doppler US makes the diagnosis; CT/MR stages the full venous problem and looks for the cause.

entries.question: What sonographic finding should immediately raise concern for portal vein occlusion on grayscale ultrasound?
entries.answer: A portal vein that is not readily seen or is nonvisualized should raise concern for portal vein occlusion. Exam pivot: The normal portal vein is usually easy to identify, so failure to see it is not a trivial finding.

entries.question: How do the portal vein and lumen typically differ in acute versus chronic portal vein thrombosis?
entries.answer: Acute thrombosis: portal-vein diameter may be enlarged; lumen may be partially or completely filled with thrombus. Chronic occlusion: portal vein may be small, echogenic, or not visible and may be accompanied by cavernous transformation. Exam pivot: A big acutely thrombosed vein and a shrunken chronically occluded/collateralized vein are not the same stage of disease.

entries.question: When does cavernous transformation begin to appear after portal vein occlusion, and what is the flow direction in those collateral vessels?
entries.answer: Cavernous transformation begins to appear about 6-20 days after occlusion and matures gradually, becoming most prominent chronically. Flow in the cavernous transformation collaterals is hepatopetal. Exam pivot: A serpiginous hepatopetal collateral network in the porta hepatis indicates chronic portal-vein bypass rather than simple stagnant flow.

entries.clinicalContext: 66-year-old patient with abdominal fullness and fatigue T4N8G2K6W1RM
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Diffuse infiltrative hepatocellular carcinoma Keyword findings: markedly heterogeneous liver; multiple refractive shadows; diffuse, infiltrative; innumerable hypervascular; wash out; fat-containing focus; Tumor in vein is present in the left portal vein Reasoning: Multifocal hypervascular hepatic tumor burden with washout and portal venous invasion is a classic aggressive HCC pattern. The combination strongly favors diffuse infiltrative HCC over other multifocal liver malignancies. Differential: Metastases Cholangiocarcinoma Combined hepatocellular cholangiocarcinoma

entries.clinicalContext: 62-year-old patient with abdominal pain and weakness U5B9H1L7C3QS
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Hepatocellular carcinoma with right portal vein tumor invasion Keyword findings: arterial hyperenhancement; invasion of right portal vein; echogenic material in the right portal vein; late, weak washout; infiltrative; right hepatic lobe Reasoning: Arterial enhancement and subsequent washout within portal venous material indicate tumor in vein rather than bland thrombus. Associated infiltrative parenchymal tumor further supports HCC with portal venous invasion. Differential (Model-inferred; not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx): Bland portal vein thrombus Cholangiocarcinoma Metastases

entries.clinicalContext: 63-year-old man with abdominal pain and fatigue Y2L7S4H9P3QC
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Hepatocellular carcinoma Keyword findings: hypervascular; washes out on portal venous phase; enhancing pseudocapsule; low intrinsic T1 signal; mildly hyperintense T2 signal Reasoning: This directly matches the source-stated MRI pattern of HCC: arterial hyperenhancement, portal venous washout, and pseudocapsule, with typical low T1 and mild T2 hyperintensity. Differential: Regenerative or dysplastic nodule Hepatic adenoma Focal nodular hyperplasia

entries.clinicalContext: 67-year-old patient with abdominal pain and increasing distention J4R8M2T6V1KD
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Hepatocellular carcinoma Keyword findings: heterogeneous, hypervascular; Numerous adjacent satellite nodules; portal vein invasion; nodular liver capsule; ascites Reasoning: A hypervascular hepatic mass with satellite nodules and portal vein invasion in a cirrhotic liver is a classic advanced HCC pattern. The background liver disease and venous invasion make benign hypervascular masses very unlikely. Differential: Metastases Cholangiocarcinoma Combined hepatocellular cholangiocarcinoma

entries.clinicalContext: 58-year-old patient with chronic abdominal discomfort N6W3P9X2L4ZT
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Hepatocellular carcinoma Keyword findings: hypoechoic, solid; chronic hepatitis; highly suspicious; further characterized with CECT, CEMR, or CEUS Reasoning: A solid hypoechoic hepatic nodule in the setting of chronic hepatitis is highly suspicious for HCC. This fits the source teaching that a solid mass in a patient with risk factors requires definitive characterization as possible HCC. Differential: Regenerative or dysplastic nodule Hepatic hemangioma Metastases

entries.question: Define hepatic adenoma.
entries.answer: 1) Source definition: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features — a hypervascular liver lesion that may enter the differential of HCC, with washout less common than in HCC. 2) Refined definition based on medical consensus: Benign hepatocellular neoplasm, usually arising in noncirrhotic liver. 3) Boundary condition: It is a benign hepatocellular tumor, not the same as focal nodular hyperplasia and not equivalent to HCC. 4) Synonyms: Hepatocellular adenoma; liver cell adenoma.

entries.question: Define focal nodular hyperplasia.
entries.answer: 1) Source definition: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features — a homogeneous hepatic mass that may show a central scar and arterial hypervascularity, but washout is uncommon. 2) Refined definition based on medical consensus: Benign hyperplastic hepatocellular lesion associated with localized vascular malformation rather than true neoplasia. 3) Boundary condition: It is a benign hyperplastic lesion, not HCC and not fibrolamellar carcinoma despite possible scar overlap. 4) Synonyms: FNH.

entries.question: Define cholangiocarcinoma.
entries.answer: 1) Source definition: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features — a primary liver malignancy that may mimic HCC but more often shows peripheral bile duct dilatation, capsular retraction, and volume loss. 2) Refined definition based on medical consensus: Malignant epithelial tumor arising from the biliary tree. 3) Boundary condition: It is a biliary epithelial primary, not a hepatocyte-derived primary liver tumor. 4) Synonyms: Bile duct carcinoma; cholangiocellular carcinoma.

entries.question: Define combined hepatocellular cholangiocarcinoma.
entries.answer: 1) Source definition: Operational definition present in article — mixed tumor sharing phenotypical and overlapping imaging characteristics of both HCC and cholangiocarcinoma. 2) Refined definition based on medical consensus: Primary liver carcinoma showing both hepatocellular and cholangiocytic differentiation. 3) Boundary condition: It is not pure HCC and not pure cholangiocarcinoma; it is a mixed primary liver carcinoma. 4) Synonyms: Mixed hepatocellular cholangiocarcinoma; combined HCC-CCA.

entries.question: Why does hepatocellular carcinoma become arterially hyperenhancing and then relatively wash out on portal venous or delayed imaging?
entries.answer: In cirrhotic hepatocarcinogenesis, the background sequence progresses from regenerative nodule to dysplastic nodule to HCC. Core states that regenerative nodules are completely supplied by the portal vein, and that most dysplastic nodules still derive blood supply from the portal vein unless high grade. As HCC develops, the lesion acquires increased neovascularity, and the article and Core describe HCC as hypervascular with arterial feeding vessels while normal liver parenchyma receives most of its blood supply from the portal vein. Because the tumor becomes preferentially supplied by hepatic arterial neovessels, it enhances more than background liver in the late arterial phase. On later phases, the surrounding liver continues to enhance through its dominant portal venous inflow while the tumor lacks the normal portal-dominant perfusion pattern, so the lesion becomes relatively hypoenhancing compared with adjacent liver (washout). This blood-supply mismatch is the key reason arterial hyperenhancement plus washout is a classic discriminator for HCC rather than regenerative or dysplastic nodules.

entries.question: Why can hepatocellular carcinoma show a nodule-in-nodule appearance within a dysplastic nodule?
entries.answer: Core explicitly frames hepatocarcinogenesis in cirrhosis as regenerative nodule → dysplastic nodule → HCC and notes that high-grade dysplastic nodules and well-differentiated HCC may overlap on imaging. A dysplastic nodule is still largely portal-supplied and may remain relatively hypoenhancing or only mildly arterialized, but once a focus of true HCC develops inside it, that malignant focus acquires increased neovascularity and behaves like HCC rather than like the parent nodule. The result is a smaller internal focus that becomes arterially hyperenhancing and later develops washout, while the larger surrounding dysplastic nodule does not show the same malignant enhancement behavior. That stepwise vascular transformation creates the classic nodule-in-nodule imaging pattern and is a direct imaging correlate of malignant evolution inside a premalignant cirrhotic nodule.

entries.question: Why are most hepatocellular carcinomas hypointense on hepatobiliary phase MRI, while focal nodular hyperplasia may be iso- or hyperintense?
entries.answer: The article states that hepatobiliary contrast uptake in liver tissue is related to the OATP8 receptor, that this transporter is downregulated in most HCCs, and that it is upregulated in focal nodular hyperplasia. Because most HCCs lose the transporter behavior that allows normal hepatocytes to take up hepatobiliary contrast, they usually retain less hepatobiliary agent than the surrounding liver and therefore appear hypointense on the hepatobiliary phase. In contrast, FNH retains or increases transporter-mediated uptake and therefore may remain iso- or hyperintense. This transporter difference explains why hepatobiliary phase imaging can help separate HCC from FNH, while also explaining the article’s pitfall that up to 10% of HCCs can still be iso- or hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase imaging.

entries.clinicalContext: 57-year-old patient with weight loss and abdominal pain F1M5R8K3Q6ZD [BT1]
entries.question: What is the key diagnostic pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Calling an echogenic solid liver lesion a hemangioma just because it looks bright on grayscale US. Safety check: In an at-risk patient, do not assume hemangioma when a nodule is > 1 cm; characterize with multiphasic CECT, CEMR, or CEUS and look for the HCC dynamic pattern rather than relying on echogenicity alone. Key discriminator: The article states HCC can be hyperechoic because of fatty metamorphosis or hypervascularity, whereas hemangioma is unusual in a cirrhotic liver and benign labeling should not be based on brightness alone. Why this error occurs: Echogenic HCC visually overlaps with common benign echogenic liver lesions.

entries.clinicalContext: 68-year-old man with abdominal pain and distention Q9V4C7M2B8LK [BT2]
entries.question: What is the key diagnostic pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Calling portal vein filling material bland thrombus without interrogating it for tumor features. Safety check: Use Doppler and contrast behavior to look for internal vascularity, arterialized waveforms, or enhancement within the venous material. Key discriminator: Bland thrombus should not contain arterial neovascularity, whereas the article shows HCC tumor in vein with marked internal vascularity and arterialized spectral tracings. Why this error occurs: Both entities occupy the portal vein lumen, but only tumor thrombus contains viable hypervascular tumor tissue.

entries.clinicalContext: 29-year-old woman with abdominal pain and weight loss M8X5R1V7K2ZD [BT3]
entries.question: What is the key diagnostic pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Seeing a central scar and reflexively calling the lesion focal nodular hyperplasia. Safety check: Step back and check whether the overall lesion behaves like a large malignant mass rather than a benign hyperplastic lesion; use the full pattern and patient context, not the scar alone. Key discriminator: Fibrolamellar carcinoma is a rare HCC subtype in young patients without chronic liver disease and is described as a large mass with a fibrous central scar, while FNH is a benign hypervascular lesion in which washout is uncommon. Why this error occurs: Both lesions can contain a central scar, so the scar by itself is a classic false reassurance cue.

entries.clinicalContext: 61-year-old patient with chronic abdominal discomfort and abnormal liver tests H3P8L2N6R5YW [BT4]
entries.question: What is the key diagnostic pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Dismissing a cirrhotic nodule as merely regenerative or dysplastic because the outer nodule looks relatively bland. Safety check: Search carefully for an internal focus that shows true HCC behavior, especially arterial hyperenhancement followed by late weak washout. Key discriminator: The article’s nodule-in-nodule case shows malignant transformation within a larger precursor nodule; regenerative and dysplastic nodules may be arterialized, but the source states they do not wash out on portal or delayed imaging like HCC. Why this error occurs: The larger background nodule can distract the reader from the smaller malignant inner component.

entries.question: What is the key hepatobiliary-phase pitfall in HCC, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Excluding HCC because a lesion is isointense or hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase imaging. Safety check: Do not let hepatobiliary-phase signal override the dynamic hallmark pattern; integrate arterial hyperenhancement, washout, capsule, and the rest of the study. Key discriminator: The article states that uptake is related to OATP8 receptor behavior and that most HCCs are hypointense, but up to 10% of HCCs can be isointense or hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase. Why this error occurs: Readers may overgeneralize the usual hepatobiliary-phase appearance into an absolute rule.

entries.clinicalContext: 71-year-old patient with abdominal fullness and fatigue L9X2C6P4T7WB [BT6]
entries.question: What is the key diagnostic pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Missing infiltrative HCC on ultrasound because there is no cleanly marginated focal mass. Safety check: Look for secondary mass effect clues, especially marked posterior displacement of hepatic vessels, and actively inspect for tumor in vein. Key discriminator: The article specifically says infiltrative tumor on US may be challenging to identify, but posterior displacement of hepatic vessels is a helpful clue and tumor in vein is often seen with large infiltrative HCC. Why this error occurs: Infiltrative tumor can blend into background liver and evade the usual find-the-round-mass search pattern.

entries.question: What percentage of adult primary liver malignancies are hepatocellular carcinomas?
entries.answer: 80-90% of all adult primary liver malignancies. Exam pivot: When you are ranking primary malignant liver tumors in an adult, HCC should be the default leading consideration.

entries.question: What proportion of hepatocellular carcinomas arise in cirrhotic livers?
entries.answer: 60-90% arise in cirrhotic liver. Exam pivot: A solid liver mass in a cirrhotic patient has a high pretest probability of HCC and should be approached that way until proven otherwise.

entries.question: What proportion of patients with noncirrhotic HBV may develop hepatocellular carcinoma?
entries.answer: Up to 30% of noncirrhotic HBV patients may develop HCC. Exam pivot: Do not require cirrhosis before considering HCC in a patient with chronic hepatitis B.

entries.question: What is the male-to-female ratio for hepatocellular carcinoma in low-incidence areas?
entries.answer: M:F = 2.5:1. Exam pivot: Male sex increases the baseline diagnostic prior for HCC, but the lesion still must be interpreted through the imaging pattern and risk background.

entries.question: What is the male-to-female ratio for hepatocellular carcinoma in high-incidence areas?
entries.answer: M:F = 8:1. Exam pivot: In high-incidence settings, the prior probability is even more male-skewed, which helps frame who is most classically affected.

entries.question: What are the major imaging criteria for HCC listed in Core page GI 107?
entries.answer: Arterial enhancement Non-peripheral washout Enhancing capsule or pseudocapsule Threshold growth Exam pivot: These are the board-style major criteria that convert a hypervascular liver lesion from possible to classic HCC-pattern thinking.

entries.question: MRI appearance pivot for hepatocellular carcinoma: what is the key MRI signal and dynamic enhancement pattern stated in the source?
entries.answer: T1WI: Typically mildly hypointense, but may be iso- or hyperintense depending on fat content or necrosis. T2WI: Typically slightly hyperintense, similar in intensity to spleen. T1WI C+: Late arterial phase hyperenhancement, portal venous phase typically hypointense, delayed or equilibrium phase washout. Pseudocapsule: Typically best seen on delayed or portal venous phase. Exam pivot: The arterial hyperenhancement plus washout plus capsule combination is the core MRI recognition pattern for HCC.

entries.question: Hepatobiliary-phase MRI pivot for hepatocellular carcinoma: what is the usual appearance, and what is the source-stated pitfall?
entries.answer: Most HCCs are hypointense on hepatobiliary phase because uptake related to OATP8 receptor is downregulated in most HCC. Pitfall: Up to 10% of HCCs can be isointense or hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase. Exam pivot: Hepatobiliary-phase appearance supports but does not overrule the classic dynamic arterial and washout pattern.

entries.question: What ultrasound surveillance interval is recommended for HCC screening in high-risk patients according to the source?
entries.answer: Every 6 months. Exam pivot: This is the standard surveillance rhythm for chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis and is a favorite board-management threshold.

entries.question: In HCC surveillance, how should a liver nodule measuring < 1 cm versus ≥ 1 cm be handled according to the source?
entries.answer: Nodule Nodule ≥ 1 cm: Characterize with CECT, CEMR, or CEUS. Exam pivot: The 1 cm threshold is the key branch point between short-interval surveillance and definitive lesion characterization.

entries.question: What diagnostic checklist rule should be applied to any solid mass ≥ 1 cm detected in a cirrhotic liver?
entries.answer: Any solid mass ≥ 1 cm detected in a cirrhotic liver is suspicious for HCC until proven otherwise. Exam pivot: This rule sharply raises the prior probability and should push you toward HCC-pattern analysis rather than benign reassurance.

entries.question: What vascular imaging finding is highly suggestive of hepatocellular carcinoma?
entries.answer: Portal vein or hepatic vein tumor invasion or tumor in vein. Exam pivot: Venous tumor invasion is one of the strongest pattern-level clues favoring HCC over many hepatic mimics.

entries.question: What Milan criteria are listed in the source for liver transplant in hepatocellular carcinoma?
entries.answer: Single tumor 2-5 cm or 3 tumors Exam pivot: This is the source-stated transplant selection threshold and is a classic management-style board fact.

entries.question: Define portal hypertension.
entries.answer: Source definition: Core gives an operational definition of increased pressure in the portal venous system. The article gives a formal definition: pressure gradient of 12 mm Hg between the main portal vein and the inferior vena cava and/or hepatic veins. Boundary condition: It is a hemodynamic state of elevated portal venous pressure with diversion into portosystemic collaterals, not merely an isolated enlarged portal vein or a single abnormal Doppler waveform. Synonyms: none explicitly stated in source.

entries.question: Why does portal hypertension produce slow portal venous flow and an increased congestion index?
entries.answer: Portal hypertension increases resistance to forward portal venous transit, so portal venous velocity falls even before the main portal vein reverses direction. At the same time, the portal vein may enlarge. Because the congestion index is the ratio of portal vein cross-sectional area to main portal vein velocity, a larger vein plus slower flow increases the congestion index. Imaging consequence: grayscale may show a dilated main portal vein, while spectral Doppler shows reduced velocity despite preserved antegrade flow until portal hypertension becomes more severe.

entries.question: Portal venous Doppler pitfall: what false interpretation can low PRF create, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking color aliasing for hepatofugal portal venous flow. Safety check / maneuver: Increase pulse repetition frequency and optimize Doppler settings before calling true flow reversal. Key discriminator: True hepatofugal flow persists after proper Doppler optimization; aliasing-related apparent reversal does not. Why it happens: Low PRF causes color wraparound in the portal venous system, creating an artifactual appearance of reversed flow.

entries.question: Portal venous Doppler pitfall in a transplant patient: what mimic can helical flow create, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking helical portal vein flow for hepatofugal flow from portal hypertension. Safety check / maneuver: Look for the elliptical color Doppler pattern and use the transplant history, especially donor-recipient main portal vein size mismatch, before calling true reversed flow. Key discriminator: Helical flow has the characteristic elliptical swirling color pattern rather than sustained true portal venous reversal. Why it happens: Helical flow commonly occurs in liver transplants when donor and recipient main portal veins are discrepant in size and can visually mimic hepatofugal flow.

entries.question: Portal venous Doppler pitfall during scanning: what operator-induced error can transiently simulate hepatofugal flow, and what maneuver resolves it?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking pressure-induced transient hepatofugal flow for true portal hypertension. Safety check / maneuver: Decrease transducer pressure and repeat the Doppler assessment. Key discriminator: The abnormal flow pattern returns to normal when probe pressure is reduced. Why it happens: Excess transducer pressure transiently increases intrahepatic resistance and can create temporary hepatofugal flow.

entries.question: Post-TIPS Doppler pitfall: which branch-flow pattern is expected in a patent TIPS, and what finding prevents miscalling it as abnormal portal venous reversal?
entries.answer: Trap: Calling hepatofugal flow in the right and left portal veins abnormal after TIPS placement. Safety check / maneuver: Confirm flow within the TIPS toward the hepatic veins and verify that the main portal vein remains hepatopetal toward the shunt. Key discriminator: In a patent TIPS, the right and left portal veins are expected to be hepatofugal toward the TIPS; if the TIPS becomes occluded, those branches re-reverse and become hepatopetal. Why it happens: The TIPS creates a low-resistance channel that redirects intrahepatic portal venous flow toward the shunt.

entries.question: What are the most common causes of portal hypertension worldwide, and what is the most common cause in the Western world?
entries.answer: Worldwide: cirrhosis and schistosomiasis are the most common causes of portal hypertension. Western world: cirrhosis is the most common cause. Exam pivot: Geography changes the default etiologic prior; cirrhosis stays the key default in Western board-style questions.

entries.question: What portal venous Doppler flow abnormality is diagnostic of portal hypertension in Core?
entries.answer: Hepatofugal (reversed) portal venous flow is diagnostic of portal hypertension in Core. Exam pivot: Slow flow supports portal hypertension, but frank flow reversal is the stronger board-level call.

entries.question: Which portosystemic shunt finding is considered diagnostic of portal hypertension in Core?
entries.answer: A recanalized paraumbilical vein is considered diagnostic of portal hypertension. Exam pivot: Not every isolated portosystemic shunt proves portal hypertension, but a recanalized paraumbilical vein does.

entries.question: What is the best first-line imaging tool for portal hypertension and the best tool for dynamic evaluation of the portal venous system?
entries.answer: Ultrasound. It is the best first-line test and the best tool for dynamic evaluation of the portal venous system because it can assess portal/hepatic venous flow direction, velocity, and waveforms, while also evaluating for collateral signs of portal hypertension. Exam pivot: If the question asks which modality best evaluates real-time portal venous hemodynamics, choose Doppler ultrasound.

entries.question: What coronary vein findings support portal hypertension on ultrasound?
entries.answer: Coronary vein dilation above the normal upper limit of 5-6 mm supports portal hypertension, and reversed flow in the coronary vein is indicative of portal hypertension. Maintenance of normal hepatopetal coronary-vein flow does not exclude portal hypertension. Exam pivot: A dilated coronary vein helps, but reversed coronary-vein flow is the more specific hemodynamic clue.

entries.question: What is the 6-week mortality in patients with variceal bleeding?
entries.answer: 10-20%. Exam pivot: Variceal hemorrhage is not just a portal-hypertension complication; it carries substantial early mortality and should be treated as a high-acuity consequence of decompensated portal hypertension.

entries.clinicalContext: 64-year-old patient with abdominal pain and weight loss
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma Keyword findings: poorly marginated hypodense mass; pancreatic head/neck; distal portal vein involvement; portal/SMV confluence; superior SMV; occluded the SMV; multiple collaterals; reconstitution of the SMV Tight reasoning: A poorly marginated hypovascular pancreatic head/neck mass with portal-mesenteric venous involvement and collateral formation is a classic invasive PDAC pattern. The associated SMV occlusion and collateral reconstitution emphasize locally advanced venous disease rather than a benign ductal process. Differential: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor Pancreatic lymphoma Pancreatic metastasis

entries.clinicalContext: 63-year-old patient with abdominal pain and weight loss

entries.answer: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma Keyword findings: T1-hypointense mass; pancreatic tail; low-signal mass; normal high-signal pancreatic parenchyma; marked restricted diffusion Tight reasoning: On MRI, PDAC is often best seen as a T1-dark mass against the intrinsically T1-bright pancreas, with added conspicuity from restricted diffusion. This is the classic MRI detection phenotype for a subtle solid pancreatic malignancy. Differential: Focal autoimmune pancreatitis Pancreatic metastasis Pancreatic lymphoma

entries.clinicalContext: 67-year-old patient with weight loss and abdominal pain

The article explicitly teaches that postcontrast MR mirrors the classic CT appearance, with diffusion increasing lesion conspicuity. Differential: Focal autoimmune pancreatitis Pancreatic lymphoma Pancreatic metastasis

entries.clinicalContext: 69-year-old patient with jaundice and abdominal pain

entries.answer: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma Keyword findings: infiltrative hypodense mass; pancreatic head; upstream pancreatic ductal dilatation; encases and severely narrows the SMV; large venous collaterals Tight reasoning: The combination of an infiltrative hypovascular head mass, upstream duct dilatation, and severe SMV compromise with collateralization is classic PDAC with advanced venous involvement. The collateral veins are a high-yield secondary sign of significant venous narrowing or occlusion. Differential: Pancreatic lymphoma Chronic pancreatitis with focal mass Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor

entries.clinicalContext: 72-year-old patient with abdominal pain and ductal obstruction symptoms

entries.answer: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma Keyword findings: upstream dilatation of the pancreatic duct; focal stricture; solid mass; biopsied and shown to be adenocarcinoma; isodense carcinoma until proven otherwise Tight reasoning: A focal main pancreatic duct stricture with upstream dilatation and EUS confirmation of a solid mass is a quintessential “secondary sign first” PDAC presentation. The article explicitly teaches that this pattern should be treated as isodense carcinoma until proven otherwise. Differential: Chronic pancreatitis with duct stricture Main-duct IPMN Focal autoimmune pancreatitis

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma Keyword findings: hypointense uncinate process mass; T1-hyperintense normal pancreatic parenchyma; relative lack of conspicuity on T2; lesion relatively hypointense; difficult to differentiate on T2 Tight reasoning: This case highlights the MRI detection pivot of PDAC: it may be much easier to see on noncontrast T1 than on T2. A T1-dark uncinate mass against T1-bright pancreas with poor T2 conspicuity is classic for adenocarcinoma. Differential: Focal autoimmune pancreatitis Pancreatic lymphoma Pancreatic metastasis

entries.clinicalContext: 70-year-old patient with weight loss and abdominal pain

This case is especially valuable for the MR enhancement behavior the article emphasizes. Differential: Pancreatic metastasis Pancreatic lymphoma Chronic pancreatitis with focal mass

The teaching point is to use the duct abnormality to find the otherwise subtle tumor. Differential: Focal autoimmune pancreatitis Chronic pancreatitis with focal mass Pancreatic lymphoma
