entries.question: Why can rectal carcinoma metastasize to the lung or bone before the liver?
entries.answer: Rectal carcinoma does not drain through a single venous route. Tumors from the upper 2/3 of the rectum can spread through the portal system to the liver and through Batson vertebral venous plexus to lumbar and thoracic vertebrae and periaortic nodes. Tumors from the lower 1/3 can also drain through the middle hemorrhoidal vein into the inferior vena cava and then to the lungs. Imaging pivot: dual venous drainage explains why rectal cancer may show lung and bone metastases before liver metastases.

entries.question: Why is extramural vascular invasion on MRI a poor prognostic sign in rectal carcinoma?
entries.answer: Extramural vascular invasion occurs when tumor extends beyond the rectal wall into veins in the mesorectal fascia. Once tumor signal is present within a vessel, expands the vessel, and disrupts the vessel border, the cancer has entered a venous conduit for extramural spread. Imaging pivot: EMVI is linked in the source with higher T and N stage, positive CRM, and distant metastases, which is why it marks poor prognosis and metastatic risk.

entries.question: What is the post-neoadjuvant MR pitfall with spiculations, and what safety check prevents the error?
entries.answer: Trap: Assuming posttreatment spiculations automatically represent residual tumor. Safety check: Compare pre- and post-neoadjuvant MR side by side and look for T2 dark fibrosis or a split scar sign; use DWI/ADC change as an adjunct. Key discriminator: Persistent intermediate T2 signal favors residual tumor, whereas dark T2 fibrosis and the split scar sign favor treatment response. Why it happens: Posttreatment desmoplastic reaction can be depicted as spiculations and may be confused with tumor.

entries.question: What is the nodal staging pitfall in rectal cancer MRI, and what safety check prevents the error?
entries.answer: Trap: Dismissing a small node as benign because it is under 5 mm. Safety check: Evaluate morphology, not size alone. Key discriminator: Round shape, irregular borders, and heterogeneous signal are suspicious; 5–9 mm nodes can be positive if 2 morphologic criteria are present, and even Why it happens: There is no safe lower size threshold, and 15% of nodes < 5 mm are metastatic in the source.

entries.question: What is the CRM measurement pitfall on rectal MRI, and what safety check prevents the error?
entries.answer: Trap: Measuring the circumferential resection margin to a lymph node or satellite nodule instead of the definitive T3 tumor border. Safety check: Measure the shortest distance from the definitive T3 tumor border to the mesorectal fascia; report nodes and satellite nodules separately. Key discriminator: Tumor ≤ 1 mm from mesorectal fascia is positive CRM and 1–2 mm is threatened. Why it happens: Multiple mesorectal structures can sit close to the fascia and distract from the source-defined CRM measurement rule.

entries.question: What percentage of rectal tumors are adenocarcinomas?
entries.answer: Adenocarcinoma accounts for 95% of rectal tumors. Exam pivot: Default to adenocarcinoma as the expected histology unless the source gives a specific alternative subtype.

entries.question: What percentage of colorectal cancer cases are due to Lynch syndrome?
entries.answer: Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) accounts for 3–5% of cases. Exam pivot: Lynch syndrome is the most common hereditary colorectal cancer association in the source and should raise suspicion for inherited risk and MSI-related biology.

entries.question: MRI appearance pivot for rectal carcinoma: what MR sequences are most important for local staging and response assessment?
entries.answer: Sequence: Non-fat-saturated T2WI sagittal and high-resolution axial T2WI (small FOV) → most important for local staging. Sequence: Coronal non-fat-saturated T2WI → best plane for sphincter involvement and least susceptible to motion artifacts. Sequence: DWI with high b value (≥ 800 sec/mm²) → assessment of tumor response to therapy and nodal detection. Sequence: Contrast-enhanced fat-saturated T1WI → local recurrence. Exam pivot: Rectal MR is the standard of care for preoperative local staging and therapy response assessment.

entries.question: MRI appearance pivot for rectal carcinoma after neoadjuvant therapy: what findings favor complete or favorable response?
entries.answer: T2WI: Split scar sign may identify complete response with very high specificity and positive predictive value. T2WI: T2 dark fibrosis at the prior tumor site favors response; persistent intermediate T2 signal favors residual tumor. DWI: Changes in ADC values between pre- and posttreatment studies predict response. Exam pivot: Side-by-side pre- and posttreatment MR improves tumor response grading.

entries.question: Ultrasound appearance pivot for rectal carcinoma: what is the key transrectal sonographic appearance and T-stage logic?
entries.answer: Sonographic feature: Hypoechoic mass with disruption of wall layers and focal or circumferential wall thickening. Wall layers: Innermost hyperechoic interface between balloon and mucosa; 2nd hypoechoic muscularis mucosae; 3rd hyperechoic submucosa; 4th hypoechoic muscularis propria; 5th hyperechoic perirectal fat or serosa. T stage: T1 preserves the middle echogenic layer; T2 keeps the outermost echogenic layer intact; T3 disrupts the outer hyperechoic ring into perirectal fat. Exam pivot: Transrectal US is best for early wall-layer staging, especially T1 versus T2.

entries.question: What are the sensitivity and specificity of transrectal ultrasonography for T0–T3 rectal cancer staging?
entries.answer: Sensitivity: 80–96%. Specificity: 75–98%. Exam pivot: Transrectal US can outperform MR for distinguishing T1 from T2, but it is limited for advanced T3/T4 disease, deep perirectal spread, and mesorectal fascia involvement.

entries.question: What is the treatment pivot between surgery-first disease and neoadjuvant therapy in rectal carcinoma?
entries.answer: T1–T2, N0, M0 (all present) → surgery. T3–T4, N1–N2, or locally unresectable (any present) → neoadjuvant chemoradiation therapy → surgery. Exam pivot: Local T and N stage on MR directly change first-line management.

entries.question: What are the key circumferential resection margin (CRM) MRI thresholds in rectal carcinoma?
entries.answer: CRM is the shortest distance from the definitive T3 tumor border to the mesorectal fascia; inferiorly the levator ani define the CRM. Tumor ≤ 1 mm from the mesorectal fascia = positive CRM; 1–2 mm = threatened CRM. CRM > 1 mm is associated with decreased local recurrence and improved survival. Exam pivot: CRM is the most important independent prognostic factor for local recurrence and poor survival.

entries.question: What MRI criteria make a lymph node suspicious in rectal carcinoma?
entries.answer: Size: Short axis ≥ 9 mm is suspicious. Morphology: Round shape, irregular borders, and heterogeneous signal are suspicious. For 5–9 mm nodes, meeting 2 morphologic criteria is suspicious; for Exam pivot: There is no size threshold below which metastasis can be excluded; 15% of nodes < 5 mm are metastatic.

entries.question: How does distance from the anal verge stratify rectal tumors, and what should you look for at each level?
entries.answer: Low rectal tumors: 0–5 cm → look for sphincter involvement. Midrectal tumors: > 5–10 cm → look for mesorectal fascia involvement. High rectal tumors: > 10–15 cm → look for peritoneal reflection involvement. Exam pivot: Tumor height changes the critical local staging target and surgical planning.

entries.question: How is T3 rectal carcinoma subclassified by depth of extramural invasion?
entries.answer: T3a: T3b: 1–5 mm. T3c: > 5–15 mm. T3d: > 15 mm. Exam pivot: The depth of invasion into mesorectal fat refines local staging beyond a simple T3 label.

entries.question: What MRI findings define extramural vascular invasion (EMVI) in rectal carcinoma, and why does it matter?
entries.answer: MRI findings: Tumor signal within a vessel, expansion of the vessel, and disruption of the vessel border in the mesorectal fascia. Prognostic significance: EMVI is associated with higher T and N stage, positive CRM, and distant metastases. Exam pivot: EMVI is a marker of poor prognosis and metastatic disease that must be reported.

entries.question: What are the best imaging tools for detection, staging, and recurrence in rectal carcinoma?
entries.answer: Detection: Barium enema or CT colonography. Staging: MR for staging and preneoadjuvant therapy restaging. Tumor recurrence and surveillance: MR, CT, PET/CT. Exam pivot: Use MR for local rectal staging and CT or PET/CT for metastatic problem solving and recurrence.

entries.clinicalContext: 62-year-old patient with rectal bleeding and change in bowel habits A1B2C3D4E5F6

entries.answer: Rectal carcinoma T staging schematic T1 tumor invades submucosa T2 tumor invades muscularis propria T3 through muscularis propria into the perirectal fat MRF(+) or MRF(-) T4a anterior peritoneal reflection T4b adjacent organs This teaching figure summarizes the source-stated T-stage progression of rectal carcinoma and highlights the key local invasion boundaries used on rectal MRI, especially the distinction between confinement to the rectal wall, extension into mesorectal fat, anterior peritoneal reflection involvement, and direct invasion of adjacent organs. Differential: (none listed in source)

entries.clinicalContext: 62-year-old patient with rectal bleeding and change in bowel habits G7H8J9K1L2M3
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Upper rectal tumor nodal drainage pattern regional nodes include the perirectal presacral sacral promontory superior rectal inferior mesenteric internal iliac nodes This figure is a review diagram of the source-stated nodal drainage pattern for upper rectal tumors. The key teaching point is the expected regional nodal pathway, particularly spread via superior rectal nodes to the inferior mesenteric chain, which helps frame nodal staging and reporting. Differential: (none listed in source)

Differential: (none listed in source)

entries.question: What are gyri in cerebral hemisphere anatomy?
entries.answer: Complex convolutions of the brain cortex.

entries.question: What are sulci, also called fissures, in cerebral hemisphere anatomy?
entries.answer: CSF-filled grooves or clefts that separate gyri.

entries.question: What are operculae in cerebral hemisphere anatomy?
entries.answer: Parts of the frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes that overhang and enclose the insula.

entries.question: What are the core gross-anatomic orientation points for the cerebral hemispheres?
entries.answer: There are 2 hemispheres of nearly equal size linked by commissural fibers. They are separated by the great longitudinal (interhemispheric) fissure, which contains the falx cerebri. A convoluted mantle of cortical gray matter overlies white matter, while deep gray nuclei and the ventricles lie centrally.

entries.question: What is the key lobar boundary created by the central sulcus?
entries.answer: It separates the frontal lobe anteriorly from the parietal lobe posteriorly.

entries.question: What is the key lobar boundary created by the Sylvian fissure?
entries.answer: It separates the frontal and parietal lobes above from the temporal lobe below.

entries.question: How is the frontal lobe bounded and what major cortical landmarks does the source emphasize?
entries.answer: It lies anterior to the central sulcus and superior to the Sylvian fissure. The precentral gyrus contains the primary motor cortex, the premotor cortex lies in the gyrus just anterior to it, and the superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri are separated by the superior and inferior frontal sulci.

entries.question: What body map orientation is emphasized for the precentral gyrus?
entries.answer: The precentral gyrus contains the primary motor cortex with a contralateral motor homunculus: head and face are lateral, while legs and feet are along the medial surface.

entries.question: How is the parietal lobe bounded and what major cortical landmarks does the source emphasize?
entries.answer: It lies posterior to the central sulcus and anterior to the parietooccipital sulcus. The postcentral gyrus contains primary somatosensory cortex; superior and inferior parietal lobules lie posterior to it; the supramarginal gyrus lies at the end of the Sylvian fissure; the angular gyrus lies ventral to the supramarginal gyrus; and the medial surface is the precuneus.

entries.question: What body map orientation is emphasized for the postcentral gyrus?
entries.answer: The postcentral gyrus contains the primary somatosensory cortex with a contralateral map: face, tongue, and lips are inferior; trunk and upper limb are superolateral; and the lower limb lies on the medial aspect.

entries.question: What normal landmarks define the occipital lobe in this source?
entries.answer: It lies posterior to the parietooccipital sulcus. The primary visual cortex is on the medial occipital lobe, and the cuneus is a medial occipital landmark.

entries.question: What major normal structures and functions are emphasized for the temporal lobe?
entries.answer: It lies inferior to the Sylvian fissure and anterior to the angular gyrus. The superior temporal gyrus contains the primary auditory cortex, the middle temporal gyrus connects with auditory, somatosensory, and visual association pathways, the inferior temporal gyrus is a higher visual association area, and the parahippocampal gyrus on the medial surface merges into the uncus.

entries.question: Where is the insula located and what covering relationship should be remembered?
entries.answer: It lies deep in the floor of the Sylvian fissure and is overlapped by the frontal, temporal, and parietal operculae.

entries.question: What are the 3 major white matter fiber classes and their key examples in this source?
entries.answer: Association fibers connect different cortical regions in the same hemisphere; the cingulum is a long association fiber beneath the cingulate gyrus. Commissural fibers connect similar cortical regions of opposite hemispheres; the corpus callosum is the largest commissural fiber. Projection fibers connect cortex with deep nuclei, brainstem, cerebellum, and spinal cord; the internal capsule is the major projection fiber.

entries.question: Which paired deep gray nuclei are included in the basal ganglia in this source?
entries.answer: The caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus.

entries.question: Which 2 sulcal landmarks most efficiently anchor lobar orientation in the cerebral hemispheres?
entries.answer: The central sulcus and the Sylvian fissure. The central sulcus separates frontal from parietal lobe, while the Sylvian fissure separates frontal and parietal lobes above from temporal lobe below.

entries.question: What imaging approach does the source recommend for evaluating the cerebral hemispheres and deep gray nuclei?
entries.answer: Multiplanar MR best evaluates the cerebral hemispheres, and multiplanar MR also best evaluates the basal ganglia and thalami.

entries.question: What modality technique does the source prefer for white matter evaluation?
entries.answer: White matter is best evaluated by diffusion tensor imaging on 1.5 or 3 Tesla MR.

entries.question: What MR approach does the source recommend for evaluating the limbic system?
entries.answer: The limbic system is best evaluated with high-resolution coronal T2 MR, T1 volume images, and FLAIR.

entries.question: What are the 5 scalp layers, and which layers surgically act together as a single unit?
entries.answer: Dermis (skin), subcutaneous fibroadipose tissue, epicranium and muscles, subaponeurotic areolar tissue, and pericranium. The first 3 layers are firmly connected and surgically act as a single layer.

entries.question: How should modality choice be matched to location in the skull, scalp, and meninges?
entries.answer: CT is often best for skull and scalp lesions. Complex skull base lesions often need bone CT plus contrast-enhanced MRI. Contrast-enhanced MRI is the best modality for meningeal processes.

entries.question: Which bones form the calvarium, and what are the major sutures that normally connect them?
entries.answer: The calvarium is composed of the frontal, parietal, occipital, temporal, and sphenoid (greater wings) bones. Major sutures are the coronal, sagittal, and lambdoid sutures. The metopic suture may be variably seen in adults.

entries.question: What are the two dural layers, and what is the expected normal enhancement pattern of dura on imaging?
entries.answer: The dura has an outer periosteal/endosteal layer and an inner meningeal layer. They are closely apposed except where they separate to enclose venous sinuses. Normal dura usually shows smooth, thin enhancement less than 2 mm.

entries.question: Where are the epidural and subdural spaces located in relation to the dura?
entries.answer: The epidural space is the potential space between the dura and the inner table of the calvarium. The subdural space is the potential space between the inner meningeal layer of the dura and the arachnoid.

entries.question: What venous sinus is shown at the calvarial apex, formed where the periosteal and meningeal dural layers separate?
entries.answer: This is the superior sagittal sinus at the midline calvarial apex. It is enclosed by the separated outer periosteal and inner meningeal dural layers; venous lakes and arachnoid granulations may be seen in relation to it.

entries.clinicalContext: Graphic of major dural sinuses and dural reflections.
entries.question: What midline dural reflection is shown inserting on the crista galli anteriorly and extending posteriorly toward the straight sinus?
entries.answer: The falx is the midline meningeal dural fold. It becomes taller posteriorly and meets the tentorium at the tentorial apex as part of normal compartmental anatomy.

entries.clinicalContext: Coronal graphic of cranial meninges and subarachnoid space.
entries.question: What normal CSF-filled space lies between the arachnoid and pia?
entries.answer: The subarachnoid space lies between arachnoid and pia, contains CSF, and contains the vessels and trabeculae covered by pia.

entries.clinicalContext: Axial T2-weighted MRI of subcortical and deep white matter.
entries.question: What normal variant fluid-filled spaces are shown in the subcortical and deep white matter?
entries.answer: Perivascular spaces are normal pial-lined interstitial fluid spaces that accompany penetrating arteries and veins. They may be conspicuous but remain a normal variant.

entries.clinicalContext: Sagittal graphic of cranial leptomeninges and cisterns.
entries.question: Which leptomeningeal layer follows the brain surface and dips into the sulci?
entries.answer: The pia closely invests the brain surface and enters the sulci, whereas the arachnoid follows the dura around the inner calvarium and does not invaginate into the sulci.

entries.clinicalContext: Graphic and MRI examples of perivascular spaces.
entries.question: Why are perivascular spaces considered normal pial-lined spaces rather than true parenchymal lesions?
entries.answer: They form where the pia invaginates along penetrating cortical arteries and veins. Because they are pial-lined interstitial fluid spaces accompanying normal vessels, they represent a normal variant rather than a mass lesion.

entries.clinicalContext: Axial bone CT showing diffuse calvarial thickening.
entries.question: When diffuse calvarial thickening is seen on bone CT, what bounded separator should be made before labeling it a benign normal variant?
entries.answer: Hair-on-end diploic marrow expansion of anemia Benign / normal-variant calvarial thickening

entries.clinicalContext: Axial bone CT through occipital bone adjacent to transverse sinus.
entries.question: What normal variant explains these sharply marginated lucent occipital bone lesions adjacent to the transverse sinus?
entries.answer: These lucent occipital bone lesions are characteristic arachnoid granulations. Their typical adjacency to a dural venous sinus and CSF-like appearance help prevent overcalling a lytic skull lesion.

entries.clinicalContext: Coronal graphic of arachnoid granulation microanatomy.
entries.question: What normal CSF-drainage structure is shown projecting from the subarachnoid space into the superior sagittal sinus?
entries.answer: An arachnoid granulation is a normal extension of the subarachnoid space and arachnoid into a venous sinus. It contains a CSF core and allows CSF drainage into the venous circulation.

entries.clinicalContext: Axial SPACE MR through occipital bone.
entries.question: What normal variant is represented by this CSF-signal lesion in the occipital bone?
entries.answer: This lesion has CSF signal intensity and a typical occipital location for an arachnoid granulation. Lack of enhancement and its relationship to venous sinuses help separate it from true skull pathology.

entries.question: What meningeal enhancement compartment pattern is shown here: leptomeningeal or dural?
entries.answer: This is leptomeningeal enhancement, which follows the pial-arachnoid surfaces and CSF spaces rather than lining the inner calvarium as a smooth pachymeningeal pattern.

entries.question: What meningeal enhancement compartment pattern is shown here: diffuse dural or leptomeningeal?
entries.answer: This is diffuse dural enhancement, a pachymeningeal pattern that lines the dura smoothly rather than tracking along sulci and cisterns like leptomeningeal enhancement.

entries.question: What classic calvarial marrow-expansion pattern is shown by the widened diploic space and radiating trabecular appearance?
entries.answer: This is the hair-on-end appearance, produced by diploic marrow widening and radiating trabeculae. It is a true abnormal pattern and should not be confused with a simple normal calvarial variant.

entries.question: What is the terminology distinction between pachymeninges and leptomeninges?
entries.answer: Pachymeninges = dura. Leptomeninges = arachnoid + pia.

entries.question: What gross anatomic features of the cranial dura are most important to remember?
entries.answer: Dense fibrocollagenous sheet with outer periosteal and inner meningeal layers. Outer layer forms the periosteum of the inner calvarium. Inner layer folds inward to form falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, and related reflections. Dural layers separate where venous sinuses are enclosed.

entries.question: How do arachnoid and pia differ in their relationship to the brain surface?
entries.answer: Arachnoid follows the dura and does not invaginate into sulci. Pia covers the brain surface, dips into sulci, and follows penetrating cortical arteries into brain.

entries.question: What are arachnoid granulations in normal cranial meningeal anatomy?
entries.answer: Endothelial-lined extensions of arachnoid and subarachnoid space into a dural venous sinus. On imaging they are seen as round or ovoid CSF-density / CSF-signal projections, most often in the transverse or sigmoid sinuses.

entries.question: What is the expected normal contrast-enhanced appearance of dura?
entries.answer: Dura normally enhances on CECT and T1 post-contrast imaging. It should be smooth and about 1-2 mm thick. Enhancement is most prominent near the vertex and least prominent under the temporal lobes. At 1.5T it may appear discontinuous; at 3T it is typically better seen as continuous curvilinear enhancement hugging the inner calvarium.

entries.question: What role do dural lymphatics play in cranial meningeal fluid clearance?
entries.answer: Brain interstitial fluid is collected in perivenous spaces and enters dural meningeal lymphatics. Dural lymphatics provide macroscopic glymphatic clearance from brain parenchyma and drain dura and paravascular spaces to cervical lymphatics.

entries.question: Why does dura enhance normally after contrast while arachnoid and pia are usually not seen as enhancing layers?
entries.answer: Dural capillaries lack endothelial tight junctions, so macromolecules such as contrast agents can leak into dura and produce normal enhancement. Arachnoid microvessels have tight junctions and are part of the blood-brain barrier, so arachnoid is normally not seen as an enhancing layer. Pia is also normally not seen on routine imaging.

entries.question: Why do normal perivascular spaces occur along penetrating arteries?
entries.answer: Pia follows penetrating cortical arteries into brain and forms perivascular spaces around them. These spaces are pial-lined and contain interstitial fluid, with CSF and interstitial fluid continuously interchanging, facilitated by AQP4 water channels.

entries.question: Within a dural venous sinus, what features favor a giant arachnoid granulation rather than thrombus?
entries.answer: Giant arachnoid granulation Dural venous sinus thrombus

entries.question: What are the 3 main parts of the midbrain, and how are they positioned relative to the cerebral aqueduct?
entries.answer: Cerebral peduncles are the anterior white matter tracts; tegmentum lies ventral to the cerebral aqueduct; tectum, or quadrigeminal plate, lies dorsal to the cerebral aqueduct and contains the superior and inferior colliculi.

entries.question: What is the arterial supply of the midbrain in this source?
entries.answer: The midbrain is supplied by vertebrobasilar circulation through small perforating branches from the basilar, superior cerebellar, and posterior cerebral arteries.

entries.question: What fibers run in the cerebral peduncles, and what separates the peduncles in the midline?
entries.answer: The cerebral peduncles, or crus cerebri, contain corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticopontine fibers; they are separated in the midline by the interpeduncular fossa.

entries.question: What does the mesencephalic tegmentum contain, and how is it related to the pons?
entries.answer: It is directly continuous with the pontine tegmentum and contains the same long tracts, cranial nerve nuclei, gray matter nuclei, and central tegmental structures.

entries.question: What structures form the tectum, and what pathways are associated with them?
entries.answer: The tectum, or quadrigeminal plate, is formed by the superior and inferior colliculi; the superior colliculi are associated with the visual pathway and the inferior colliculi with the auditory pathway.

entries.question: What are the key anatomic relationships of the oculomotor nucleus and oculomotor nerve in the midbrain?
entries.answer: CNIII nuclei are at the superior colliculus level, paramedian and anterior to the cerebral aqueduct. The Edinger-Westphal parasympathetic nuclei lie dorsal to the CNIII nucleus in the periaqueductal gray. CNIII fibers course anteriorly through the midbrain and exit at the interpeduncular fossa.

entries.question: What are the key anatomic relationships of the trochlear nucleus and trochlear nerve in the midbrain?
entries.answer: CNIV nuclei are at the inferior colliculus level, paramedian and anterior to the cerebral aqueduct, and dorsal to the medial longitudinal fasciculus. CNIV fibers course posteriorly around the cerebral aqueduct, decussate in the superior medullary velum, and exit the dorsal midbrain just inferior to the inferior colliculus.

entries.question: What midbrain structures are emphasized as visible on imaging, and what structures are localized mainly by typical position rather than direct resolution?
entries.answer: CNIII and CNIV can be seen as they exit the midbrain. Substantia nigra and red nucleus are well seen. CN nuclei and white matter tracts can be identified by typical location but are not resolved on imaging.

entries.question: What normal imaging pitfall involving the cerebral aqueduct should not be overcalled as intrinsic midbrain pathology?
entries.answer: The cerebral aqueduct may show variable signal due to flow artifact.

entries.question: What interpretive mistake should be avoided when reviewing midbrain nuclei and long tracts on conventional imaging?
entries.answer: Do not claim direct resolution of midbrain cranial nerve nuclei or long white matter tracts on conventional imaging; the source supports identification by typical location, not direct visualization.

entries.question: Why is the trochlear nerve localized dorsally rather than in the interpeduncular region when reviewing the midbrain?
entries.answer: Because CNIV fibers course posteriorly around the cerebral aqueduct, decussate in the superior medullary velum, and exit the dorsal midbrain just inferior to the inferior colliculus.

entries.question: What is the pons?
entries.answer: Bulbous midportion of the brainstem that relays information from brain to cerebellum.

entries.question: What are the 2 main parts of the pons, and what broadly characterizes each?
entries.answer: Ventral or anterior pons is predominantly white matter tracts; dorsal tegmentum contains cranial nerve nuclei, gray matter nuclei, and white matter tracts.

entries.question: Which adjacent cisterns bracket the pons, and what cranial nerves do they contain?
entries.answer: Prepontine cistern lies anterior to the pons and contains CNV and CNVI; CPA cistern lies lateral to the pons and contains CNVII and CNVIII.

entries.question: What fibers make up the ventral pontine belly?
entries.answer: Longitudinal corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticopontine tracts plus multiple transverse pontine fibers; the ventral pons may be referred to as the pontine bulb or belly.

entries.question: Which major tegmental white matter tracts are described in the dorsal pons even though they are not resolved on conventional imaging?
entries.answer: Medial lemniscus, medial longitudinal fasciculus, lateral lemniscus, trapezoid body, spinothalamic tract, and central tegmental tract.

entries.question: Where are the major trigeminal nuclei concentrated in relation to the pons?
entries.answer: CNV nuclei extend throughout the brainstem and upper cord, but the bulk of the motor, main sensory, and mesencephalic nuclei is located in the pons.

entries.question: Where is the abducens nucleus located within the pons?
entries.answer: In the pontine tegmentum near the midline, just anterior to the 4th ventricle.

entries.question: Why does the facial colliculus form in the floor of the 4th ventricle?
entries.answer: Because axons of CNVII loop around the CNVI nucleus, creating a bulge in the floor of the 4th ventricle.

entries.question: What are the 3 main CNVII nuclei within the pons, and where are they located?
entries.answer: Motor, superior salivatory, and solitary tract nuclei; they are located in the ventrolateral aspect of the tegmentum of the lower pons.

entries.question: Where are the major CNVIII nuclei located?
entries.answer: Vestibular nuclei lie beneath the lateral recess along the floor of the 4th ventricle, and the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei lie on the lateral surface of the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

entries.question: What cranial nerve root entry and exit zones are specifically visualized at the pons?
entries.answer: CNV root entry zone is at the midlateral pons; CNVI exits anteriorly at the pontomedullary junction; CNVII exits laterally at the pontomedullary junction; CNVIII enters the brainstem posterior to CNVII at the pontomedullary junction.

entries.question: What key limitation of routine pontine imaging should guide normal review?
entries.answer: Cranial nerve nuclei are not resolved on conventional imaging, and specific white matter tracts are identified by expected location rather than direct resolution.

entries.question: What is the vertebrobasilar arterial supply to the pons?
entries.answer: The pons is supplied by vertebrobasilar circulation, including medial branches of the superior cerebellar arteries and perforating branches of the basilar artery and thalamoperforator arteries.

entries.question: Why is diffusion-weighted imaging especially important when acute pontine ischemia is suspected?
entries.answer: Because acute pontine ischemia is often not seen on routine CT or routine MR, so DWI is specifically recommended when suspicion remains high.

entries.question: What pitfall should be avoided when evaluating a fusiform or unusual mass in the cerebellopontine angle region?
entries.answer: Do not limit consideration to schwannoma or meningioma; posterior circulation aneurysm must also be considered when the lesion is fusiform or otherwise unusual.

entries.question: Where should a lesion localize if it produces both CNVI and CNVII palsies?
entries.answer: The facial colliculus region in the dorsal lower pons, because CNVII fibers loop around the CNVI nucleus there.

entries.question: How is the vermis organized, and which fissure separates superior from inferior vermis?
entries.answer: Superior vermis: lingula, central lobule, culmen, declive, folium. Inferior vermis: tuber, pyramid, uvula, nodulus. The horizontal (petrosal) fissure separates superior from inferior vermis.

entries.question: Which deep cerebellar nucleus is the main directly appreciable imaging anchor, and how should the others be localized?
entries.answer: Dentate nucleus is the main deep nucleus to look for; it is the lateral group and has a heavily folded band with a medial hilum. Fastigial nucleus is a medial vermian nucleus and should be localized in deep midline white matter near the vermis. Globose and emboliform nuclei are intermediate nuclei, localized between vermis and hemisphere, medial to dentate.

entries.question: Which arterial territories are most useful for cerebellar stroke localization?
entries.answer: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the inferior cerebellar hemispheres; anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the anterolateral aspect of the cerebellar hemispheres; superior cerebellar artery supplies the superior cerebellar hemisphere and also supplies the superior cerebellar peduncle, dentate nucleus, and part of the middle cerebellar peduncle.

entries.question: Why is the nodulus a classic overcall trap on cerebellar imaging?
entries.answer: The nodulus lies just posterior to and may project into the fourth ventricle, so it can be mistaken for a fourth ventricular lesion. Stay safe by first identifying the fourth ventricle, midline vermis, and superior cerebellar peduncles, then confirming the expected midline nodular cerebellar position.

entries.question: Why is the flocculus a classic cerebellopontine angle pseudolesion?
entries.answer: Flocculus, together with nodulus, forms the flocculonodular lobe and may appear as tissue in the CPA cistern, creating a false impression of a lesion. Verify its expected location in the CPA region relative to the anterior cerebellar surface, nearby peduncular landmarks, and the normal flocculonodular anatomy before overcalling a mass.

entries.question: Why does the cerebellum show an arbor vitae pattern on sagittal imaging?
entries.answer: The cerebellar white matter core branches into medullary laminae that occupy the central lobules and are covered by cerebellar cortex; in sagittal section this highly branched white matter pattern creates the arbor vitae, or tree of life.

entries.question: What structures should anchor first-pass orientation on high-resolution MRI review of the CPA-IAC region?
entries.answer: Start with the CPA cistern, then the IAC, then the fundus, then the cochlea, and finally the pontomedullary junction where CNVIII enters the brainstem.

entries.question: What is the CPA-IAC cistern?
entries.answer: It is the CSF space in the cerebellopontine angle and internal auditory canal that contains CNVII, CNVIII, and the AICA loop.

entries.question: Which normal non-neural structures can occupy the CPA cistern and matter for overcall prevention?
entries.answer: AICA loop, flocculus of the cerebellum in the posteromedial CPA, and choroid plexus that may pass through the foramen of Luschka into the CPA cistern.

entries.question: How are CNVII and the divisions of CNVIII arranged in the IAC fundus?
entries.answer: Use “seven-up, coke down”: CNVII anterosuperior, cochlear nerve anteroinferior, superior vestibular nerve posterosuperior, and inferior vestibular nerve posteroinferior.

entries.question: What are the key anatomic landmarks of the IAC fundus?
entries.answer: Crista falciformis is the horizontal crest dividing superior from inferior compartments; Bill bar is the vertical crest in the superior fundus but is not visible on CT or MR; the cochlear aperture is the outlet to the cochlea; the macula cribrosa is perforated bone between the IAC and vestibule.

entries.question: What is the normal course of the cochlear nerve from inner ear to brainstem?
entries.answer: It begins from auditory axons arising from the spiral ganglion, travels in the anteroinferior quadrant of the IAC, joins the superior and inferior vestibular nerves at the porus acusticus to form the CNVIII bundle in the CPA cistern, then enters the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction and bifurcates to the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei.

entries.question: What is the normal position of the facial nerve in the CPA-IAC corridor?
entries.answer: Its root exit zone is at the pontomedullary junction, it travels anterior to CNVIII in the CPA cistern, and it occupies the anterosuperior quadrant of the IAC.

entries.question: What normal landmarks are best established on bone CT through the IAC fundus and cochlea?
entries.answer: The labyrinthine facial nerve exits the anterosuperior fundus, the cochlear aperture connects the anteroinferior fundus to the cochlea, the modiolus is seen within the cochlea, and the macula cribrosa lies along the posterolateral fundal wall toward the vestibule.

entries.question: Why does high-resolution thin-section T2 MR imaging work well for screening the CPA-IAC region in uncomplicated unilateral SNHL?
entries.answer: Because the CPA-IAC cistern and fundus are CSF-filled, so high-signal fluid outlines the low-signal nerves and the horizontal crista falciformis, allowing the nerve compartments and relationships to be assessed on thin-section imaging.

entries.question: What is the imaging approach to cochlear portion of CNVIII evaluation in uncomplicated versus complex unilateral SNHL?
entries.answer: For uncomplicated unilateral SNHL, screen with high-resolution thin-section T2 MR through the CPA-IAC. For complex unilateral SNHL, add whole-brain and posterior fossa sequences: begin with whole-brain axial T2 and FLAIR, then conclude with thin-section axial and coronal post-contrast T1 imaging of the posterior fossa and CPA-IAC. Bone CT is reserved for bony indications such as trauma, otosclerosis, and Paget disease.

entries.question: What normal CPA-IAC pitfall can mimic a cranial nerve or a tiny acoustic schwannoma on high-resolution MRI?
entries.answer: An AICA loop can appear as a flow void on high-resolution T2 MR and may mimic a cranial nerve; subtle enhancement in the IAC on post-contrast T1 may then be mistaken for a small acoustic schwannoma.

entries.question: What normal variant in the walls of the IAC can mimic an IAC tumor on post-contrast T1 MR?
entries.answer: Marrow space foci in the walls of the IAC can mimic an IAC tumor on T1 post-contrast MR.

entries.question: What clinical pattern is most typical for CPA-IAC lesions, and what should make you widen the differential beyond an acoustic schwannoma pattern?
entries.answer: CPA-IAC lesions most commonly present with unilateral SNHL; cochlear nerve injury produces SNHL and tinnitus. Facial nerve dysfunction is uncommon for a CPA-IAC lesion, so if CNVII is involved, consider nonacoustic schwannoma causes such as facial nerve schwannoma or metastatic disease.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: What is the key structural distinction between dural venous sinuses and cerebral veins?
entries.answer: Dural venous sinuses are large endothelial-lined trabeculated venous channels formed within dural folds/reflections; cerebral veins are thin-walled valveless veins that cross the subarachnoid space and pierce arachnoid/inner dura to enter a dural sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: How are the dural venous sinuses broadly grouped in this overview?
entries.answer: Anteroinferior group: cavernous sinus, superior/inferior petrosal sinuses, clival plexus, sphenoparietal system. Posterosuperior group: superior sagittal, inferior sagittal, straight, transverse, sigmoid, and occipital sinuses.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: What are the high-yield venous drainage territory rules in the intracranial venous system?
entries.answer: Venous territories are more variable than arterial territories, but key rules are: 1) Drainage is generally radial and centrifugal except in deep cerebral structures. 2) Much of the middle/superior cerebral surface drains by cortical veins to the superior sagittal sinus. 3) Posterior/inferior temporal lobe and adjacent parietal territory drain by the vein of Labbé to the transverse sinus. 4) Insular and perisylvian regions drain toward the sphenoparietal sinus and cavernous sinus. 5) Deep white matter and basal ganglia drain by medullary/subependymal veins to the internal cerebral veins, vein of Galen, and straight sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: How are the internal cerebral veins formed, and what visible landmarks help localize them?
entries.answer: The septal and thalamostriate veins join to form the paired internal cerebral veins. Localize them by first identifying the frontal horns and foramen of Monro; the septal veins curve around the pillars of the fornix, and the paired ICVs then course posteriorly as paramedian deep veins.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: What are the key localization and formation pearls for the vein of Galen in this source?
entries.answer: The great cerebral vein (vein of Galen) is formed posteriorly where the paired internal cerebral veins and basal veins of Rosenthal converge. At the upper foramen of Monro/pineal region level, it can appear U-shaped, curving above the pineal gland and beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: How should the basal vein of Rosenthal be localized on routine cross-sectional imaging?
entries.answer: Use the midbrain and tentorial edge as anchors. The basal vein of Rosenthal courses around the midbrain and then runs posteriorly toward its confluence with the internal cerebral veins at the vein of Galen.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: How do the superficial and deep middle cerebral veins drain?
entries.answer: The superficial middle cerebral vein drains into the sphenoparietal sinus and then the cavernous sinus, whereas the deep middle cerebral vein drains into the basal vein of Rosenthal and then the vein of Galen.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: What modality and acquisition approach pearls are emphasized for reviewing the intracranial venous system?
entries.answer: MRV and CTV are excellent for general overview of dural sinuses and cerebral veins, but DSA is best for detailed delineation. For MR venography, source images should be obtained perpendicular to the main axis of the dural sinus being evaluated, for example coronal images for the superior sagittal sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: What skull base venous connections provide collateral drainage around the cavernous sinus?
entries.answer: The cavernous sinus communicates richly with the intercavernous plexus, clival venous plexus, superior/inferior petrosal sinuses, ophthalmic veins, pterygoid venous plexus, and venous plexus near the foramen ovale. These intra- to extracranial channels can provide collateral venous drainage if the cavernous sinus becomes occluded.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: What normal dural sinus variant commonly mimics venous occlusion on MRV or CTV?
entries.answer: Normal transverse sinus asymmetry. A transverse sinus may be smaller, hypoplastic, or even segmentally atretic, especially compared with the opposite side, and this should not be mistaken for occlusion.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: In a dural sinus, what bounded differential should be considered when a round or ovoid CSF-equivalent filling defect is seen, especially in the transverse sinus?
entries.answer: Giant arachnoid granulation vs dural sinus thrombus

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: What normal enhancing venous structure along the anterior pons can be overcalled as leptomeningeal disease on post-contrast MRI?
entries.answer: The anterior pontomesencephalic venous plexus. Faint enhancement along the anterior belly of the pons may be normal venous plexus rather than meningitis or leptomeningeal carcinomatosis.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Intracranial Venous System Overview
entries.question: What is the key bounded differential when one transverse sinus is clearly smaller than the other on venous imaging?
entries.answer: Normal transverse sinus asymmetry/hypoplasia vs transverse sinus occlusion

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: What are dural venous sinuses anatomically, and what normal intraluminal structures may they contain?
entries.answer: They are endothelial-lined venous channels contained between the periosteal and meningeal dural layers. They are often fenestrated, septated, and multichanneled. They may contain arachnoid villi and arachnoid granulations, which project into the sinus lumen.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: How should you localize the major midline dural venous sinuses on routine imaging?
entries.answer: First identify the falx and the falcotentorial junction. The superior sagittal sinus runs along the superior falx at the inner calvarial vault. The inferior sagittal sinus, when present, runs in the free inferior falx above the corpus callosum. The vein of Galen lies under the splenium and above the pineal gland, joining the straight sinus at the falcotentorial junction. The straight sinus then courses posteroinferiorly toward the torcular.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: What normal course and variation pattern should you expect for the superior sagittal sinus?
entries.answer: It appears as a curvilinear channel hugging the inner calvarial vault at the falx-calvarial junction. It may begin as anteriorly as the crista galli or as posteriorly as the coronal suture. It collects superficial cortical veins, increases in caliber as it courses posteriorly, and terminates at the venous sinus confluence, sometimes running off midline posteriorly.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: How do you follow the normal lateral dural venous runoff from the confluence to the neck?
entries.answer: The torcular Herophili is formed by the union of the superior sagittal sinus, straight sinus, and transverse sinuses. The transverse sinuses run laterally along the tentorial attachment to the posterior petrous temporal bone. The sigmoid sinuses are the anteroinferior continuations of the transverse sinuses with a gentle S-shaped course. They terminate by becoming the internal jugular veins.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: What is the key compartment rule for the cavernous sinus and its contents?
entries.answer: The cavernous sinus is an irregular, trabeculated venous compartment along the sides of the sella. The cavernous internal carotid artery and cranial nerve number 6 are the only structures that lie within the cavernous sinus itself. Cranial nerve numbers 3 and 4 and divisions 1 and 2 of cranial nerve number 5 lie in the lateral dural wall. The medial dural wall is often inapparent on imaging.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: Which venous pathways should you actively recall when reviewing the cavernous sinus region?
entries.answer: Tributaries include the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins and the sphenoparietal sinus. The cavernous sinuses communicate inferiorly with the pterygoid venous plexus, medially with the contralateral cavernous sinus, and posteriorly with the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses and the clival venous plexus. Use the sella, petrous apex, clivus, and jugular bulb as practical skull-base anchors for these channels.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: Which dural venous structures are usually conspicuous versus variably visualized on routine studies?
entries.answer: Usually conspicuous on contrast-enhanced cross-sectional studies, MRV, or CTV: superior sagittal sinus, straight sinus, transverse sinuses, sigmoid sinuses, and jugular bulbs. Variably visualized or smaller/inconstant: inferior sagittal sinus, superior and inferior petrosal sinuses, sphenoparietal sinus, occipital sinus, and clival venous plexus. For the less conspicuous channels, localize them relative to the falx, tentorium, petrous ridge, sella, clivus, and jugular bulb rather than expecting a crisp standalone structure every time.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: What source-supported review pearls help when reading venographic studies of the dural sinuses?
entries.answer: Examine source MRV and CTV images, not just reprojected views. On DSA, early venous phase emphasizes superficial cortical and anastomotic veins while the sinuses are faint; midvenous phase best opacifies the major dural sinuses; late venous phase washes out cortical veins so subependymal veins and arachnoid granulations become more conspicuous. In a perfectly straight AP venous view, the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses, internal cerebral vein, and vein of Galen overlap in the midline. Oblique AP venous views are especially useful for evaluating sinus occlusion. DSA is rarely required to diagnose dural sinus occlusion.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: What deep venous structures form the vein of Galen on axial imaging?
entries.answer: At the tentorial apex, the internal cerebral veins and the basal veins of Rosenthal converge to form the vein of Galen. The internal cerebral vein also arcs posteriorly from the anterior thalamostriate vein toward the vein of Galen.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: A less conspicuous transverse sinus on venography should prompt what bounded distinction?
entries.answer: Normal hypoplastic or asymmetric transverse sinus Dural venous sinus occlusion

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: What common skull-base venous finding can mimic pseudoocclusion?
entries.answer: Marked jugular bulb asymmetry with turbulent or inhomogeneous flow and enhancement is common and can simulate occlusion. The safety move is to expect side-to-side size variability and to follow continuity from the sigmoid sinus into the jugular bulb on source images.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: What classic normal filling defect in a dural sinus is easy to overcall as thrombus?
entries.answer: A giant arachnoid granulation. It is a normal round or ovoid cerebrospinal-fluid-equivalent filling defect within a dural sinus. It is especially common in the transverse and sigmoid sinuses, but it can also be seen in the superior sagittal sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: What normal MRI appearance in the posterior superior sagittal sinus can be mistaken for thrombus if reviewed carelessly?
entries.answer: A normal flow void caused by fast venous flow in the posterior aspect of the superior sagittal sinus. The safety move is to remember that dark posterior sinus signal can be normal and to correlate with sequence context and contrast-enhanced images before diagnosing thrombosis.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
entries.question: Why are arachnoid granulations normally seen within dural venous sinuses?
entries.answer: They are extensions of the subarachnoid space and arachnoid that protrude through the dural wall into the venous sinus lumen. Their physiologic role is to return cerebrospinal fluid to the venous circulation.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What is the core drainage sequence of the deep cerebral venous system?
entries.answer: Medullary veins → subependymal veins → septal/thalamostriate venous confluence → paired ICVs → vein of Galen; the BVRs are the other major tributaries of the vein of Galen, and the vein of Galen joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What is the normal course of the septal vein, and where does it usually join the thalamostriate vein?
entries.answer: The septal vein courses posteriorly along the septum pellucidum and usually joins the thalamostriate vein at the interventricular foramen of Monro to form the internal cerebral vein.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What is the normal course and key imaging role of the thalamostriate vein?
entries.answer: The thalamostriate vein receives caudate/terminal veins, courses anteriorly between the caudate nucleus and thalamus, curves over the caudate, and terminates at Monro by uniting with the septal vein to form the ICV. On AP venous imaging it helps define the size and outer margin of the lateral ventricle and has a characteristic double-curve appearance.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: How should you localize the internal cerebral veins on routine MRI or venography?
entries.answer: Localize them as paired paramedian veins running posteriorly in the cavum veli interpositi/velum interpositum just above the roof/body of the 3rd ventricle. Key anchors: below the fornices and corpus callosum splenium, above the pineal gland and 3rd ventricle, and beginning near the foramen of Monro.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What is the cavum veli interpositi, and why is it important for deep venous localization?
entries.answer: It is the space within the double-layered tela choroidea of the 3rd ventricle that communicates posteriorly with the quadrigeminal cistern. It is important because the paired ICVs course posteriorly within this space.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What territory is drained by the ICVs, the vein of Galen, and their tributaries?
entries.answer: They drain an ovoid deep periventricular territory surrounding the lateral and 3rd ventricles, including the caudate nuclei, putamen/globus pallidus, thalamus, internal capsule, deep medullary white matter, and medial temporal lobes.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What landmarks should you identify first when reviewing the deep cerebral veins?
entries.answer: Start with the foramen of Monro, the lateral ventricular margins and roof of the 3rd ventricle, the pineal/quadrigeminal cistern region, and the falcotentorial apex. Then trace the paired ICVs posteriorly to the vein of Galen and straight sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What deep cerebral veins are usually visible on routine MR/venography, and which are often not?
entries.answer: ICVs and the vein of Galen are usually well seen on CTV/MRV, and the ICVs can be seen on axial T1 post-contrast MRI as linear paramedian veins just above the 3rd ventricle. Smaller subependymal veins are usually inapparent on routine post-contrast MRI, and the subependymal and medullary veins are not generally visualized on standard MRV.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What is the normal course and classification pearl of the basal vein of Rosenthal?
entries.answer: The BVR begins at the medial temporal lobe, curves around the midbrain in the ambient/quadrigeminal cisterns, and joins the ICVs to form the vein of Galen. Although it drains into the deep venous system, the BVR is actually a superficial cerebral vein.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What is the normal relationship of the direct lateral and terminal veins to the stria terminalis?
entries.answer: Direct lateral veins collect caudate-body tributaries as they course along the stria terminalis, which marks the border between the caudate and thalamus. A terminal vein may also course along this groove and join the caudate and septal veins to form the thalamostriate vein.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: How is the normal vein of Galen formed, and where does it course?
entries.answer: The normal vein of Galen is a short U-shaped midline vein formed by union of the paired ICVs and BVRs. It curves posteriorly and superiorly under the corpus callosum splenium in the quadrigeminal cistern and joins the inferior sagittal sinus at the falcotentorial apex to form the straight sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What is the key embryologic sequence that forms the definitive vein of Galen?
entries.answer: By the 7th–8th fetal weeks, the choroid plexus drains through a temporary midline primitive median prosencephalic vein (MPV) that courses posteriorly toward the falcine sinus. By the 10th week, the ICVs annex the choroid plexus drainage, the MPV regresses, and its caudal remnant unites with the developing ICVs to form the definitive vein of Galen.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: Why is the lateral MRV projection more useful than the submentovertex projection for major deep cerebral venous patency?
entries.answer: Because overlap of many vessels on the submentovertex projection largely obscures the deep cerebral veins, whereas the lateral projection better displays the main deep outflow pathway from the ICVs into the vein of Galen and straight sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What normal variant at the septal/thalamostriate confluence can be mistaken for distortion of the deep venous anatomy?
entries.answer: A long septal vein may join the thalamostriate and direct lateral veins well behind the foramen of Monro. This is a normal variant rather than abnormal displacement of the deep venous system.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What faint post-contrast enhancement along the superolateral ventricular margin should not be overcalled as pathology?
entries.answer: It can represent confluence of the deep medullary white-matter veins draining into a subependymal vein.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Deep Cerebral Veins
entries.question: What normal limitation of standard MRV should keep you from overcalling absence of the smaller deep veins?
entries.answer: The subependymal and medullary veins are not generally visualized on standard MRV, even when the major deep venous pathway is patent.

entries.question: What are the subarachnoid spaces and why do cisterns form within them?
entries.answer: The SASs are CSF-filled spaces between pia and arachnoid. Trabeculae, septa, and membranes subdivide this communicating space into smaller compartments called cisterns, which expand especially at the brain base, around the brainstem, and at the tentorial incisura.

entries.question: How do the cranial cisterns communicate with each other and with the ventricular system?
entries.answer: The cranial cisterns normally communicate freely with one another and with the ventricles through the foramina of Magendie and Luschka. Because cranial nerves and major arteries/veins traverse them, they also create pathways for disease spread and surgical access.

entries.question: What is the Liliequist membrane and which cisterns does it separate?
entries.answer: Liliequist membrane is a thin arachnoid membrane that separates the suprasellar, interpeduncular, and prepontine cisterns.

entries.question: What is the velum interpositum and where is its cistern located?
entries.answer: The velum interpositum is a double layer of tela choroidea (pia). Its cistern lies above the 3rd ventricle, contains the internal cerebral veins and medial posterior choroidal arteries, and may remain open posteriorly as a cavum veli interpositi communicating with the quadrigeminal cistern.

entries.question: What is the choroidal fissure?
entries.answer: The choroidal fissure is a narrow pial-lined channel between the SAS and the ventricles and is the site of choroid plexus attachment in the lateral ventricles.

entries.question: Which supratentorial and peritentorial cisterns should anchor localization around the sella and midbrain?
entries.answer: Use this map: suprasellar cistern above the pituitary; interpeduncular cistern between the cerebral peduncles; ambient cisterns wrapping around the midbrain and linking the suprasellar and quadrigeminal cisterns; quadrigeminal cistern behind the pineal gland and tectum beneath the splenium; cistern of the velum interpositum above the 3rd ventricle.

entries.question: Which midline infratentorial cisterns should anchor localization in the posterior fossa?
entries.answer: Prepontine cistern lies between the upper clivus and anterior pons; premedullary cistern extends from the pontomedullary junction to the foramen magnum between lower clivus and medulla; superior cerebellar cistern lies between the upper vermis and straight sinus; cisterna magna lies between the medulla and occiput below and behind the inferior vermis.

entries.question: How do you localize the paired lateral posterior fossa cisterns?
entries.answer: The cerebellopontine cistern lies between the anterolateral pons/cerebellum and the petrous temporal bone. The cerebellomedullary cistern extends from the dorsal margin of the inferior olive laterally around the medulla.

entries.question: What are the key fissures and their associated cisternal relationships?
entries.answer: The interhemispheric fissure separates the cerebral hemispheres; its inferior part contains the cistern of the lamina terminalis and its upper part the pericallosal cistern. The Sylvian fissure separates the frontal and temporal lobes anteriorly, courses laterally to cover the insula, and contains the MCA and middle cerebral vein.

entries.question: What are the key contents of the suprasellar cistern?
entries.answer: The suprasellar cistern contains the infundibulum, optic chiasm, and circle of Willis.

entries.question: What are the key contents of the interpeduncular cistern?
entries.answer: The interpeduncular cistern contains CN III, the basilar artery bifurcation, and the posterior thalamoperforating arteries.

entries.question: What structures define the ambient cisterns and their retropulvinar extensions?
entries.answer: The ambient cisterns wrap around the midbrain, connect the suprasellar and quadrigeminal cisterns, and contain CN IV, P2 PCA segments and branches, the SCAs, and the basal veins of Rosenthal. The retropulvinar cisterns are the lateral extensions of the ambient cisterns posterior to the thalami.

entries.question: What are the key landmarks and contents of the quadrigeminal cistern?
entries.answer: The quadrigeminal cistern lies behind the pineal gland and tectum, under the splenium, and between the cerebellar vermis and the colliculi. It contains the pineal gland, CN IV, P3 PCA segments, medial and lateral posterior choroidal arteries, and the vein of Galen with tributaries.

entries.question: Which features distinguish the cistern of the velum interpositum from the 3rd ventricle on imaging?
entries.answer: Cistern of the velum interpositum vs 3rd ventricle

entries.question: What are the key contents of the prepontine cistern?
entries.answer: The prepontine cistern contains the basilar artery, AICA, CN V, and CN VI and lies between the upper clivus and the anterior pons.

entries.question: What structures course through the premedullary and cerebellomedullary cisterns?
entries.answer: The premedullary cistern contains the vertebral arteries, anterior spinal artery, PICAs, and CN XII. The cerebellomedullary cistern contains CN IX, X, and XI as it wraps laterally around the medulla.

entries.question: What are the key contents of the cerebellopontine cistern?
entries.answer: The cerebellopontine cistern contains CN V, CN VII, CN VIII, AICA, and the petrosal vein.

entries.question: What are the key landmarks and contents of the cisterna magna?
entries.answer: The cisterna magna lies behind the lower medulla and upper cervical cord and below the cerebellar hemispheres; it is continuous with the spinal SAS. The vertebral arteries and PICAs normally traverse it, and the cerebellar tonsils often have dense trabecular attachments with tonsillohemispheric PICA branches nearby.

entries.question: What defines the superior cerebellar cistern?
entries.answer: The superior cerebellar cistern lies above the vermis and cerebellar hemispheres, between the upper vermis and the straight sinus, and connects with the ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns. It contains SCA branches and the superior vermian and precentral cerebellar veins.

entries.question: Which vessels normally travel in the interhemispheric and Sylvian fissures?
entries.answer: The interhemispheric fissure contains the falx cerebri with the inferior sagittal sinus and the ACA with branches. The Sylvian fissure contains the MCA from M1 through M3 segments and the middle cerebral vein.

entries.question: What common vascular variant can be seen near the basilar apex and interpeduncular region?
entries.answer: Duplication of the superior cerebellar artery is a common anatomic variant.

entries.question: Why can the cistern of the velum interpositum communicate with the quadrigeminal cistern?
entries.answer: The velum interpositum forms from folding/overgrowth of the cerebral hemispheres over the diencephalon, creating a double layer of tela choroidea (pia). If this potential space remains open posteriorly, it communicates with the quadrigeminal cistern and is termed a cavum veli interpositi.

entries.question: Why can Liliequist membrane matter for CSF flow and third ventriculostomy?
entries.answer: Because it is a true arachnoid partition spanning from the dorsum sella toward the mammillary/mesencephalic region; when anatomically complete it separates the suprasellar, interpeduncular, and prepontine cisterns, can obstruct CSF flow, and may require perforation during 3rd ventriculostomy.

entries.question: What normal Meckel cave relationship helps prevent overcalling it as an isolated cystic space?
entries.answer: CSF in Meckel cave normally communicates freely with the prepontine and cerebellopontine angle cisterns and contains trigeminal fascicles. Verify continuity with adjacent cisterns and the expected CN V location rather than treating it as a separate isolated collection.

entries.question: What is the normal communication pathway of the ventricular system, and where is bulk CSF resorbed?
entries.answer: Lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → 3rd ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → 4th ventricle → foramina of Luschka and Magendie → subarachnoid space; bulk CSF resorption is via arachnoid granulations near the superior sagittal sinus.

entries.question: Which structures should anchor a first-pass review of the ventricular system on routine MRI or CT?
entries.answer: Start with the visible CSF spaces in sequence: lateral ventricles, 3rd ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, 4th ventricle, then the outlets at Luschka and Magendie and the inferior obex. Once those anchors are set, place the recesses and choroid plexus relative to them.

entries.question: Where is choroid plexus normally expected, and where is it normally absent, within the ventricular system?
entries.answer: Expected: roof of the 3rd ventricle, body and atrium of the lateral ventricle, temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, and inferior roof/lateral recess region of the 4th ventricle. Absent: frontal horns, occipital horns, cerebral aqueduct, and foramen of Magendie.

entries.question: What are the key boundary anchors of the lateral ventricle on routine imaging?
entries.answer: Frontal horn: corpus callosum roof, caudate lateral wall/floor, septum pellucidum medial wall. Body: corpus callosum roof, dorsal thalamus floor, fornix medially, caudate body/tail laterally. Temporal horn: caudate tail roof and hippocampus along the medial wall/floor. Atrium is the confluence of the horns and contains the glomi of the choroid plexus; the occipital horn is white-matter lined.

entries.question: How do you anchor a normal 3rd ventricle review on imaging?
entries.answer: Identify the thin midline slit between the thalami. Anterior boundary: lamina terminalis and anterior commissure. Roof: tela choroidea and choroid plexus. Floor: optic chiasm region, infundibulum/tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, and midbrain tegmentum. Posterior boundary: pineal region with habenular and posterior commissures. Recesses: optic, infundibular, suprapineal, and pineal.

entries.question: How do you anchor a normal 4th ventricle review on imaging?
entries.answer: Find the diamond-shaped infratentorial ventricle along the dorsal pons and upper medulla. Roof: superior and inferior medullary vela. Walls/floor region: dorsal pons and medulla with adjacent cerebellar peduncles. Key outpouchings are the paired posterior superior recesses, paired lateral recesses, and the fastigium. It communicates with the subarachnoid space via Luschka and Magendie and continues inferiorly to the obex/central canal.

entries.question: What are the tela choroidea and choroidal fissure, and why do they matter on imaging?
entries.answer: The tela choroidea is a double layer of pia. The choroidal fissure is a narrow pial-lined channel between the subarachnoid space and the ventricles and is the lateral ventricular attachment site of the choroid plexus. On imaging, they matter because normal choroid plexus location reflects this attachment pattern.

entries.question: How can the foramina of Monro be localized safely on routine imaging?
entries.answer: First identify the frontal horns and the 3rd ventricle, then look for their connection at the junction of the lateral and 3rd ventricles. The anterior columns of the fornix descend toward the mammillary bodies and form the anterior border of the foramen of Monro.

entries.question: What is the obex, and why is it a useful inferior anchor for fourth ventricular review?
entries.answer: The obex is the inferior termination of the 4th ventricle in the upper cord; it marks the transition between the intracranial ventricular system and the central canal of the spinal cord.

entries.question: Which ventricular and choroid plexus findings are usually normal variants rather than pathology?
entries.answer: Ventricular variants include cavum septi pellucidi, cavum vergae, and cavum veli interpositi. Choroid plexus variants include calcification and xanthogranulomas, which may make the glomi look lobulated or cystic.

entries.question: What ventricular shape cues should reassure you on routine imaging, and what change should raise concern for obstruction?
entries.answer: Normal temporal horns are thin and crescentic, bounded medially by the hippocampi. The 3rd ventricle is usually thin/slit-like and narrow in transverse dimension. Frontal horn lateral margins are normally concave from the caudate nuclei. Rounding of the temporal horns or widening/outward convexity of the 3rd ventricle should raise concern for obstruction.

entries.question: What normal finding near the foramen of Luschka can mimic an enhancing mass, and what keeps you safe?
entries.answer: Normal choroid plexus may protrude through the 4th ventricular lateral recess into the medullary cisterns via the foramina of Luschka. This is an expected normal extension, not an enhancing mass.

entries.question: On coronal scans, which normal CSF spaces can be mistaken for the 3rd ventricle, and what keeps them separate?
entries.answer: The interpeduncular cistern and the thin linear interhemispheric fissure inferior to the frontal horns can be mistaken for the 3rd ventricle on coronal imaging.

entries.question: What flow-related pitfall can simulate an intraventricular mass in the ventricular system?
entries.answer: Spin dephasing from pulsatile CSF flow can mimic an intraventricular mass, including a colloid-cyst-type impression.

entries.question: Why can the cerebral aqueduct look either bright or dark on T2-weighted MRI?
entries.answer: The aqueduct contains CSF, which can give increased T2 signal, but pulsatile/high-flow CSF can also create spin dephasing and relative signal loss; the same normal channel can therefore appear bright or dark.

entries.question: Why is choroid plexus found only in specific ventricular regions?
entries.answer: Choroid plexus forms where the tela choroidea contacts the ependymal lining of the ventricles: roof of the 3rd ventricle, body and temporal horn of the lateral ventricle via the choroidal fissure, and inferior roof of the 4th ventricle. Because of that attachment pattern, it is not expected in the frontal horns, occipital horns, cerebral aqueduct, or foramen of Magendie.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: What is the basic map of the ventricular system and the normal CSF flow pathway?
entries.answer: Four communicating ependymal-lined CSF spaces: paired lateral ventricles, 3rd ventricle, and 4th ventricle. Normal flow: lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → 3rd ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → 4th ventricle → foramina of Luschka and Magendie → subarachnoid space. Bulk CSF resorption occurs via arachnoid granulations near the superior sagittal sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: What are the tela choroidea and choroidal fissure, and why do they matter in ventricular anatomy?
entries.answer: Tela choroidea is a double layer of pia formed during brain folding. The choroidal fissure is a narrow pial-lined channel between subarachnoid space and ventricle that serves as the attachment site of choroid plexus in the lateral ventricles. Together they explain where choroid plexus normally forms and attaches.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: Where is choroid plexus normally located within the ventricular system?
entries.answer: Normal locations: anteromedial body, atria/glomi, and temporal horns of the lateral ventricles; roof of the 3rd ventricle; inferior/posterior roof and lateral recess region of the 4th ventricle. Normal no-plexus zones: frontal horns, occipital horns, cerebral aqueduct, and foramen of Magendie.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: Why is choroid plexus found only in specific parts of the ventricles rather than throughout the ventricular system?
entries.answer: Because choroid plexus forms only where tela choroidea contacts ventricular ependyma: the roof of the 3rd ventricle, the body and temporal horn of the lateral ventricle via the choroidal fissure, and the inferior roof/lateral recess region of the 4th ventricle. It is therefore absent from the frontal horns, occipital horns, cerebral aqueduct, and foramen of Magendie.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: Which landmarks should anchor a first-pass review of the lateral ventricles on MRI or CT?
entries.answer: Find the paired C-shaped ventricles arching around and above the thalami, then orient by frontal horn → body → atrium → temporal horn/occipital horn. Use the septum pellucidum medially, caudate along the lateral margin of the frontal horn/body, thalamus in the body, and hippocampus along the medial temporal horn.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: What forms the frontal horn of the lateral ventricle?
entries.answer: Roof: corpus callosum. Lateral wall and floor: caudate nucleus. Medial wall: septum pellucidum. On imaging the frontal horns normally keep concave lateral margins from the caudate nuclei, and choroid plexus is not normally present here.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: What forms the body of the lateral ventricle?
entries.answer: Roof: corpus callosum. Floor: dorsal thalamus. Medial wall/floor: fornix. Lateral wall/floor: body and tail of the caudate nucleus. On axial and coronal imaging, the thalamus and caudate are the main deep-gray anchors for the ventricular body.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: How do you localize the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, and what is its normal shape?
entries.answer: Find the inferior/anterior limb of the C-shaped lateral ventricle. Roof: tail of the caudate nucleus. Medial wall/floor: hippocampus. The normal temporal horn is thin and crescentic; rounding should raise concern for obstruction.
