entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: What is the atrium of the lateral ventricle, and how does it differ from the occipital horn?
entries.answer: The atrium is the confluence of the body, temporal horn, and occipital horn and normally contains the glomi of the choroid plexus. The occipital horn is surrounded by white matter and normally contains no choroid plexus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: How do you localize the foramina of Monro on normal imaging?
entries.answer: They are the Y-shaped channels connecting the paired lateral ventricles with the 3rd ventricle. Use the transition from the lateral ventricular body/frontal horn region into the 3rd ventricle and the anterior columns of the fornix, which form the anterior border, as the key landmarks.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: What are the main boundaries of the 3rd ventricle?
entries.answer: It is a midline slit-like cavity between the thalami. Anterior: lamina terminalis and anterior commissure. Lateral: thalami. Roof: tela choroidea and choroid plexus. Floor: optic chiasm, infundibulum/tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, and midbrain tegmentum. Posterior: pineal gland plus habenular and posterior commissures.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: Which recesses of the 3rd ventricle are most useful to recognize on imaging?
entries.answer: Anterior/inferior recesses: rounded optic recess above the optic chiasm and pointed infundibular recess extending into the stalk. Posterior recesses: thin suprapineal recess and pointed pineal recess projecting into the pineal stalk.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: What are the key recesses and outlets of the 4th ventricle?
entries.answer: Posterior superior recesses are thin blind-ending pouches capping the tonsils. Lateral recesses curve anteriorly under the brachium pontis, contain choroid plexus, and communicate with the subarachnoid space via the foramina of Luschka. The fastigium is the dorsal pointed midline outpouching, and inferiorly the ventricle ends at the obex where it communicates with the central canal.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: Which normal ventricular shape clues argue against obstruction on routine MRI or CT?
entries.answer: Temporal horns should remain thin and crescentic. The 3rd ventricle should usually stay narrow/slit-like rather than widened or outwardly convex. The 4th ventricle should keep its normal diamond-shaped contour down to the obex.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: What normal finding in the region of the foramina of Luschka should not be mistaken for an enhancing mass?
entries.answer: Normal choroid plexus can protrude through the lateral recesses/foramina of Luschka into the medullary cisterns. Stay safe by confirming continuity with expected choroid plexus in the lateral recess and its expected location at the 4th ventricular outlet.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: What normal CSF-related imaging phenomenon can mimic an intraventricular mass?
entries.answer: Spin dephasing from pulsatile CSF flow can mimic a small intraventricular lesion such as a colloid cyst. The cerebral aqueduct may be barely visible and can show either increased T2 signal from CSF or signal loss from high flow, so an apparent focal abnormality should be checked across sequence and level.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: Why can the cerebral aqueduct appear either bright or dark on T2-weighted imaging?
entries.answer: Its appearance depends on CSF flow. Visible/slower CSF can contribute increased T2 signal, whereas higher-velocity flow can cause signal loss from flow-related dephasing. This is why the aqueduct may be barely visible or change conspicuity across studies and sequences.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: Which normal CSF spaces are common mimics of the 3rd ventricle on routine scans?
entries.answer: The interpeduncular cistern on coronal scans and the interhemispheric fissure/cistern of the lamina terminalis inferior to the frontal horns can be mistaken for the 3rd ventricle. Use adjacent landmarks such as optic pathways, anterior cerebral arteries within the fissure, and the expected midline ventricular boundaries to keep the spaces separate.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: CSF spaces::Ventricles and Choroid Plexus
entries.question: Why should the occipital horns be reviewed carefully even though they normally contain no choroid plexus?
entries.answer: The occipital horns are a common dependent site where subtle intraventricular blood may collect. On a normal review, knowing that choroid plexus should be absent here helps you notice unexpected dependent material instead of dismissing it.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What is the safest first-pass anchor system for localizing deep neck spaces on CT or MRI?
entries.answer: Above the hyoid, start with the paired fat-filled PPS and the airway: PMS is medial, MS anterolateral, PS lateral, and CS posterior; behind the mucosal tube lie RPS and then PVS. At and below the hyoid, shift to the central VS, with CS lateral, RPS posterior, PVS deepest/posterior, and ACS as the anterior inferior continuation of the SMS.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Which deep cervical fascial layers define the major deep neck spaces?
entries.answer: SL-DCF surrounds the MS and PS in the SHN and acts as the investing layer around neck structures including sternocleidomastoid and trapezius in the IHN. ML-DCF defines the deep margin of the PMS and circumscribes the VS. DL-DCF surrounds the PVS and contributes the alar fascia, which separates the true RPS from the danger space. The carotid sheath is formed by contributions from all three layers.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What makes the parapharyngeal space the key suprahyoid localization anchor?
entries.answer: The PPS is a paired prestyloid fat-filled space that extends from the skull base to the posterosuperior SMS. It lies between PMS medially and the MS/PS laterally, with CS posteriorly, and contains fat plus the pharyngeal venous plexus. Because it is centrally placed and fat-filled, its displacement pattern helps localize the compartment of origin of adjacent lesions.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: A deep neck lesion displaces the parapharyngeal space posteromedially. Which surrounding suprahyoid space is the most likely compartment of origin?
entries.answer: Masticator space; Pharyngeal mucosal space; Parotid space; Carotid space

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: How should the carotid space be localized above and below the hyoid?
entries.answer: In the SHN, the CS is poststyloid and posterior to the PPS; in the IHN it lies lateral to the VS and RPS. It begins at the inferior jugular foramen and carotid canal and extends to the aortic arch. Major contents include the carotid artery and internal jugular vein; at the hyoid and below, the main routinely emphasized contents are the common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: How do you localize the retropharyngeal space and danger space on routine imaging?
entries.answer: Localize the RPS posterior to the PMS in the SHN and posterior to the VS in the IHN. The true RPS lies anterior to the alar fascia and the danger space posterior to it; both course inferiorly, with fusion of the alar fascia to ML-DCF around about T3. On routine studies, use the anterior mucosal/visceral tube and the posterior PVS as the practical landmarks.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What is the key imaging pitfall when separating the true retropharyngeal space from the danger space?
entries.answer: Do not imply that the alar fascia is usually directly visible on routine CT or MR. It is typically too thin to see, so the true RPS and danger space are usually assigned by expected position; the plane may become more apparent when edema outlines it.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What structures belong to the perivertebral space, and how is it subdivided?
entries.answer: The PVS lies behind the RPS and around the spine from skull base to clavicle. DL-DCF completely surrounds it and sends a slip laterally that divides it into prevertebral and paraspinal components. The prevertebral component contains vertebral body, prevertebral and scalene muscles, veins, arteries, brachial plexus, and phrenic nerve; the paraspinal component contains posterior vertebral elements, levator scapulae, and paraspinal muscles.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: How does the visceral space organize the infrahyoid neck on cross-sectional imaging?
entries.answer: The VS is an infrahyoid-only compartment that extends into the mediastinum and is circumscribed by the ML-DCF. Superiorly it contains laryngeal and hypopharyngeal structures plus infrahyoid strap muscles; more inferiorly it contains thyroid, parathyroids, trachea, esophagus, recurrent laryngeal nerve, and paratracheal nodes.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What is the anterior cervical space, and what is its key continuity relationship?
entries.answer: The ACS is the inferior extension of the SMS into the infrahyoid neck. Recognizing that continuity helps connect the suprahyoid and infrahyoid maps instead of treating the ACS as an unrelated new space.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Which normal landmark helps prevent confusion between a parotid space lesion and a carotid space lesion near the parotid tail?
entries.answer: Use the posterior belly of the digastric muscle. At the mandibular body level it separates the parotid tail from the carotid space; posteromedial displacement favors a parotid-space lesion, while anterolateral displacement favors a carotid-space lesion.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What are the key imaging boundaries and practical implication of the buccal space? What are its contents?
entries.answer: The BS is bounded medially by buccinator, posteriorly by the MS, laterally by the PS, and anteriorly by superficial facial muscles and investing fascia; inferiorly it blends with the SMS. It contains fat, minor salivary glands, parotid duct, lymph nodes, facial veins, facial/angular/buccal arteries, and buccal branches of facial and mandibular nerves.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Which ultrasound landmark divides the sublingual space from the submandibular space, and how are the two spaces positioned relative to it?
entries.answer: The mylohyoid muscle is the key divider. The SLS lies deep to the mylohyoid plane, whereas the SMS lies superficial to it. On ultrasound, the sublingual gland is seen as a homogeneous hyperechoic structure lateral to the geniohyoid/genioglossus muscles, while the submandibular gland is recognized more laterally and sits astride the mylohyoid and posterior belly of digastric.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Why is Doppler useful in the submental region when a tubular structure could represent either vessel or duct?
entries.answer: Color flow within branches of the lingual artery confirms vessel and helps distinguish it from a dilated submandibular duct, which sits alongside the lingual vessels and may otherwise be mistaken for them on grayscale ultrasound.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What are the key ultrasound landmarks of the carotid sheath in the upper and midcervical neck?
entries.answer: At the upper cervical level, identify the internal and external carotid arteries and the internal jugular vein; at the bifurcation, the external carotid artery is usually more medial and smaller than the internal carotid artery. Below the bifurcation and in the midcervical neck, the main carotid sheath structures are the common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve; the vagus nerve usually lies between the artery and vein and appears as a small round hypoechoic nodule with a central echogenic dot. Deep cervical lymph nodes commonly lie along and anterior to these vessels and are normally elliptical with an echogenic hilum and hilar vascularity.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: How do you localize the brachial plexus roots in the lower neck on CT or MR?
entries.answer: First identify the prevertebral component of the PVS and the anterior and middle scalene muscles. The brachial plexus roots exit the neural foramina, pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles, and then enter the posterior carotid-space fat on their way to the axilla. At the thoracic inlet, the right subclavian artery also passes between the anterior and middle scalenes.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Why is parapharyngeal space displacement such a useful localizer for suprahyoid masses?
entries.answer: Because the PPS is a centrally placed prestyloid fat-filled space bordered by PMS, MS, PS, and CS from different directions. A lesion in one of those surrounding compartments pushes the PPS away in a predictable direction, making the displacement pattern a practical map of compartment of origin.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: Which landmarks should anchor a first-pass oral cavity review on MRI or CT?
entries.answer: Start with the oral tongue and floor of mouth, then find the mylohyoid sling, the paired submandibular glands below it, and the paired genioglossus muscles with the fatty lingual septum in the midline. Finally confirm the posterior oral cavity boundary at the palatoglossus/anterior tonsillar pillar and remember that the lingual tonsil and posterior third of the tongue belong to the oropharynx.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: How do you localize the sublingual space, and which spread pathways must be checked when a lesion is centered there?
entries.answer: Localize SLS as the deep oral tongue compartment superomedial to the mylohyoid and lateral to the genioglossus. Check for anterior cross-midline spread under the tongue frenulum and posterior spread into the superior SMS and inferior parapharyngeal space at the posterior edge of the mylohyoid.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: How do you localize the submandibular space, and what structures dominate it clinically and radiologically?
entries.answer: Localize SMS inferolateral to the mylohyoid, superior to the hyoid, and deep to the platysma. It is the only fascia-lined oral cavity space. Its dominant occupants are the submandibular gland and level I nodes, so most SMS masses are glandular or nodal in origin.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: What is the root of tongue on oral cavity imaging, and what finding suggests a lesion is primary to it?
entries.answer: ROT is the deep midline oral tongue above the mylohyoid sling and below the extrinsic tongue muscles. It is formed by the paired genioglossus muscles and the fibrofatty lingual septum. A lesion that bows the genioglossus muscles laterally away from each other should be considered primary to the ROT.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: What landmarks keep the oral cavity from being misextended posteriorly into the oropharynx?
entries.answer: The oral tongue is the anterior two thirds of the tongue; the posterior third is base of tongue/lingual tonsil and belongs to the oropharynx. The palatoglossus underlies the anterior tonsillar pillar and serves as the oral cavity-oropharynx dividing line. Caption support adds the circumvallate papillae as a useful superficial landmark of this transition.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: What makes the retromolar trigone a high-yield oral cavity subsite on imaging review?
entries.answer: The RMT is a small triangular mucosal region directly behind the last mandibular molar and is really the most posterior part of the alveolar ridge. Its importance comes from adjacency to the pterygomandibular raphe, a fibrous band connecting buccinator to superior pharyngeal constrictor from the medial pterygoid plate hamulus down to the posterior mylohyoid ridge region, creating a superior perifascial spread route.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: What three clinical questions drive most oral cavity CT and MR examinations?
entries.answer: Most oral cavity cross-sectional studies are performed for: 1) staging oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma and nodes, 2) searching for abscess and its cause, and 3) deciding whether a submandibular space mass is nodal or glandular.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: What is the fallback reading strategy when an oral cavity lesion is encountered without helpful clinical history?
entries.answer: Assign the lesion to its space of origin first—OMS, SLS, SMS, or ROT—then apply the space-specific differential framework. This space-first localization strategy is the core problem-solving approach for deep oral cavity lesions.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: Which muscles form the floor of mouth, and which one is the key separator of sublingual and submandibular spaces?
entries.answer: The floor of mouth is formed by the mylohyoid and geniohyoid muscles. The key separator is the mylohyoid, which forms the muscular sling that divides SLS above from SMS below and lateral.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: When a mass is centered in the submandibular space, what is the first practical distinction to make?
entries.answer: First decide whether the mass is arising from the submandibular gland or from the level IA/IB nodal chain. That distinction immediately shifts the differential into glandular versus nodal disease. If CECT is equivocal for a small gland lesion but clinical suspicion remains high, ultrasound or MR can be used as problem-solving exams.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: Why is enhanced fat-saturated MR considered superior to CT for staging oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma?
entries.answer: MR is less degraded by dental amalgam artifact and better delineates deep soft tissue extent and perineural tumor. That combination makes it a stronger exam than CT when the key question is how far the tumor extends beyond the mucosal surface.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: Why is contrast-enhanced CT with mandible and maxilla bone windows preferred for suspected oral cavity infection?
entries.answer: CECT readily shows abscesses in any oral cavity space, and bone windows better reveal common causes such as dental decay, apical cyst, mandibular osteomyelitis, and submandibular duct stone.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: What is the key routine-MR overcall trap when reviewing the oral cavity on a closed-mouth study?
entries.answer: Do not overclaim visualization of the oral mucosal surface or the small neurovascular contents of SLS and SMS on routine closed-mouth MR. The safer move is to anchor to the mylohyoid sling, paired genioglossus muscles, lingual septum, and the larger deep spaces, which are much better delineated.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Oral Cavity Overview
entries.question: What common boundary mistake can mislocalize a posterior tongue finding out of the oral cavity framework?
entries.answer: Do not label the lingual tonsil or posterior one third of the tongue as oral cavity. Use the anterior tonsillar pillar/palatoglossus boundary and the circumvallate papilla transition to keep posterior tongue-base and lingual-tonsil findings in the oropharynx rather than the oral cavity.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: How are the suprahyoid neck and infrahyoid neck defined, and which named spaces belong to each?
entries.answer: SHN extends from the skull base to the hyoid bone and includes the PMS, PPS, MS, PS, CS, BS, RPS, PVS, SMS, and SLS. IHN lies below the hyoid and includes the VS, PCS, ACS, CS, RPS, and PVS; several of these continue into the mediastinum.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What should anchor a first-pass review of the suprahyoid and infrahyoid neck on cross-sectional imaging?
entries.answer: Use the PPS as the central SHN anchor because it is paired and fat-filled, then place PMS medially, MS anterolaterally, PS laterally, CS posteriorly, and RPS/PVS posteriorly. In the IHN, start with the VS centrally, then localize CS laterally and RPS/PVS posteriorly; use prevertebral muscles and major vessels as the posterior and lateral truth landmarks.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Which 3 layers of deep cervical fascia organize the neck spaces, and what are their key radiologic roles?
entries.answer: SL-DCF surrounds the MS and PS in the SHN and invests the infrahyoid neck, enclosing sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. ML-DCF forms the deep margin of the PMS in the SHN and circumscribes the VS in the IHN. DL-DCF surrounds the PVS in both SHN and IHN, contributes to the carotid sheath, and gives rise to the alar fascia that separates true RPS from DS.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Why is the parapharyngeal space the key localization anchor in the suprahyoid neck?
entries.answer: The PPS is a bilateral prestyloid, fat-filled SHN space that extends from the skull base to the posterosuperior submandibular space. It is bordered by PMS medially and by MS and PS laterally, with CS and lateral RPS posteriorly. Because it is centrally placed and normally fatty, it is easy to recognize and its displacement pattern helps define the space of origin of larger SHN masses.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Why can displacement of parapharyngeal fat localize the space of origin of a suprahyoid neck mass?
entries.answer: The PPS sits centrally in the lateral SHN and is surrounded by the major paired spaces, so enlargement of one neighboring space pushes the fat in a characteristic direction. The displacement pattern therefore reflects which compartment is expanding rather than requiring the mass itself to stay neatly confined to one space.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What parapharyngeal space displacement patterns point to the major suprahyoid neck spaces?
entries.answer: PMS mass -> PPS laterally. MS mass -> PPS posteromedially. PS mass -> PPS medially. CS mass -> PPS anteriorly. Lateral RPS nodal mass -> PPS anterolaterally.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Which suprahyoid spaces have the key skull-base interactions, and what are the high-yield contacts?
entries.answer: MS has the broadest skull-base abutment and receives CN V3. PS relates to the stylomastoid foramen and CN VII. CS begins at the jugular foramen and carotid canal region and contains CN IX-XII. PMS abuts the basisphenoid / foramen lacerum region. PPS has relatively bland skull-base contact without a major critical structure at that interface.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: How are the retropharyngeal space and danger space organized longitudinally?
entries.answer: RPS lies posterior to PMS in the SHN and posterior to VS in the IHN. The alar fascia, a slip of DL-DCF, divides the anterior true RPS from the posterior DS. RPS begins at the clivus and extends to about T3, where the alar fascia fuses with ML-DCF; DS continues inferiorly into the mediastinum and down toward the diaphragm.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Why can retropharyngeal disease spread into the mediastinum?
entries.answer: At roughly the T3 level, the alar fascia fuses with the middle layer of deep cervical fascia, creating the classic fascial trapdoor. This permits material in the retropharyngeal region to enter the danger space, which then continues inferiorly into the mediastinum.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: How is the perivertebral space organized, and what are its key contents?
entries.answer: PVS lies behind the RPS and around the spine from skull base to clavicle. DL-DCF completely surrounds it and sends a fascial slip laterally to divide it into prevertebral and paraspinal compartments. Prevertebral PVS contains vertebral body, prevertebral and scalene muscles, vessels, brachial plexus, and phrenic nerve; paraspinal PVS contains posterior vertebral elements, levator scapulae, and paraspinal muscles.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What are the extent and major contents of the carotid space above and below the hyoid?
entries.answer: CS begins at the inferior jugular foramen / carotid canal region and extends inferiorly to the aortic arch. In the SHN it contains CN IX-XII, the internal jugular vein, and carotid artery. In the IHN, the major contents simplify to the common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What is the fascial composition of the carotid sheath?
entries.answer: The carotid sheath is a tricontributed fascial envelope: SL-DCF, ML-DCF, and DL-DCF all participate in forming it in both SHN and IHN.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What defines the visceral space, and what structures normally traverse it?
entries.answer: VS is an IHN space circumscribed by ML-DCF and extending inferiorly into the mediastinum. It contains the thyroid and parathyroid glands, trachea, esophagus, recurrent laryngeal nerve, and paratracheal nodes; at more superior infrahyoid levels it also includes laryngeal and hypopharyngeal structures and strap muscles.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Which normal landmark helps distinguish a parotid-space lesion from a carotid-space lesion?
entries.answer: Use the posterior belly of the digastric muscle. It separates the parotid tail from the carotid space, so its direction of displacement helps localize the lesion: parotid-space lesions displace it posteromedially, whereas carotid-space lesions displace it anterolaterally.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What ultrasound landmark divides the sublingual space from the submandibular space?
entries.answer: The mylohyoid muscle is the key divider: the sublingual space lies deep to the mylohyoid plane, whereas the submandibular space lies superficial to it.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What is the key normal landmark of the submandibular region on ultrasound?
entries.answer: The submandibular gland is the key structure because it is readily recognized by its homogeneous echotexture and it sits astride the mylohyoid and posterior belly of the digastric muscles.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: How does Doppler help avoid mistaking a lingual arterial branch for the submandibular duct in the submental region?
entries.answer: Color or power Doppler confirms flow within branches of the lingual artery, whereas the submandibular duct does not show arterial flow. Use Doppler when a tubular structure near the lingual vessels could be either vessel or duct.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: At the carotid bifurcation on transverse ultrasound, how can you usually distinguish the external carotid artery from the internal carotid artery?
entries.answer: The external carotid artery is usually smaller and more medial than the internal carotid artery at the bifurcation.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: On midcervical ultrasound, what normal structure can mimic a small hypoechoic nodular lesion in the carotid sheath?
entries.answer: The vagus nerve. It normally lies between the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein and appears as a small, round, hypoechoic structure with a central echogenic dot.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What is the usual normal ultrasound appearance of upper and midcervical deep cervical lymph nodes?
entries.answer: They are typically elliptical and hypoechoic with a preserved echogenic hilum and normal hilar vascularity.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: How do you localize the brachial plexus roots in the lower neck on cross-sectional imaging?
entries.answer: First identify the anterior and middle scalene muscles in the prevertebral component of the PVS. The brachial plexus roots lie between those muscles and then course laterally with the subclavian artery toward the axilla.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What are the key contents and fascial position of the posterior cervical space?
entries.answer: PCS lies between SL-DCF and DL-DCF, begins near the mastoid tip, and extends to the clavicle with most of its volume in the IHN. It contains fat, CN XI, and the spinal accessory nodal chain.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What structures define the pharyngeal mucosal space on imaging?
entries.answer: PMS is the mucosal compartment medial to the PPS and anterior to the RPS. It contains mucosa, minor salivary glands, the lymphatic ring, and constrictor muscles; at the nasopharyngeal level it includes structures such as torus tubarius and adenoids, and at the oropharyngeal level it includes the tonsillar pillars and palatine and lingual tonsils. Its deep margin is formed by ML-DCF on the nonairway side.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: Why can disease spread easily through the buccal space?
entries.answer: The buccal space does not have complete fascial coverings separating it from adjacent spaces. Because its boundaries are incomplete, disease can spread across it more readily than through fully fascially enclosed compartments.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Suprahyoid Neck Overview
entries.question: What anatomic feature allows disease to spread between the suprazygomatic and infrazygomatic portions of the masticator space?
entries.answer: There is no horizontal fascial barrier at the zygomatic arch, so the masticator space communicates across that level and disease can spread between its suprazygomatic and infrazygomatic components.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: Which posterior landmarks separate the oral cavity from the oropharynx on imaging?
entries.answer: The oral cavity is separated posteriorly by the soft palate, anterior tonsillar pillars, and circumvallate papillae. The lingual tonsil lies posterior to that boundary and belongs to the oropharynx, not the oral cavity.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: Which 4 regions should organize a first-pass oral cavity imaging review?
entries.answer: Use a 4-region framework: 1) OMS = central oral cavity proper plus lateral vestibules 2) SLS = non-fascial-lined space superomedial to mylohyoid 3) SMS = space inferolateral to mylohyoid 4) ROT = genioglossus-geniohyoid complex plus lingual septum.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: How do you distinguish the oral cavity proper from the oral vestibule on imaging?
entries.answer: The oral cavity proper is bounded by the alveolar arches, roofed by the hard palate and maxillary alveolar ridge, floored by FOM mucosa, and contains the mobile anterior two thirds of the tongue. The oral vestibule lies lateral to the oral cavity proper, with buccal mucosa laterally, gingival mucosa medially, and superior/inferior gingivobuccal sulci where buccal mucosa reflects onto maxilla and mandible.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: What is the key imaging landmark of the floor of mouth, and what spaces does it separate?
entries.answer: The mylohyoid muscle sling is the principal landmark of the floor of mouth. It separates the sublingual space superomedially from the submandibular space inferolaterally, except at its posterior free margin.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: How do you localize the sublingual space on routine CT or MR imaging?
entries.answer: Localize it by first identifying the mylohyoid and the paramidline genioglossus-geniohyoid complex. The sublingual space lies below FOM mucosa , superomedial to mylohyoid , and lateral to the genioglossus-geniohyoid complex . It forms a horizontal horseshoe beneath the oral tongue, communicates anteriorly beneath the frenulum, and empties posteriorly into the posterior SMS and inferior PPS.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: How do you localize the submandibular space on routine CT or MR imaging?
entries.answer: The submandibular space is the vertical horseshoe inferolateral to the mylohyoid and above the hyoid/anterior neck. It is bounded superficially by platysma, lined by the superficial layer of deep cervical fascia, contains the superficial submandibular gland, level IA/IB nodes, facial vessels, and anterior bellies of digastric, and continues inferiorly as the anterior cervical space. There is no vertical fascia dividing right and left SMS .

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: What forms the root of tongue on imaging, and where does it extend?
entries.answer: The root of tongue is formed by the genioglossus-geniohyoid complex together with the lingual septum . It extends inferiorly to the hyoid and mylohyoid sling and anteriorly to the mandibular symphysis at the genial tubercles.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: Why is the retromolar trigone and pterygomandibular raphe region a high-yield oral cavity landmark?
entries.answer: The retromolar trigone is the small triangular mucosal region behind the last mandibular molar over the anterior mandibular ramus and is an anatomic crossroads linking the oral cavity, oropharynx, soft palate, buccal space, floor of mouth, masticator space, and PPS. The pterygomandibular raphe lies beneath RMT mucosa, extending from the posterior mandibular mylohyoid line to the hamulus where buccinator and superior pharyngeal constrictor meet.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: Which oral cavity structures are best localized topographically rather than expected as crisply resolved routine CT/MR targets?
entries.answer: Do not expect the lingual nerve, distal CN IX, or CN XII to be uniformly crisp routine CT/MR targets. Instead localize them by the surrounding visible anchors: mylohyoid inferiorly, the genioglossus-geniohyoid complex medially, the anterior margin of hyoglossus posteriorly, and the sublingual gland/submandibular duct/deep submandibular gland laterally and centrally within the SLS.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: Which landmarks should anchor a first-pass axial review of the lower oral cavity?
entries.answer: Start with the central oral cavity proper and any lateral vestibular air . Then identify the mylohyoid sling , the paired genioglossus muscles and lingual septum , and classify what lies superomedial versus inferolateral to mylohyoid. Inferiorly, confirm the expected SMS occupants and borders: submandibular gland, digastric, and platysma.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: When is water distention preferable to puffed cheek for oral cavity imaging?
entries.answer: Prefer water distention when you need better evaluation of the dependent posterior tongue , posterior buccal/gingival mucosa , superior and inferior GBS , RMT , or the pterygomandibular raphe / medial pterygoid region . It is also better when severe submucosal or postoperative fibrosis prevents adequate air distention. It cannot be performed with an orocutaneous fistula and may be difficult with large flap reconstruction or edentulous patients.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: What are the best targets and main limitation of the open-mouth maneuver?
entries.answer: Open-mouth imaging helps small hard palate , soft palate , upper alveolus , retromolar trigone , and gingivobuccal sulcus lesions, and can also uncover some oropharyngeal lesions obscured by dental artifact. Motion artifact is common; a stabilizing device such as a syringe may be placed between the teeth.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: Why are small gingival, buccal, retromolar trigone, and oral tongue lesions often difficult to detect on routine CT/MR?
entries.answer: They are hidden by apposition of mucosal and tongue surfaces . Lips and cheeks lie against gingival surfaces of the maxillary and mandibular alveolus, and the tongue lies against the hard palate and lingual alveolar surfaces, so subtle focal thickening may not separate from adjacent normal mucosa on static imaging.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: Why does the puffed cheek maneuver improve oral cavity lesion conspicuity?
entries.answer: Air distends the oral vestibule and separates the buccal/labial mucosa from the gingival mucosa while also moving the tongue away from the hard palate and teeth. This better outlines the oral tongue and buccinator muscle and can reduce the practical impact of dental hardware artifact for anterior oral cavity lesions.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: What normal variant in the mylohyoid can mimic pathology in the floor of mouth?
entries.answer: The mylohyoid boutonniere is a cleft at the junction of the anterior one third and posterior two thirds of the mylohyoid muscle. It may be prominent and contain fat, vessels, and sometimes accessory salivary tissue, so it can simulate abnormal floor-of-mouth tissue if its expected location is not recognized.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: What maneuver-related pitfall can create pseudolesions in the posterior oral cavity and oropharynx during puffed cheek imaging?
entries.answer: An inadvertent Valsalva maneuver can distend the posterior oral tongue, RMT, and posterior GBS, but it may also elevate and posteriorly displace the tongue. That can partially obscure the posterior oral cavity and oropharynx and create pseudolesional appearances.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Anatomy Oral Cavity
entries.question: What normal posterior floor-of-mouth configuration can be mistaken for abnormal sublingual-space tissue?
entries.answer: The deep portion of the submandibular gland normally hooks around the posterior free edge of the mylohyoid and can plug the posterior sublingual space.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: Which structures should anchor a first-pass axial CT/MR review when assigning cervical lymph node levels?
entries.answer: Use the submandibular glands, SCM, carotid sheath/vessels, hyoid bone, cricoid cartilage, clavicle, and top of the manubrium as the core anchors; add the prevertebral muscles when localizing retropharyngeal nodes. The level map is created by drawing boundary lines along these structures separately on each side of the neck.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: How is level I defined, and how are levels IA and IB separated?
entries.answer: Level I lies below the mylohyoid, above the inferior margin of the hyoid, and anterior to transverse lines drawn along the posterior margins of the submandibular glands. Level IA contains submental nodes between the medial margins of the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles. Level IB contains submandibular nodes posterior and lateral to the medial margin of the anterior belly of digastric, around the submandibular gland.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: What is the practical axial rule for classifying level II nodes in the suprahyoid neck?
entries.answer: Level II extends from the skull base to the lower margin of the hyoid body, anterior to a transverse line along the posterior SCM border and posterior to a transverse line along the posterior submandibular gland edge. Within 2 cm of the skull base, a node lateral, anterior, or posterior to the carotid sheath is level II; a node medial to the ICA there is retropharyngeal rather than level II.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: What feature separates a level IIA node from a level IIB node?
entries.answer: A level IIB node lies posterior to the IJV with a visible fat plane between the node and the vein. A posterior node that directly contacts the IJV without an interposed fat plane is still classified as level IIA.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: Why is the hyoid bone such a high-yield landmark in cervical nodal level classification?
entries.answer: Its inferior margin marks the transition from level II internal jugular nodes above to level III nodes below. It also sits at the carotid bulb level, which helps explain why suprahyoid medial nodes are judged relative to the ICA while infrahyoid medial nodes are judged relative to the CCA/carotid bulb.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: How is level III localized on axial imaging?
entries.answer: Level III is the mid internal jugular chain between the lower margin of the hyoid and the lower margin of the cricoid cartilage. It lies anterior to the transverse line along the posterior SCM border and lateral to the medial margin of the CCA/carotid bulb; nodes medial to that carotid margin belong to level VI.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: What nodal-level transitions are marked by the inferior margin of the cricoid cartilage?
entries.answer: It separates level III internal jugular chain nodes above from level IV nodes below and also marks the inferior extent of level VA; below this point, posterior-chain nodes become level VB rather than VA.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: When should a lower lateral neck node be called supraclavicular rather than level IV or VB?
entries.answer: If any portion of the clavicle is seen on that side of the axial image, a node lateral to the medial margin of the CCA is classified as supraclavicular. If the clavicle is not yet visible on that side, the same lower lateral node is classified as level IV anteriorly or level VB posteriorly.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: How are levels VI and VII defined on axial imaging?
entries.answer: Level VI contains visceral-compartment nodes from the lower margin of the hyoid to the top of the manubrium, including prelaryngeal, pretracheal, and paratracheal groups; these nodes lie medial to the medial margin of the CCA/carotid bulb. Level VII contains superior mediastinal nodes between the carotid arteries from the top of the manubrium to the innominate vein.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: How do you localize lateral and medial retropharyngeal nodes on cross-sectional imaging?
entries.answer: Retropharyngeal nodes within 2 cm of the skull base lie medial to the ICA. Lateral retropharyngeal nodes sit on the anterolateral surface of the prevertebral muscles, just medial to the carotid space; medial retropharyngeal nodes lie in the paramedian retropharyngeal space and are less often seen.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: How should parotid and facial nodal groups be described in reports?
entries.answer: Parotid nodes are described as intraglandular or extraglandular nodes within the parotid fascia and drain to the upper internal jugular chain (level II). Facial nodal groups do not carry standard cervical level numbers and should be described by their anatomic location, such as mandibular, buccinator, infraorbital, malar, or retrozygomatic.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: What morphology and size rules define a normal cervical node on routine imaging?
entries.answer: Most normal cervical nodes are not visualized. When seen, they are usually oval and smoothly marginated, often with a central fatty hilum. Usual short-axis criterion in older adults is < 10 mm, with exceptions for slightly larger level II jugulodigastric and level I submandibular nodes; lateral retropharyngeal nodes should be < 6 mm; any visible medial retropharyngeal node in an adult is abnormal. Long-axis diameter is usually < 12-15 mm in levels II-III, although the jugulodigastric node may exceed 15 mm in younger adults.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: What is the expected MRI appearance of normal cervical lymph nodes?
entries.answer: Cervical nodes are characteristically low signal on T1, intermediate signal on T2, and more conspicuous on fat-suppressed T2 or STIR because surrounding fat is suppressed. A fatty hilum may be appreciable in benign nodes.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: What ultrasound features favor a benign or normal cervical lymph node?
entries.answer: Benign cervical nodes are typically ovoid or elliptical, hypoechoic, and contain an echogenic hilum. Power Doppler should show hilar vascularity; in reactive nodes, cortical hypertrophy may occur but the hilum and radiating hilar vascularity are preserved.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: Why can a normal-sized cervical node still harbor early metastatic disease?
entries.answer: Metastatic tumor cells arriving through afferent lymphatics are first deposited in the subcapsular sinus just beneath the outer cortex, so micrometastatic disease may be present before the node enlarges enough to exceed size thresholds. High-resolution ultrasound can help by interrogating this peripheral cortical region.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: Why do fat-suppressed T2 and STIR sequences improve cervical node conspicuity?
entries.answer: They suppress surrounding fat, which increases the visibility of smaller nodes around the carotid space and can also make adjacent lymphoid tissue such as lingual tonsil tissue more conspicuous.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: What normal-mimic pitfall can simulate a lateral retropharyngeal node after radiation, and what keeps the read safe?
entries.answer: Benign postradiation hypertrophy of the superior cervical sympathetic ganglion can mimic an enlarged lateral retropharyngeal node. It typically lies medial to the ICA at the C2-C3 transverse process level and shows a central black dot on axial postcontrast CT/MR and a central black line on coronal or sagittal images.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: What lower-neck mimic can be mistaken for supraclavicular adenopathy near the venous angle?
entries.answer: The distal thoracic duct on the left or the right lymphatic duct on the right can mimic supraclavicular lymphadenopathy because of their location near the carotid sheath and the internal jugular-subclavian venous angle.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: Which ultrasound features best separate a benign/reactive cervical node from a metastatic node?
entries.answer: Benign/reactive cervical node; Metastatic cervical node

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: What scan extent is recommended for cervical nodal staging in head and neck SCCa versus thyroid/cervical esophageal cancer?
entries.answer: For head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, scan from skull base to clavicles because neck SCCa does not normally drain into the mediastinum. For thyroid or cervical esophageal cancer, extend from skull base to the carina to include the superior mediastinum; MRI is preferred for thyroid cancer when iodinated CT contrast could interfere with I-131 radioiodine treatment decisions.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: Which named cervical nodes are especially high-yield, and why?
entries.answer: Jugulodigastric node: level II node just above the hyoid near the posterior belly of digastric; commonly larger than surrounding nodes and is the first sentinel node for the face, mouth, pharynx, and tonsils. Rouviere node: highest retropharyngeal node within 2 cm of the skull base. Delphian node: prelaryngeal/precricoid node, not normally identified on imaging. Juguloomohyoid node: level III node near the intermediate tendon of the omohyoid, classically linked to tongue drainage. Virchow (signal) node: lowest internal jugular chain node; if no neck primary is found, consider thoracic or abdominal primary carried via the thoracic duct, especially on the left.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
entries.question: If a lymph node lies across an axial boundary between two adjacent levels, how should it be assigned?
entries.answer: Assign it to the level that contains most of the node's cross-sectional area. The boundary lines themselves should be drawn separately for each side of the neck.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the basic shape and extent of the orbit?
entries.answer: A cone- or pyramid-shaped bony cavity extending from the orbital rim/orbital septum anteriorly to the orbital apex posteriorly.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: Which bones contribute to the bony orbit?
entries.answer: Frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, maxillary, palatine, ethmoid, and lacrimal bones.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: How are the orbital walls organized by bone?
entries.answer: Roof = frontal + sphenoid; medial wall = sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal, frontal process of maxilla; floor = sphenoid, palatine, maxillary orbital process; lateral wall = greater sphenoid wing near apex plus frontal and zygomatic bones anteriorly.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What are the key anatomic relationships of the orbit to adjacent skull base and sinus structures?
entries.answer: The orbit is superior to the maxillary sinus, lateral to the ethmoid sinus, and its roof forms the floor of the anterior cranial fossa; the apex lies at the transition between anterior and central skull base.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: How should you define the orbital base and apex on imaging?
entries.answer: The anterior base is the orbital rim peripherally with soft tissues centrally; the posterior apex is the crowded foraminal/fissural region where the orbit meets the skull base.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What fraction of orbital volume is occupied by the globe and by orbital fat?
entries.answer: The globe occupies about one third of orbital volume, while orbital fat occupies about one half.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What covers the intraorbital optic nerve?
entries.answer: Pia, arachnoid, and dura cover the optic nerve.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: How can the extraaxial optic pathway be segmented from posterior to anterior?
entries.answer: Optic tract → optic chiasm → cisternal optic nerve → intracanalicular optic nerve → intraorbital optic nerve.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: Why is the optic nerve sheath clinically and anatomically important as a normal imaging concept?
entries.answer: It is a dural reflection continuous with intracranial dura, linking the intraorbital optic nerve-sheath complex to intracranial meningeal anatomy.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: How do you define the intraconal and extraconal orbital spaces?
entries.answer: Intraconal space lies behind the globe within the conical boundaries of the rectus muscles; extraconal space lies outside that cone between muscles and orbital walls.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What practical imaging anchor defines the muscle cone?
entries.answer: The rectus muscles form a cone converging toward the annulus of Zinn at the apex, with the optic nerve-sheath complex centered in the intraconal space.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: Why is orbital fat one of the most important normal imaging landmarks in the orbit?
entries.answer: Normal orbital fat outlines the globe, extraocular muscles, optic nerve-sheath complex, and vessels, making compartmental localization practical on CT and MR.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the expected normal CT/MR appearance of the extraocular muscles?
entries.answer: They have density on CT and signal on MR similar to other skeletal muscle, and they normally show prominent gadolinium enhancement on MR.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the key normal relationship between the superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris?
entries.answer: The superior rectus lies inferior to the levator palpebrae superioris, and the levator courses above it anteriorly toward the eyelid.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the key normal distinction between the inferior oblique and inferior rectus on imaging?
entries.answer: The inferior rectus lies along the floor of the orbit, while the inferior oblique is a separate oblique muscle that can be seen in oblique cross section and should not be mistaken for the inferior rectus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the annulus of Zinn?
entries.answer: A tendinous ring formed by thickened periorbita at the orbital apex that passes over the optic canal and partially encircles the medial superior orbital fissure.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: Which key structures are associated with or pass through the annulus of Zinn?
entries.answer: The four rectus muscles, superior oblique, and levator palpebrae superioris arise from it; CN III, CN VI, the nasociliary branch of V1, and the optic nerve pass through the annular/apical region.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the optic strut and why is it a key orbital apex landmark?
entries.answer: The optic strut is part of the lesser wing of the sphenoid and separates the optic canal from the superior orbital fissure.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the typical origin and normal intraorbital course of the ophthalmic artery?
entries.answer: It is the first intradural branch of the ICA, enters the apex along the inferolateral aspect of the optic canal/optic nerve, then usually passes over the optic nerve and continues anteriorly along the medial orbit.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the normal course and drainage of the superior ophthalmic vein?
entries.answer: It forms medially from the angular and supraorbital veins, passes near the trochlea and medial to the superior oblique, crosses the anterior optic nerve region, then courses posteriorly along the superolateral border of the optic nerve to the superior orbital fissure and cavernous sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the normal imaging expectation for the inferior ophthalmic vein?
entries.answer: It is smaller and more variable than the superior ophthalmic vein, usually lies just above the inferior rectus, and may drain to the superior ophthalmic vein, directly to the cavernous sinus, or through the inferior orbital fissure to the pterygoid plexus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the periorbita and how is it continuous with surrounding tissues?
entries.answer: The periorbita is the dense connective tissue lining the inner orbital bones; it is continuous anteriorly with facial periosteum and posteriorly with the periosteal layer of dura through the orbital foramina and fissures.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: How should you think about the orbital septum on routine imaging?
entries.answer: It is a thin anterior connective-tissue barrier arising from orbital periosteum at the rim and inserting into lid structures; on routine CT/MR it is usually inferred rather than directly seen.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the function of Tenon capsule?
entries.answer: It is a fibrous connective tissue capsule surrounding the globe and separating it from retrobulbar fat; a potential space between Tenon capsule and episclera helps allow smooth ocular motility.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: How are the orbital and palpebral lobes of the lacrimal gland arranged?
entries.answer: The larger orbital lobe lies in the superotemporal bony fossa, while the smaller palpebral lobe lies inferiorly and is separated by the levator aponeurosis.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: Why is Whitnall ligament worth knowing in normal orbital anatomy?
entries.answer: It is a superior transverse suspensory ligament running from the trochlea to the lateral orbital wall, attaching to the levator aponeurosis and superior rectus and likely acting as a fulcrum for levator function.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: Why are the lacrimal fossa and lacrimal sac considered preseptal structures?
entries.answer: Because the medial orbital septum and medial rectus check ligament attach posterior to the posterior lacrimal crest, leaving the lacrimal fossa/sac anterior to the septal boundary.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: How should you interpret asymmetry in superior ophthalmic vein size on routine imaging?
entries.answer: The superior ophthalmic vein can be quite variable in size and may be normally asymmetric.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the expected normal postcontrast appearance of the optic nerve and its sheath?
entries.answer: The optic nerve itself should not enhance, but the optic nerve sheath dura may show subtle normal enhancement.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What CT technique is recommended for orbital evaluation?
entries.answer: Thin-section axial and coronal imaging (≤2 mm), multislice isovoxel acquisition with multiplanar reformations, soft-tissue algorithm plus bone windows in at least one plane.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What MR technique is recommended for dedicated orbital evaluation?
entries.answer: Use thin sections (about 3–4 mm), small field of view (about 12–16 cm), axial and coronal T1 precontrast, axial and coronal STIR or T2 fat-sat, and axial and coronal postcontrast T1 fat-sat; coverage should span roof to floor axially and back of pons through globe coronally.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: Why is a routine postcontrast brain MRI often inadequate for detailed orbital optic nerve evaluation?
entries.answer: Because dedicated orbital imaging needs thinner sections and fat suppression to evaluate the optic nerve and sheath well; routine brain protocols usually do not provide that detail.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the main role of ultrasound in orbital imaging?
entries.answer: Ultrasound is the first-line modality for intraocular lesions because it is noninvasive and readily available.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: What is the first major step in the imaging approach to an orbital lesion?
entries.answer: Localize it first: globe (intraocular vs transscleral), optic nerve vs nerve-sheath complex, intraconal vs conal vs extraconal orbit, lacrimal gland, isolated vs multifocal/transspatial process, and any direct intracranial extension.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
entries.question: After localization, what imaging features should be assessed for an orbital lesion?
entries.answer: Determine whether it is solid or cystic, whether it contains fluid, fat, blood, or soft tissue, whether it is well defined or infiltrative, whether there is bony remodeling or destruction, and the degree/homogeneity of enhancement.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What structures are included in the sinonasal region in this overview?
entries.answer: The sinonasal region includes the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, and surrounding structures. The named paranasal sinuses are maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: Which structures define the basic normal boundaries of the nasal cavity?
entries.answer: The nasal cavity is a triangle divided in the midline by the septum. Its roof is the horizontal cribriform plate, floor is the hard and soft palate, and lateral boundary is the lateral nasal wall with attached turbinates.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: How should the anterior and posterior openings of the nasal cavity be localized?
entries.answer: Anteriorly, identify the nasal pyriform aperture at the mucocutaneous junction level. Posteriorly, identify the posterior choana, which connects the nasal cavity to the nasopharynx.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What are the major normal components of the nasal septum?
entries.answer: The anterior septum is cartilaginous. The bony septum is formed by the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid posterosuperiorly, the vomer posteroinferiorly, and the maxillary crest along the undersurface.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What defines the normal pyriform aperture of the nose?
entries.answer: The pyriform aperture is the pear-shaped anterior bony aperture at the limen nasi. Its superior margin is the lower margin of the nasal bone, and its inferolateral margin is formed by thin sharp maxillary bone margins that curve medially to join the premaxilla at the anterior nasal spine.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: How do the turbinates organize the nasal meati on imaging?
entries.answer: The superior, middle, and inferior turbinates project medially into the nasal cavity. The region below and lateral to each turbinate is the corresponding superior, middle, or inferior meatus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: Which turbinate landmark points toward the natural sphenoid sinus ostium?
entries.answer: The tail of the superior turbinate points medially toward the natural ostium of the sphenoid sinus in the sphenoethmoidal recess, making it a very important surgical landmark.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: How does the basal lamella of the middle turbinate help organize the ethmoid sinuses?
entries.answer: The vertical portion attaches to the cribriform plate on coronal CT, while the middle and posterior portions extend laterally to the lamina papyracea on sagittal CT. Its lateral attachment separates anterior from posterior ethmoid air cells, which have separate drainage pathways.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What is the compact surgical sequence of the 5 obliquely oriented ethmoturbinal lamellae?
entries.answer: From anterior to posterior: 1st lamella = uncinate process; 2nd = ethmoid bulla; 3rd = ground/basal lamella of the middle turbinate; 4th = basal lamella of the superior turbinate; 5th = basal lamella of the supreme turbinate. The 3rd lamella is most important because it separates anterior and posterior ethmoid air cells.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: Which sinuses drain into the superior meatus and sphenoethmoidal recess?
entries.answer: The posterior ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses drain into the superior meatus at the sphenoethmoidal recess; this is the posterior ostiomeatal complex.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What structures make up the practical middle-meatus ostiomeatal complex map?
entries.answer: The key OMC structures are the uncinate process, ethmoid bulla, hiatus semilunaris, maxillary infundibulum, and middle meatus. The hiatus semilunaris is the semilunar region between the uncinate process and ethmoid bulla.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What normally drains into the inferior meatus?
entries.answer: The nasolacrimal duct drains anteriorly into the inferior meatus and is covered by the mucosal Hasner valve.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: Trace the normal drainage pathway of the maxillary sinus.
entries.answer: The maxillary sinus drains through its superomedial maxillary ostium into the ethmoid/maxillary infundibulum, then through the hiatus semilunaris into the middle meatus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: How do anterior and posterior ethmoid air cells differ in normal drainage?
entries.answer: Anterior ethmoid cells drain to the anterior recess of the hiatus semilunaris and middle meatus around the ethmoid bulla, with some drainage into the ethmoid infundibulum. Posterior ethmoid cells drain to the superior meatus and sphenoethmoidal recess.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: How does the frontal sinus normally drain?
entries.answer: The frontal sinus drains along the funnel-shaped frontal recess into the middle meatus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: Where does the sphenoid sinus normally drain?
entries.answer: The sphenoid sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess in the posterior nasal cavity.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What is the ethmoid bulla, and why is it a useful middle-meatus landmark?
entries.answer: The ethmoid bulla is a dominant anterior ethmoid air cell that protrudes inferomedially into the infundibulum or hiatus semilunaris, helping define the superior aspect of the ostiomeatal complex.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What structures form the ethmoid roof and olfactory fossa margin?
entries.answer: The ethmoid roof is formed superolaterally by the horizontal fovea ethmoidalis of the orbital plate of the frontal bone and medially by the vertical lateral lamella of the cribriform plate, just lateral to the horizontal cribriform plate of the nasal roof.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: How does the Keros classification stratify olfactory fossa depth?
entries.answer: Keros type I = 1-3 mm lateral lamella height; type II = 4-7 mm; type III = 8-16 mm. Increasing type means increasing vertical height of the lateral lamella and greater olfactory fossa depth.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What is concha bullosa in the sinonasal normal-variant map?
entries.answer: Concha bullosa is pneumatization of a turbinate, usually the middle turbinate.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: How do you localize an infraorbital ethmoid cell? Eponym?
entries.answer: A Haller cell is an ethmoid air cell that extends into the inferomedial orbital floor.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: Where is the agger nasi cell in the frontal recess map?
entries.answer: The agger nasi cell is the most anterior air cell and involves the lacrimal bone or frontal process of the maxilla. It forms an anteroinferior frontal recess landmark.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: Which air cells border the frontal recess anteriorly and posteriorly?
entries.answer: Anteriorly, the frontal recess is bordered by the agger nasi cell inferiorly and Kuhn cells superiorly. Posteriorly, it is bordered by the bulla ethmoidalis, frontal bullar cells, suprabullar cells, and supraorbital ethmoid cells.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What are the Kuhn frontal recess cell types described in the source captions?
entries.answer: Type I = single frontal recess cell above the agger nasi; type II = multiple cells in the frontal recess; type III = single cell reaching the frontal sinus; type IV = single isolated cell within the frontal sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What is the safest CT method to identify an Onodi cell?
entries.answer: Look for a horizontal septum in the upper sphenoid sinus on coronal CT, then trace whether the air cell is continuous with a posterior ethmoid air cell on sagittal or axial images. An Onodi cell is a posterior ethmoid air cell with prominent superolateral pneumatization and close optic nerve relationship.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: Why is the lamina papyracea a key normal boundary on sinonasal CT?
entries.answer: The lamina papyracea is the paper-thin lateral wall of the ethmoid sinuses and the shared wall with the orbit. It separates ethmoid air cells from extraconal fat and the medial rectus region.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: Which exits organize the pterygopalatine fossa around the posterior maxillary sinus?
entries.answer: The lateral exit is the pterygomaxillary fissure into the masticator space. The superior exit is the inferior orbital fissure. The medial exit is the sphenopalatine foramen into the posterolateral nose.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What is the key sinonasal relationship of the sphenopalatine foramen?
entries.answer: The sphenopalatine foramen connects the superior meatus/posterolateral nasal cavity with the pterygopalatine fossa lateral to it. The source notes it as the site of origin of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: How can the sphenoid lateral recess help localize foramen rotundum and the vidian canal on coronal images?
entries.answer: Use the lateral recess of the sphenoid sinus as the anchor: the vidian canal lies inferomedially in the sphenoid body, while foramen rotundum lies superolaterally.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What normal pathway connects the lateral hard-soft palate junction to the pterygopalatine fossa?
