entries.answer: Zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture displaced lateral orbital wall fracture bone fragment protrudes extraconal fat near the lateral rectus muscle Lateral orbital wall involvement is a key limb of a ZMC fracture and helps separate this pattern from a pure inferior orbital blowout fracture, which spares the lateral orbital wall. In the context of the same facial trauma pattern, this orbital wall component supports ZMC alignment injury. Differential: Complex midfacial fracture Transfacial (Le Fort) fracture Inferior orbital (blowout) fracture

entries.clinicalContext: 26-year-old man with facial trauma and swelling H2C7B4T9M6QZ
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture walls of the left maxillary sinus left zygomatic arch lateral orbital wall classic features The 3D image shows the classic multi-limb ZMC pattern, with concurrent involvement of the maxillary sinus walls, zygomatic arch, and lateral orbital wall. That combination fits a complete ZMC fracture better than an isolated arch fracture or other single-compartment orbital injury. Differential: Complex midfacial fracture Transfacial (Le Fort) fracture Zygomatic arch fracture Inferior orbital (blowout) fracture

entries.clinicalContext: 36-year-old patient with chronic facial asymmetry after prior trauma J5R8P2N7X4LK
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Remote zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture with enophthalmos left enophthalmos increased orbital volume remote fracture left lateral orbital wall zygomaticosphenoid suture The key chronic clue is enophthalmos from increased orbital volume together with a remote lateral orbital wall fracture at the zygomaticosphenoid suture, which is an important alignment landmark in ZMC injury. This supports prior ZMC malalignment rather than a new isolated soft-tissue process. Differential (Model-inferred; not listed in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx): Inferior orbital (blowout) fracture Silent sinus syndrome Naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture

entries.clinicalContext: 24-year-old man with facial trauma and cheek pain Q7M4N2P8R5TX [DD1]
entries.question: CT of the face. Based on the image, name 4 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
entries.answer: Complex midfacial fracture Transfacial (Le Fort) fracture Zygomatic arch fracture Inferior orbital (blowout) fracture

entries.question: Define Zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture.
entries.answer: Source definition: Fracture complex with fracture lines involving the zygomatic arch, lateral orbital wall, anterior and lateral walls of the maxillary sinus, and orbital floor. Boundary condition: This is a zygoma-based multi-limb midface fracture, not an isolated zygomatic arch fracture, pure inferior orbital blowout fracture, or Le Fort fracture. Synonyms: Trimalar fracture; tripod fracture; displaced ZMC fracture may be called quadripod or quadramalar fracture.

entries.question: Why can a displaced or angulated zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture produce enophthalmos?
entries.answer: A classic ZMC fracture includes the lateral orbital wall and orbital floor as part of the fractured zygoma-based complex. When the fracture is displaced or angulated, the zygoma rotates and the bony orbit enlarges, increasing orbital volume; the globe then sits farther posteriorly, producing enophthalmos. The article also notes that failure to restore alignment at the zygomaticosphenoid suture can leave rotational deformity and persistent orbital volume expansion.

entries.question: Why can the zygomatic arch component of a zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture cause trismus?
entries.answer: When the zygomatic arch is depressed as part of a ZMC fracture, it can mechanically impinge on the temporalis muscle or the coronoid process of the mandible. That impingement restricts mandibular excursion and produces trismus. This is why the arch component matters functionally even when attention is drawn to the orbital or maxillary components.

entries.question: Common pitfall: what does calling this a 'tripod fracture' risk missing, and what is the safety check?
entries.answer: Trap: Focusing on the 3 classic radiographic limbs and overlooking the lateral orbital wall / zygomaticosphenoid component. Safety check: On thin-slice CT, deliberately inspect the zygomaticosphenoid suture and lateral orbital wall for displacement, angulation, or telescoping. Key discriminator: A complete ZMC fracture is a tetrapod fracture involving 4 articulations. Why the error occurs: Older terminology came from radiograph-era pattern recognition and undercalls the posterior orbital component.

entries.question: Common pitfall: how do you avoid mistaking an isolated zygomatic arch or blowout fracture for a ZMC fracture?
entries.answer: Trap: Labeling any cheek or orbital fracture as ZMC without proving the full zygoma-centered fracture pattern. Safety check: Require combined involvement of the zygomatic arch, lateral orbital wall / zygomaticosphenoid region, and zygomaticomaxillary buttress / maxillary sinus wall complex. Key discriminator: Isolated zygomatic arch fracture lacks maxillary wall and lateral orbital wall involvement, while inferior orbital blowout fracture spares the arch and lateral orbital wall. Why the error occurs: The fractures are anatomically adjacent and all can follow blunt facial trauma.

entries.question: What proportion of facial fractures are zygomatic fractures?
entries.answer: 17% of facial fractures. Exam pivot: This is common enough that ZMC injury should stay high on the midface trauma differential.

entries.question: Which age/sex group is most commonly affected by zygomaticomaxillary complex fractures?
entries.answer: Teenage to young adult males. Exam pivot: In the typical trauma demographic, keep ZMC fracture high on the list when cheek projection, numbness, trismus, or orbital asymmetry are present.

entries.question: What is the most common mechanism of injury for a zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture?
entries.answer: Direct blow to the cheek (malar eminence), often during assault. Exam pivot: A cheek-directed impact should prompt an active search for the full ZMC fracture pattern rather than only an isolated arch fracture.

entries.question: Best CT protocol for suspected zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture?
entries.answer: Thin-slice 0.6-1.0 mm axial bone algorithm CT. Reformat in the coronal plane. 3D reformatted images are very helpful for displacement and angulation in surgical planning. Exam pivot: ZMC reduction depends on precise alignment assessment, so thin slices and multiplanar review matter.

entries.question: What 4 articulations are involved in a complete zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture?
entries.answer: Zygomaticofrontal suture at the lateral orbital rim. Zygomaticomaxillary buttress from the inferior orbital rim and floor through the maxillary sinus walls. Zygomaticotemporal suture along the zygomatic arch. Zygomaticosphenoid suture along the lateral orbital wall. Exam pivot: Think tetrapod, not tripod.

entries.question: Which landmark is most sensitive for evaluating overall ZMC alignment?
entries.answer: The zygomaticosphenoid suture. Displacement, angulation, or telescoping there is a sensitive sign of overall ZMC malalignment and rotational deformity. Exam pivot: If alignment looks equivocal elsewhere, check this suture carefully.

entries.question: Which sensory deficit is common in ZMC fracture, and how often does it occur?
entries.answer: Impaired sensation or anesthesia of the cheek / upper lip from infraorbital nerve injury; >90% of cases. Exam pivot: Cheek or upper-lip numbness strongly supports infraorbital nerve involvement in midface trauma.

entries.question: When is surgical exposure indicated for a zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture?
entries.answer: When the fracture is angulated or severely comminuted. Exam pivot: Degree of angulation and comminution directly affects fixation strategy and cosmetic / orbital restoration.

entries.question: Define frontobasal fracture.
entries.answer: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features: fracture involving the anterior skull base, especially the floor of the anterior cranial fossa, at the interface of frontal sinus, orbital roofs, cribriform plate, ethmoid roof, and sometimes planum sphenoidale. Boundary condition: It is a descriptive anterior skull base zone-of-injury diagnosis, not a single fixed fracture line or a complete report by itself. Synonyms: Anterior skull base fracture involving the frontobasal region

entries.question: Define frontal sinus posterior table fracture.
entries.answer: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features: fracture involving the back wall of the frontal sinus toward the brain. Boundary condition: It is the frontal sinus component that raises concern for communication with the anterior cranial fossa and dura; it is not equivalent to an isolated anterior table fracture. Synonyms: Posterior table frontal sinus fracture

entries.question: Define orbital roof fracture.
entries.answer: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features: fracture through the orbital roof, which is both the ceiling of the orbit and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa. Boundary condition: It is both an orbital fracture and an anterior skull base fracture when it creates orbit-intracranial communication. Synonyms: Superior orbital wall fracture

entries.question: Define cribriform plate fracture.
entries.answer: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features: fracture through the thin perforated bone where olfactory nerve fibers pass from nasal cavity to olfactory bulbs. Boundary condition: It is a high-risk anterior skull base fracture location for CSF rhinorrhea and olfactory injury; it is not just a routine nasal fracture. Synonyms: Cribriform fracture

entries.question: Define NOE fracture.
entries.answer: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features: naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture involving central midface structures including medial orbital walls, nasal bones, lacrimal bones, ethmoid complex, and often frontal sinus outflow region. Boundary condition: It is not only a facial fracture; it may extend into the anterior skull base and frontal sinus drainage pathway. Synonyms: Naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture; nasoorbitoethmoid fracture

entries.question: Define CSF rhinorrhea.
entries.answer: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features: CSF leak into the nasal cavity due to communication between subarachnoid space and sinonasal cavity. Boundary condition: It is an anatomic communication problem; routine trauma CT identifies risk features rather than directly proving active CSF flow unless specialized imaging is performed. Synonyms: CSF leak through the nose

entries.question: Define pneumocephalus.
entries.answer: No formal definition provided in source; operational definition derived from described features: intracranial air. Boundary condition: In frontobasal trauma it usually indicates communication between air-containing sinonasal spaces and the intracranial compartment; tension pneumocephalus is the emergency form with mass effect. Synonyms: Intracranial air

entries.question: Why is compartment communication the central mechanism in frontobasal fractures?
entries.answer: The frontobasal region is a thin junctional platform between frontal lobes, frontal sinus, orbits, ethmoid sinuses, nasal cavity, and anterior skull base. When trauma breaks the bony barriers, spaces that should remain separate may communicate: brain with sinonasal cavity, orbit with intracranial compartment, or frontal sinus with intracranial compartment. The imaging consequence is that small skull base defects, sinus opacification, pneumocephalus, orbital injury, and fracture trajectory become more important than simply naming the broken bone.

entries.question: Why do cribriform plate and ethmoid roof fractures raise concern for CSF rhinorrhea?
entries.answer: The cribriform plate and ethmoid roof form a thin central skull base barrier between the subarachnoid space above and the nasal cavity or ethmoid air cells below. A fracture crossing this region can create a dural/skull base defect, allowing CSF-containing intracranial spaces to communicate with the sinonasal tract. On routine CT, the radiologist does not directly see active CSF flow, but the mechanism explains why skull base defect, adjacent ethmoid or sinonasal fluid, and pneumocephalus are risk features.

entries.question: Why does pneumocephalus matter in frontobasal trauma?
entries.answer: Pneumocephalus is intracranial air. In frontobasal trauma, its presence usually means that an air-containing sinonasal cavity or frontal sinus has communicated with the intracranial compartment through a skull base or posterior table defect. The imaging pivot is not just the air itself, but the implication that a compartment barrier has been violated; therefore report amount, location, and any mass effect.

entries.question: Why can frontobasal fractures lead to delayed mucocele or chronic sinus problems?
entries.answer: The frontal sinus drains through the frontal recess into the middle meatus. If fractures involve the frontal sinus floor, anterior ethmoid region, or nasofrontal outflow tract, drainage can be obstructed even when the acute bony injury is the dominant finding. The imaging consequence is that the radiologist must inspect the outflow pathway because obstruction can later produce chronic sinusitis or mucocele formation.

entries.question: Why can cribriform plate fractures cause anosmia?
entries.answer: The cribriform plate is the perforated anterior skull base bone traversed by olfactory nerve fibers as they pass from the nasal cavity to the olfactory bulbs. A fracture in this region can injure or disrupt those fibers. The radiology pivot is that the nerve injury may not be directly visible, but the fracture location explains anosmia.

entries.question: Why can orbital roof fractures produce both orbital and intracranial findings?
entries.answer: The orbital roof is simultaneously the ceiling of the orbit and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa. A fracture can displace fragments inferiorly into the orbit or superiorly toward the cranial fossa and can create communication between the orbit and intracranial compartment. This explains why CT review must include the globe, retrobulbar hematoma, extraocular muscles, proptosis, optic canal/orbital apex region, pneumocephalus, and intracranial hemorrhage.

entries.question: What is the trap when reporting an anterior frontal fracture, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: calling it a frontal bone fracture and stopping there. Safety check: explicitly inspect and report posterior frontal sinus table, orbital roof, cribriform plate/ethmoid roof, nasofrontal outflow tract, pneumocephalus, intracranial hemorrhage, and orbital injury risk. Discriminator: a clinically meaningful report identifies violated barriers and complications, not only the named bone. Why it happens: the superficial frontal fracture is visually obvious, while small skull base defects can be subtle.

entries.question: What is the trap with frontal sinus fractures, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: treating anterior table and posterior table fractures as equivalent. Safety check: separate anterior table, posterior table, and both-table involvement in the report. Discriminator: anterior table is mainly cosmetic/structural, whereas posterior table is the wall toward the anterior cranial fossa and raises concern for dural/intracranial communication. Why it happens: both are frontal sinus fractures, but their risk profiles differ.

entries.question: What is the trap when reviewing the cribriform plate region, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: scrolling quickly through axial images and missing a subtle central skull base fracture. Safety check: use thin-section coronal bone images, compare sides, and trace the skull base from one orbit to the other. Discriminator: tiny cortical breaks, step-offs, asymmetry, ethmoid fluid, displaced ethmoid roof fragments, and intracranial air localize the risk. Why it happens: the lateral lamella/cribriform region is thin and fractures can be subtle.

entries.question: What is the trap with orbital roof fractures, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: treating the injury as only an orbital fracture. Safety check: inspect for intracranial communication, pneumocephalus, anterior cranial fossa fragment displacement, frontal lobe injury, and orbital compartment complications. Discriminator: the orbital roof is also the floor of the anterior cranial fossa. Why it happens: orbital findings can distract from the skull base role of the same bone.

entries.question: What is the trap with NOE trauma, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: focusing only on nasal bones and medial orbit while missing anterior skull base and frontal sinus drainage involvement. Safety check: inspect cribriform plate, ethmoid roof, frontal sinus outflow region, and medial canthal tendon attachment region. Discriminator: NOE trauma can extend into the frontobasal skull base and can cause traumatic telecanthus when the tendon-bearing central fragment is displaced or comminuted. Why it happens: the injury looks facial, but its consequences may be skull base and lacrimal/orbital.

entries.question: What is the trap when small pneumocephalus is present in frontobasal trauma, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: reporting only small pneumocephalus without explaining the communication it implies. Safety check: search for the adjacent skull base, posterior table, cribriform, ethmoid roof, or sinus roof defect and report location, amount, and mass effect. Discriminator: pneumocephalus indicates intracranial air and therefore a violated barrier. Why it happens: the air volume may be small, but the anatomic implication is high value.

entries.question: What is the trap with nasofrontal outflow tract involvement, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: undercalling outflow obstruction because it is not the most dramatic acute fracture finding. Safety check: inspect the frontal sinus floor, anterior ethmoid region, frontal recess, and nasofrontal outflow pathway when frontal sinus or NOE components are present. Discriminator: outflow involvement predicts chronic obstruction, sinusitis, or mucocele risk. Why it happens: acute trauma attention often goes to displaced fragments, hemorrhage, and pneumocephalus.

entries.question: What is the trap in high-energy combined craniofacial trauma, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: listing every fracture randomly without surgical organization. Safety check: group findings by surgical relevance: frontal sinus anterior table, posterior table, nasofrontal outflow tract, orbital roof, cribriform/ethmoid roof, pneumocephalus, intracranial hemorrhage, orbital compartment risk, and CSF leak risk. Discriminator: organized compartment-based reporting is more actionable than an unstructured bone inventory. Why it happens: complex trauma creates visual chaos.

entries.question: What are the three major barriers to assess in frontobasal trauma?
entries.answer: Brain to sinonasal cavity; orbit to intracranial compartment; frontal sinus to intracranial compartment.

entries.question: What is the frontobasal anatomy checklist?
entries.answer: Frontal sinus anterior/posterior tables; orbital roofs; ethmoid roof; cribriform plate; planum sphenoidale.

entries.question: What is the key frontal sinus question in frontobasal trauma?
entries.answer: Is the posterior table fractured? If yes, evaluate for intracranial communication, pneumocephalus, dural violation risk, intracranial hemorrhage, and displaced posterior table fragments.

entries.question: What is the main significance of an isolated anterior table frontal sinus fracture?
entries.answer: It is primarily a cosmetic/structural injury and does not necessarily create intracranial communication.

entries.question: What should be inspected when both frontal sinus tables are fractured?
entries.answer: Inspect the nasofrontal outflow tract because obstruction can lead to chronic sinus problems or mucocele formation.

entries.question: What CT findings should be sought in orbital roof fracture?
entries.answer: Depression into the orbit; elevation into the anterior cranial fossa; orbital hematoma; superior rectus/levator-related involvement; proptosis; globe injury; pneumocephalus.

entries.question: How should the cribriform plate and ethmoid roof be reviewed on CT?
entries.answer: Use coronal thin-section bone images, compare right and left, and trace the skull base from one orbit to the other.

entries.question: What findings raise concern for cribriform/ethmoid roof injury?
entries.answer: Tiny cortical breaks; step-off; asymmetry; displaced ethmoid roof fragments; ethmoid air cell fluid; intracranial air.

entries.question: Which anterior skull base region is described as especially thin and weak?
entries.answer: The lateral lamella of the cribriform plate.

entries.question: What complications should be considered when a fracture crosses the cribriform plate, fovea ethmoidalis, or lateral lamella?
entries.answer: Possible dural tear, CSF leak, anosmia, and meningitis risk.

entries.question: What are the suspicious fracture locations for CSF rhinorrhea in the source text?
entries.answer: Cribriform plate; ethmoid roof; sphenoid sinus roof; posterior table of frontal sinus; sometimes planum sphenoidale.

entries.question: What CT features identify risk anatomy for CSF leak?
entries.answer: Skull base defect; adjacent sinus opacification; pneumocephalus; fracture crossing a CSF-containing space.

entries.question: What should be reported for pneumocephalus in frontobasal trauma?
entries.answer: Presence, amount, location, and any mass effect.

entries.question: What orbital structures should be checked in frontobasal/orbital roof trauma?
entries.answer: Globe; lens position; retrobulbar hematoma; extraocular muscles; optic canal region; superior orbital fissure region; orbital apex.

entries.question: What is the key structure in NOE fractures?
entries.answer: Medial canthal tendon attachment; displacement or comminution of the tendon-bearing central fragment can cause traumatic telecanthus.

entries.question: Why do NOE fractures matter in a frontobasal report?
entries.answer: They can extend into the anterior skull base, cribriform plate, ethmoid roof, and frontal sinus drainage pathway.

entries.question: What are the five practical pattern groups for frontobasal fractures?
entries.answer: Frontal sinus table fractures; orbital roof fractures; cribriform plate/ethmoid roof fractures; NOE-associated anterior skull base fractures; complex craniofacial fractures.

entries.question: What should a complex frontobasal trauma report group by surgical relevance?
entries.answer: Frontal sinus anterior table; posterior table; nasofrontal outflow tract; orbital roof; cribriform/ethmoid roof; pneumocephalus; intracranial hemorrhage; orbital compartment risk; CSF leak risk.

entries.question: What is the recommended CT review sequence from the source text?
entries.answer: Brain/soft tissue windows; frontal sinus; orbital roofs; cribriform/ethmoid roof; planum sphenoidale/sphenoid sinus roof; orbits; face.

entries.question: What should be checked first on brain/soft tissue windows?
entries.answer: Frontal lobe contusions; extra-axial hemorrhage; subarachnoid hemorrhage; pneumocephalus; mass effect.

entries.question: What should be checked at the frontal sinus on bone windows?
entries.answer: Anterior table; posterior table; displacement; comminution; sinus opacification; outflow tract involvement.

entries.question: How should the orbital roofs be traced?
entries.answer: Trace each orbital roof from anterior to posterior and look for depression into the orbit or elevation into the cranial fossa.

entries.question: What posterior central skull base areas should be checked for extension?
entries.answer: Planum sphenoidale and sphenoid sinus roof.

entries.question: What facial fracture patterns should be searched for when frontobasal trauma is present?
entries.answer: NOE fracture; Le Fort pattern; zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture; nasal bone fracture; maxillary sinus wall fractures; pterygoid plate fractures.

entries.question: What is the best one-line mental model for frontobasal fracture imaging?
entries.answer: It is a zone of injury where frontal lobes, frontal sinus, orbits, ethmoid sinuses, nasal cavity, and anterior skull base meet.

entries.question: What wording makes a frontobasal fracture report clinically useful?
entries.answer: Specify involved structures and complications, such as posterior frontal sinus table, orbital roof, cribriform plate, pneumocephalus, sinus opacification, intracranial hemorrhage, orbital risk, and CSF leak risk.

entries.question: What phrase should not be the endpoint of the report?
entries.answer: Multiple facial fractures or frontal bone fracture without compartment, skull base, sinus outflow, orbital, and CSF leak risk assessment.

entries.question: What is the central reporting principle for frontobasal fractures?
entries.answer: The surgeon needs to know which compartments are connected, which barriers are violated, and which complications are likely.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: Wha is the asterisk
entries.answer: 31 : Supraorbital ethmoid cells. The supraorbital ethmoid cell (*) extend to the orbital plate of the frontal bone. The anterior ethmoid foramen (red arrows) is easily identified by pneumatization of the supraorbital ethmoid cell.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Interfrontal sinus septal cell. The interfrontal sinus septal cell (*) is located between the frontal sinuses. This cell drains into frontal recess (red dotted line).

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Fig. 34 : Posterior ethmoid cell (PC) and postreme ethmoid cell (PSC) The superior nasal turbinate (fourth basal lamella; yellow arrows in a, b) separates the posterior and postreme ethmoid cells. Posterior ethmoid cell can invade into the roof of the maxillary sinus behind the Haller cell (c, d).

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Onodi cells. Onodi cells (OC), or sphenoethmoidal cells, represent invasion of the postreme ethmoid cells above the sphenoid sinus. These cells can contact the optic nerve (a, b) and internal carotid artery(c). Pneumatization may extend to the anterior clinoid process (*

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Aspergillosis of the Onodi cell. Aspergillosis of the Onodi cell in a 60-year-old man with right visual disturbance. Right Onodi cell (*) invades the anterior clinoid process, with local inflammation (yellow arrows) involving the right optic nerve. As part of the ethmoid sinus, this structure should not be confused with the sphenoid sinus (**). Aspergillus was identified in the specimen postsurgery.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Frontal cells: Type 1 (a, b), Type 2 (c, d), and Type 3 (e, f). Frontal cells (*) are located above the agger nasi cells (AN). Frontal cells form the anterior wall of the drainage pathway from the frontal sinus (yellow dotted line), and encroach on the frontal recess or frontal sinus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Haller cells. Haller cells (red arrow) are located at the medial floor of the maxillary sinus below the ethmoid bulla (EB). When small, they may be similar appearance to the infraorbital canal (c, d). Due to their location next to the infundibulum, Haller cells may obstruct sinus drainage. (Uncinate process [*] posterior ethmoid cell [PC] Infraorbital canal [yellow arrow])

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Pneumatization of the crista galli. Anterior ethmoid cells extending to the crista galli.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Inflammation of the frontal bullar cells. Frontal bullar cells are opacified (*). The frontal sinus is clear because the frontal recess is not involved.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Suprabullar and frontal bullar cells. Suprabullar cells (Fig a, b *) do not extend to the frontal sinus in contrast to frontal bullar cells (Fig c, d **). The frontal recess may be narrow between the agger nasi cells (AN) and suprabullar or frontal bullar cells (b). (Ethmoid bulla [EB])

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Sinus lateralis (the lateral sinus of Grunwald, suprabullar recess, and retrobullar recess). The sinus lateralis(retrobullar recess, red dotted line, b-d) is the space between the ethmoid bulla (EB) and the third basal lamella (yellow dotted line). When ethmoid bulla dose not extend to the roof, the sinus lateralis continues to frontal recess (suprabullar recess, blue dotted line, c). The ethmoid bulla opens posteriorly into lateral recess (** in b). (Agger nasi cell [AN],suprabullar cell [*])

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Anterior and posterior ethmoid foramina. The medial notch of the orbit is a useful landmark for identifying the ethmoid foramen. The posterior ethmoid artery is located 10-12 mm behind anterior ethmoid foramen.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: Where does this defect most likely occur
entries.answer: Dehiscence of the lamina papyracea with medial herniation of orbital fat. Bony dehiscence occurs most often at the insertion of the basal lamella.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: 18 : Concha bullosa of the superior turbinate. Concha bullosa may occur in the superior turbinate, a structure derived from the fourth lamella. This variant may cause headache.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Attachment of the middle turbinate. The insertion of the middle turbinate can be divided into 3 parts. The first or vertical part attaches to the cribriform plate. The second or oblique part attaches to the basal lamella or lamina papyracea. The third or horizontal part attaches to the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone. These attachments help to stabilize the middle turbinate.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: 14 : Torus lateralis. The torus lateralis (green arrows) represents an ethmoid bulla without pnenumatization. (Agger nasi cell [AN])

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Ethmoid bulla. The ethmoid bulla (EB) is located in the anterior air cells and is usually the largest cell. EB is formed by pneumatization of the second basal lamella. (Agger nasi cell [AN], uncinate process [UP], sinus lateralis [SL], frontal recess [FR])

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Agger nasi cells. Agger nasi cells (green arrows) are the most anterior of the ethmoid cells. The agger nasi cells drain to the middle nasal meatus (orange arrows).The agger nasi cells are located posteromedial to the lacrimal sac and are the anatomical landmark for this sac during surgery.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.question: What is happening in here with the uncinate process and frontal recess
entries.answer: Four different attachments of the uncinate process. When the uncinate process attaches to ethmoid bulla or lamina papyracea (red arrows, a and b), the frontal recess opens directly into middle meatus. When the attachment is at the skull base or middle turbinate (red arrows, c and d), the frontal recess opens into the ethmoid infundibulum. Yellow dotted line shows drainage pathway. (Lamina terminalis (*))

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Sinonasal Overview
entries.answer: Pneumatized uncinate process. Pneumatized uncinate process (red arrow) is believed to represent extension of agger nasi cells. In this case, the agger nasi cell extends to the uncinate process (yellow arrow, c).

entries.question: Identify: recent trauma
entries.answer: T2-weighted MRI showing blood in the arterial wall and narrowing of the lumen of the left internal carotid. This is also known as the “crescent sign,” a hallmark of internal carotid artery dissection.

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: HNF1A-mutated hepatic adenoma Caption-derived keyword findings: subcapsular, encapsulated mass not very vascular almost isointense to background liver marked signal loss from the mass no retained contrast encapsulated, pale, tan mass with diffuse and focal lipid Fat-rich, encapsulated hepatic mass with opposed-phase signal loss and absent delayed gadoxetate retention fits the HNF1A-mutated subtype. The lack of retained hepatobiliary contrast is the key separation from FNH, while diffuse lipid supports this adenoma subtype. Differential: Focal nodular hyperplasia Hepatocellular carcinoma Hypervascular metastases

entries.clinicalContext:
54-year-old woman with abdominal discomfort T9W2K6RJ4XQ1

Gadoxetate is the contrast agent
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Hepatic adenoma Caption-derived keyword findings: slightly hyperintense to a normal-appearing liver no signal dropout from the lesion central scar is quite hyperintense mass is hypervascular retains less contrast material than normal liver encapsulated mass with blood pooling and foci of hemorrhage This case teaches the atypical FNH mimic problem: a hypervascular mass with a scar-like feature could suggest FNH, but reduced 20-minute hepatobiliary contrast retention and hemorrhagic pathology support adenoma. The source warns that a minority of adenomas can be iso- to hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase, so hepatobiliary signal is powerful but not absolute. Differential: Focal nodular hyperplasia Hepatocellular carcinoma Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma Hypervascular metastases

entries.clinicalContext: 35-year-old woman with right upper quadrant pain N4C8V2LP9MDA
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Inflammatory hepatic adenoma Caption-derived keyword findings: hepatic mass several hyperintense foci represent hemorrhage heterogeneous mass slight hyperintensity represent lipid increased enhancement in the nonnecrotic and nonhemorrhagic portions Hemorrhagic foci, heterogeneity, lipid, and enhancement of viable portions match the inflammatory subtype pattern described by the source, which is often hypervascular and may show hemorrhage. The teaching pivot is to recognize hemorrhagic hypervascular adenoma rather than treating the lesion as a generic hypervascular mass. Differential: Focal nodular hyperplasia Hepatocellular carcinoma Hypervascular metastases

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with abdominal pain H6R1Q8TZ5WPK
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Inflammatory hepatic adenoma Caption-derived keyword findings: very large, sharply demarcated, mostly homogeneous mass small focus of hemorrhage hypervascularity with enlarged vessels often encapsulated with focal hemorrhage encapsulated mass hyperintense foci central focus of hyperintensity A large sharply demarcated hypervascular mass with vessels, hemorrhage, and capsule/pseudocapsule fits inflammatory hepatic adenoma in this source. The discriminating pattern is a hypervascular heterogeneous adenoma with hemorrhagic components rather than a homogeneous FNH-type lesion. Differential: Focal nodular hyperplasia Hepatocellular carcinoma Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma Hypervascular metastases

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with abdominal pain A3L9D5XQ2VNR
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Hepatic adenoma Caption-derived keyword findings: brightly enhancing mass focal calcification solid mass with calcification capsule around the mass focal calcification a less common feature Arterial enhancement with a capsule and focal calcification is compatible with adenoma, while the source emphasizes that calcification is less common and ultrasound is not specific. This case is useful because it prevents over-reliance on a single modality or a single feature. Differential: Focal nodular hyperplasia Hepatocellular carcinoma Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma Hypervascular metastases

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?

entries.question: Define Inflammatory hepatic adenoma.
entries.answer: Source definition: Most common hepatic adenoma subtype, including lesions previously called telangiectatic hepatic adenoma, associated with oral contraceptives, obesity, and alcohol use. Boundary condition: It is an HA subtype with persistent hypervascularity and bleeding risk, not FNH despite possible mimicry. Synonyms: Inflammatory HA; telangiectatic HA legacy terminology.

entries.question: Define HNF1A-mutated hepatic adenoma.
entries.answer: Source definition: Second most common hepatic adenoma subtype, associated with diabetes and familial hepatic adenomatosis, characterized by diffuse lipid deposition within adenomas. Boundary condition: It is a fat-rich adenoma subtype, not focal fat or FNH. Synonyms: HNF1A-mutated HA; HNF-alpha 1 mutated adenoma.

entries.question: Define CTNNB1-mutated hepatic adenoma.
entries.answer: Source definition: Least common hepatic adenoma subtype associated with beta-catenin mutation, more likely in men, androgenic steroid users, metabolic syndrome, and glycogen storage disease, with highest malignant transformation risk. Boundary condition: It is a high-risk HA subtype, not conventional HCC, although malignant transformation can occur. Synonyms: Beta-catenin-mutated HA; CTNNB1-mutated HA.

entries.question: Define Hepatic adenomatosis.
entries.answer: Source definition: No strict definition; generally more than 10 adenomas, associated with glycogen storage disease, steatosis, and diabetes. Boundary condition: It is a multiplicity pattern of adenomas, not a separate malignant diagnosis. Synonyms: Adenomatosis.

entries.question: Define Focal nodular hyperplasia.
entries.answer: Source definition: Benign liver mass that contains Kupffer cells and biliary ductules and may be confirmed with sulfur colloid or HIDA behavior in the proper context. Refined operational definition based on the allowed source set: A benign hepatocellular lesion that typically homogeneously enhances and retains hepatobiliary contrast, used as the key benign mimic of hepatic adenoma. Boundary condition: It is not hepatic adenoma; presence of bile ductules/Kupffer cells explains uptake behavior. Synonyms: FNH.

entries.question: Define Hepatocellular carcinoma.
entries.answer: Source definition: Most common primary liver tumor, classically a hypervascular liver mass in a patient with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis until proven otherwise. Boundary condition: It is malignant and locally invasive; invasion, metastases, and tumor-in-vein distinguish it from benign adenoma when present. Synonyms: HCC.

entries.question: Why does hepatic adenoma usually lack HIDA uptake and hepatobiliary-phase retention compared with FNH?
entries.answer: Core and RadPrimer describe hepatic adenoma as hepatocellular tissue without bile ducts/bile ductules. HIDA uptake depends on biliary handling, and hepatobiliary-phase gadoxetate retention requires functioning hepatobiliary uptake/excretion behavior. FNH contains bile ductules and Kupffer cells, so it can show HIDA uptake and sulfur-colloid/hepatobiliary retention; adenoma usually lacks that machinery, so it shows paucity of HIDA uptake and often no substantial delayed gadoxetate retention. This mechanism is the key imaging discriminator between adenoma and FNH.

entries.question: Why does HNF1A-mutated hepatic adenoma show opposed-phase signal dropout?
entries.answer: The source states that the mutated HNF1A gene promotes lipogenesis and hepatocellular proliferation, producing diffuse lipid deposition within the adenoma. When fat and water are present within the same voxel, opposed-phase GRE T1 imaging cancels part of the signal, so the lesion loses signal compared with in-phase imaging. This connects the subtype biology to the practical MR discriminator: homogeneous intralesional fat favors HNF1A-mutated adenoma.

entries.question: Why can inflammatory hepatic adenoma show persistent hypervascularity and T2 hyperintensity/atoll-type appearance?
entries.answer: RadPrimer attributes persistent hypervascularity through arterial and venous phases to sinusoidal dilation, peliotic areas, and abnormal vessels. Those vascular/sinusoidal spaces create a hypervascular lesion and can produce T2 hyperintensity, including a peripheral atoll-type distribution in a subset of inflammatory adenomas. The imaging pivot is that this vascular inflammatory subtype can mimic FNH, so subtype risk factors and hepatobiliary-phase behavior must be checked.

entries.question: Why are hepatic adenomas prone to hemorrhage and why does size matter?
entries.answer: The source describes hepatic adenoma as a hepatocellular neoplasm with absent portal/central veins and bile ducts and scattered thin-walled unpaired vascular channels. This abnormal vascular architecture, combined with arterial supply and subtype-specific vascularity, explains why adenomas can hemorrhage or rupture. Larger lesions have more tissue and vascular substrate at risk, which is why incidentally discovered adenomas greater than 5 cm are usually resected and why hemorrhage is a central board complication.

entries.question: What is the pitfall when a hepatobiliary-phase liver lesion looks like FNH, and what safety check prevents the error?
entries.answer: Trap: Assuming hepatobiliary-phase uptake/retention always proves FNH. Safety check: Check for inflammatory HA risk factors and the full imaging pattern, because a minority of adenomas are iso- to hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase and inflammatory HA can mimic FNH. Key discriminator: FNH usually retains gadoxetate and contains bile ductules/Kupffer cells; adenoma often lacks substantial retention, but exceptions exist. Why it happens: Both lesions are hepatocellular and hypervascular, so hepatobiliary-phase behavior can overlap.

entries.question: What is the pitfall when a hepatic adenoma is found in a man or in glycogen storage disease, and what safety check prevents the error?
entries.answer: Trap: Treating all adenomas as low-risk benign lesions. Safety check: Identify malignant-risk factors: male sex, glycogen storage disease, anabolic steroid use, CTNNB1-mutated subtype, and size greater than 5 cm. Key discriminator: CTNNB1-mutated adenoma carries the highest malignant transformation risk and is relatively more associated with men and glycogen storage disease. Why it happens: The word adenoma sounds benign, but the subtype/risk context changes management urgency.

entries.question: What is the nuclear medicine pitfall in separating FNH from hepatic adenoma, and what safety check prevents the error?
entries.answer: Trap: Assuming sulfur colloid alone always separates FNH from adenoma. Safety check: Remember FNH can be variable on sulfur colloid, while HIDA helps because FNH contains biliary ductules and adenoma lacks bile ductules. Key discriminator: FNH should demonstrate HIDA uptake; hepatic adenoma usually shows paucity/lack of HIDA uptake. Why it happens: Kupffer-cell sulfur colloid behavior can vary, especially in FNH, so the bile-ductule-based HIDA discriminator is often cleaner.

entries.question: What is the sex distribution of hepatic adenoma stated by the source, and why does it matter?
entries.answer: Fact: 98% are seen in females; males are uncommon unless anabolic steroid use or glycogen storage disease is present. Exam pivot: A hepatic adenoma in a man should trigger higher concern for high-risk context and malignant transformation.

entries.question: What is the typical age group for hepatic adenoma stated by the source?
entries.answer: Fact: Young women in the childbearing age group, predominantly in the 3rd and 4th decades. Exam pivot: This demographic helps rank HA above HCC in a young noncirrhotic woman with a hypervascular hepatic mass.

entries.question: What proportion of hepatic adenomas are inflammatory subtype?
entries.answer: Fact: Inflammatory HA is the most common subtype, accounting for 40-50% of HAs. Exam pivot: Inflammatory subtype should be a default subtype consideration when a hepatic adenoma is hypervascular and hemorrhagic.

entries.question: What proportion of hepatic adenomas are HNF1A-mutated subtype?
entries.answer: Fact: HNF1A-mutated HA is the 2nd most common subtype, accounting for 30-35% of HAs. Exam pivot: Diffuse intralesional fat with opposed-phase signal dropout should raise this subtype strongly.

entries.question: What proportion of hepatic adenomas are CTNNB1-mutated subtype?
entries.answer: Fact: CTNNB1-mutated HA is the least common subtype, accounting for 10-15% of HAs. Exam pivot: Even though least common, it is the highest malignant-risk subtype, especially in men/steroid/glycogen-storage contexts.

entries.question: What percentage of patients with von Gierke type I glycogen storage disease have multiple adenomas according to the source?
entries.answer: Fact: Multiple adenomas occur in 60% of affected patients. Exam pivot: Multiple adenomas in glycogen storage disease should not be treated as a routine low-risk incidental multiplicity pattern.

entries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what is the key subtype/risk framework?
entries.answer: Inflammatory HA: most common; persistent hypervascularity; highest bleeding risk. HNF1A-mutated HA: diffuse lipid/opposed-phase dropout; least aggressive. CTNNB1-mutated HA: least common; highest malignant transformation risk. Unclassified: does not fit other subtype profiles. Exam pivot: subtype changes imaging expectations and risk stratification.

entries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what CT attenuation and enhancement pattern is expected?
entries.answer: Noncontrast CT: hemorrhage may appear as hyperdense foci; fat may be present; calcification is focal and about 5%. Postcontrast: typically arterial hyperenhancement, becoming iso- or hypoattenuating to liver on portal venous/delayed phases. Capsule: pseudocapsule/encapsulation may be present and can enhance late. Exam pivot: fat/hemorrhage and arterial hypervascularity support HA, but overlap with other hypervascular liver lesions remains.

entries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what MRI signal and enhancement pattern is expected?
entries.answer: T1WI: heterogeneous; increased signal from fat/recent hemorrhage; decreased signal from necrosis, calcification, or old hemorrhage. T2WI: heterogeneous; increased signal from old hemorrhage/necrosis; decreased signal from fat/recent hemorrhage. Postcontrast: heterogeneous arterial hypervascular enhancement; delayed pseudocapsule may be hyperintense. Exam pivot: MR is better than CT for lipid and hemorrhage.

entries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what gadoxetate-enhanced MRI behavior is source-supported?
entries.answer: Many adenomas show no substantial uptake or retention on delayed imaging. Up to 26% of adenomas are iso- to hyperintense to liver; 8% of FNHs may show hypointensity. Inflammatory HA can mimic FNH. Exam pivot: hepatobiliary-phase signal is highly useful but not absolute.

entries.question: For HNF1A-mutated hepatic adenoma, what MRI appearance is expected?
entries.answer: Diffuse lipid deposition within HA. Most evident as signal dropout on opposed-phase GRE T1WI due to homogeneous intralesional fat. Hyper- to isointense on T1WI; iso- to slightly hyperintense on T2WI. Only moderate arterial enhancement and no persistent venous/delayed enhancement. Exam pivot: homogeneous opposed-phase dropout is the subtype clue.

entries.question: For inflammatory hepatic adenoma, what MRI appearance is expected? What about percentages of some of the expected findings?
entries.answer: Persistent hypervascularity through arterial and venous phases. Iso- to mildly hyperintense on T1WI. Increased T2 signal, homogeneous or peripheral atoll distribution in 40% of cases. MR/clinical evidence of hemorrhage up to 30%. Exam pivot: hypervascular hemorrhagic adenoma with atoll-type T2 signal can mimic FNH.

entries.question: For CTNNB1-mutated hepatic adenoma, what MRI appearance is source-supported?
entries.answer: No distinctive MRI pattern is established. Usually hypervascular with evidence of hemorrhage or necrosis within tumor. Exam pivot: recognize the subtype mainly by risk context and malignant potential rather than a specific MRI signature.

entries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what sonographic appearance is source-supported?
entries.answer: Core: no specific ultrasound features distinguish adenoma from other hepatic masses; it may be hyperechoic, isoechoic, or hypoechoic. RadPrimer: complex heterogeneous hyper-/hypoechoic mass with anechoic areas; capsule may be seen. Color Doppler: hypervascular tumor, large peripheral arteries/veins, and intratumoral veins. Exam pivot: intratumoral veins are absent in FNH and can help distinguish adenoma.

entries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what nuclear medicine appearance is source-supported?
entries.answer: Tc-99m sulfur colloid: usually photopenic; RadPrimer states cold in 80% and warm in 20%. HIDA: usually lack of uptake because adenoma lacks biliary ductules; RadPrimer notes increased activity in some. Gallium: no uptake. Exam pivot: HIDA uptake favors FNH over adenoma because FNH contains biliary ductules.

entries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what are the key source-supported malignant transformation risk factors?
entries.answer: Male sex: 10x more frequent malignant degeneration than in women on a per-case basis. Concomitant glycogen storage disease; anabolic steroid use; CTNNB1-mutated subtype. Mass size greater than 5 cm. Exam pivot: these features change an adenoma from routine benign lesion to high-risk lesion.

entries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what are the main source-supported treatment pivots?
entries.answer: Adenoma less than 5 cm: observation and discontinuation of oral contraceptives or other steroids. Adenoma greater than 5 cm and near surface: surgical resection; consider transcatheter embolization. Any beta-catenin adenoma: resection independent of size. Pregnancy should be avoided due to increased rupture risk. Exam pivot: size, surface location, pregnancy risk, and beta-catenin status drive management.

entries.question: For hepatic adenomatosis, what threshold and consequence are source-supported?
entries.answer: No strict definition; generally more than 10 adenomas. May number more than 100 adenomas. Associated with glycogen storage disease, steatosis, and diabetes. May cause hepatic dysfunction and hemorrhage. Exam pivot: multiplicity can be a disease-risk framework, not just incidental multiple benign masses.

entries.question: For hepatic adenoma versus FNH, what is the key hepatobiliary/nuclear medicine discriminator?
entries.answer: FNH: contains Kupffer cells and bile ductules; may retain gadoxetate and demonstrate HIDA uptake. Hepatic adenoma: lacks bile ducts/bile ductules; often no delayed gadoxetate retention and paucity/lack of HIDA uptake. Exam pivot: FNH is usually the benign mimic to actively separate from adenoma.

entries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what is the best imaging tool recommended by the source?
entries.answer: Use a combination of chemical shift, T2, and T1 pre- and postcontrast MRI, with optional gadoxetate-enhanced MRI. Exam pivot: MR characterizes lipid, hemorrhage, enhancement, and hepatobiliary behavior better than a single CT or ultrasound feature.

entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Transient hepatic attenuation difference due to portal vein thrombosis Keyword findings: thrombosis of the posterior branch of the right portal vein compensatory increased flow through the hepatic artery ascites uniform enhancement of the liver portal vein thrombus Reasoning: Arterial-phase regional hepatic hyperenhancement occurs in the territory of a thrombosed portal vein branch, and the liver becomes uniformly enhancing on portal venous phase while the thrombus remains visible. This supports a transient perfusion abnormality from decreased portal inflow with compensatory arterial flow. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

entries.question: Define transient hepatic attenuation/intensity difference (THAD/THID).
entries.answer: Source definition: Transient increase in hepatic attenuation, or intensity on MRI, appearing as segmental wedge-shaped areas of enhancement during arterial-phase CT or MRI, which become isoattenuating/isointense during portal venous phase due to regional variations in the balance between hepatic arterial and portal venous blood flow. Boundary condition: It is a transient perfusion phenomenon, not a mass by itself; a separate underlying lesion may still be present. Synonyms: THAD = transient hepatic attenuation difference; THID = transient hepatic intensity difference.

entries.question: Why can decreased portal venous inflow produce THAD or THID?
entries.answer: In the arterial phase, iodinated contrast reaching the liver through the hepatic artery is normally diluted in the sinusoids by unopacified portal venous blood in an approximate 3:1 portal-to-arterial contribution. If portal venous inflow is decreased by segmental portal vein thrombosis, compression/occlusion by mass, extrinsic compression, or elevated sinusoidal pressure, the affected territory receives relatively greater arterial contribution. This produces arterial-phase regional hyperenhancement, which becomes isoattenuating/isointense once portal venous enhancement equilibrates in later phases.

entries.question: Why can increased arterial inflow produce THAD or THID?
entries.answer: Any process that increases hepatic arterial inflow can make a region of liver enhance more strongly during arterial-phase imaging. Source-supported causes include peripheral AP shunts in cirrhosis, hypervascular masses drawing increased arterial flow by sump or siphon effect, and posttraumatic or congenital AV fistula. The abnormality is transient because the portal venous phase restores more uniform parenchymal enhancement, so the perfusion territory fades relative to liver.

entries.question: How does SVC obstruction create medial left lobe or segment 4 THAD?
entries.answer: SVC obstruction can divert venous return through collateral pathways: subclavian vein -> internal mammary vein -> recanalized paraumbilical vein -> left portal vein -> medial left lobe/quadrate lobe -> hepatic veins -> IVC -> right atrium. This alternative venous inflow can densely opacify the medial left lobe or segment 4 during arterial-phase CT or MRI, producing a third-inflow THAD. The same collateral-flow physiology explains the hot quadrate/medial segment sign on Tc-sulfur colloid scans in SVC obstruction.

entries.question: Why can biliary obstruction produce a lobar THAD?
entries.answer: The source states that biliary obstruction or cholangitis can elevate sinusoidal pressure and regionally decrease portal flow. When portal inflow is reduced in the affected territory, hepatic arterial contribution becomes relatively more conspicuous during arterial-phase imaging. This produces a lobar or segmental THAD that fades when portal venous phase enhancement becomes more uniform.

entries.clinicalContext: 67-year-old man with midepigastric pain and weight loss C8M2L5Q7R9VX [BT1]
entries.question: What is the major pitfall on this case, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Calling the perfusion wedge the whole lesion and missing the small causative tumor. Safety check: Inspect the apex of every wedge-shaped THAD on portal venous-phase and arterial-phase images. Key discriminator: The THAD is wedge-shaped and perfusional, while the causative tumor is a small rounded lesion at the apex of the wedge/triangle. Why it happens: The perfusion abnormality can be larger and more conspicuous than the small mass that causes it.

entries.question: What is the major pitfall on this case, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Overestimating HCC tumor size by including adjacent THAD/perfusion abnormality as tumor. Safety check: Compare arterial and portal venous phases and separate the discrete tumor foci from the transient wedge-shaped perfusion territory. Key discriminator: The HCC masses show washout, while the THAD becomes less evident on portal venous phase. Why it happens: Tumor and adjacent perfusion abnormality can both be hypervascular on arterial phase.

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with chest discomfort H4Q7N2L9X5RK [BT3]
entries.question: What is the major pitfall on this case, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Misinterpreting medial left hepatic lobe enhancement from collateral venous flow as a hepatic mass. Safety check: Look for SVC occlusion, chest wall collateral veins, intrahepatic collaterals, and densely opacified medial segment/segment 4. Key discriminator: Third-inflow enhancement follows collateral venous pathways rather than forming a discrete spherical or oval mass. Why it happens: Alternative venous inflow can create focal hepatic hyperenhancement and nuclear medicine hot pseudolesions.

entries.question: For THAD, what CT appearance is expected?
entries.answer: - Arterial phase: peripheral wedge-shaped increased attenuation with straight margins. - Portal venous/delayed phases: becomes isodense and inconspicuous. - CT may show the cause: focal hepatic/perihepatic mass, portal vein thrombosis, or hepatic vein thrombosis. Exam pivot: If it persists or behaves like a mass, do not call it pure THAD.

entries.question: For THID, what MRI appearance is expected?
entries.answer: - Arterial phase gadolinium-enhanced MRI: areas of hyperenhancement. - Venous/delayed phases: becomes isointense to liver. - T2/DWI: no corresponding signal abnormality unless an underlying lesion is present. Exam pivot: Absence of a T2/DWI correlate supports vascular phenomenon rather than structural lesion.

entries.question: For THAD/THID, what ultrasound appearance is source-supported?
entries.answer: - Ultrasound: no corollary findings are expected. - Exception: contrast-enhanced ultrasound with microbubble contrast agent may show a correlate. Exam pivot: Do not invent grayscale or Doppler findings for THAD unless contrast-enhanced ultrasound is specifically being used.

entries.question: For THAD/THID, what nuclear medicine pseudolesions are source-supported?
entries.answer: - Tc sulfur colloid: hot accumulation in the left lobe/quadrate region can occur with SVC obstruction. - FDG PET/CT: hot accumulation can occur within a THAD. Exam pivot: Tracer hot spots caused by perfusion/third inflow can be misinterpreted as tumor.

entries.question: What are the three major mechanism buckets for THAD/THID?
entries.answer: - Decreased portal flow: portal vein thrombosis, mass compression/occlusion, elevated sinusoidal pressure. - Increased arterial inflow: AP shunts, hypervascular masses, AV fistula. - Third inflow: alternative venous supply such as gallbladder venous drainage or paraumbilical/paradiaphragmatic collaterals. Exam pivot: The enhancement pattern is the clue; the mechanism tells you where to search for the cause.

entries.question: What contrast timing/protocol details are source-supported for evaluating THAD/THID?
entries.answer: - Best tool: CECT with arterial and portal venous-phase imaging. - Arterial phase: 25-40 seconds after IV bolus. - Contrast: >100 mL volume and >=3 mL/sec injection rate. - Portal venous phase: 60-80 seconds after IV bolus. Exam pivot: The diagnosis depends on proving arterial conspicuity with venous/delayed fading.

entries.question: What is the diagnostic checklist pearl for a wedge-shaped THAD?
entries.answer: Look carefully for a small hepatic tumor at the apex of the wedge-shaped THAD. Exam pivot: The THAD may be the larger perfusion sign, while the true neoplastic cause may be a small rounded lesion at the apex.

entries.question: How do the main THAD mimics differ from true THAD?
entries.answer: - Hypervascular liver mass: spherical/oval, may wash out, and should be separate from THAD. - Focal confluent fibrosis: delayed-phase wedge with capsular retraction/volume loss, often segment 4. - Hemangioma: nodular discontinuous peripheral enhancement or flash fill, tracking blood pool. - Focal fatty sparing: high-attenuation normal liver in fatty liver, often segments 4A/4B near gallbladder fossa, more evident on nonenhanced CT/MRI. Exam pivot: Shape, phase behavior, and background liver separate perfusion from mimic.

entries.question: Which tumors are source-stated to invade or obstruct hepatic veins/portal veins in THAD-related cases?
entries.answer: Tumor invading or obstructing veins: hepatocellular carcinoma > cholangiocarcinoma > metastases. Exam pivot: Portal venous invasion/obstruction can create THAD and carries poor prognosis related to the underlying tumor.

entries.question: What phase behavior distinguishes THAD from a true hypervascular mass?
entries.answer: THAD is arterial-phase wedge hyperenhancement that becomes isoattenuating/isointense on portal venous and delayed phases; a true mass is spherical/oval and may persist or wash out.

entries.question: Define child abuse.
entries.answer: Source definition: Any act or failure to act by a parent/caretaker that causes harm or imminent risk of harm to a child. Boundary condition: This is a maltreatment/safety diagnosis, not a specific fracture morphology by itself. Synonyms/related terms: nonaccidental trauma or injury (NAT, NAI), child abuse and neglect, battered child syndrome, Kempe-Silverman syndrome.

entries.question: Why are posterior rib fractures highly specific for nonaccidental trauma in infants?
entries.answer: In the source-described mechanism, an assailant holds the infant with hands wrapped around the chest: fingertips contact the posterior ribs while thumbs are anterior. AP compression during squeezing and shaking levers the posterior ribs against the transverse processes. That force concentration produces posterior rib fractures, which are therefore the most common location and most specific rib fracture pattern for abuse. Imaging consequence: acute fractures may be difficult to diagnose, but healing posterior callus along multiple ribs becomes a highly specific radiographic clue.

entries.question: Why can acute pediatric rib fractures be occult initially but become visible on follow-up radiographs?
entries.answer: Acute rib fractures may show only a subtle vertical or oblique lucency in the rib short axis, and the line is often not visible when nondisplaced or when the fracture plane is poorly oriented relative to the x-ray beam. With time, fracture healing progresses through inflammation, soft callus, hard callus, and remodeling. Callus and subperiosteal new bone formation may become visible after 7-10 days, ranging from rib broadening to nodular or bulbous callus. Imaging consequence: follow-up skeletal survey can confirm suspected fractures and reveal additional fractures that were occult on the initial study.

entries.question: Why can costochondral junction fractures resemble classic metaphyseal lesions?
entries.answer: RadPrimer states that costochondral junction fractures disrupt the physis similar to a Salter-Harris injury. Because the anterior rib costochondral junction functions as a metaphyseal-equivalent growth-region injury, the acute projection-dependent appearance can resemble a classic metaphyseal lesion, including arcuate density, bucket-handle morphology, triangular corner fragment, fissure, or transverse lucency. With healing, sclerosis or growth disturbance can develop, including flaring, nodular enlargement, or cartilage invagination. Imaging consequence: the anterior rib injury should not be dismissed as a generic rib fracture when it has CML-like morphology.

entries.question: What pitfall should be avoided, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking normal rotated sternal ossification centers for true bulbous posterior rib callus on oblique radiographs. Safety check: Correlate location/projection with other views and problem-solving imaging when needed; in this case, bone scan confirms true right rib fractures and identifies additional medial left posterior rib fractures. Key discriminator: Sternal ossification centers are projectional normal structures, while true fractures show healing/callus or focal radiotracer activity. Why it happens: On oblique views, sternal ossification centers can project over posterior ribs and visually mimic callus.

entries.question: What false attribution should be avoided when evaluating pediatric rib fractures?
entries.answer: Trap: Attributing posterior rib fractures in a child to cardiopulmonary resuscitation by default. Safety check: Check fracture location and age; source states pediatric CPR-related rib fractures are very rare, less than 1%, and most involve anterior ribs. Key discriminator: Posterior rib fractures are highly specific for abuse, while rare CPR fractures tend to be anterior/lateral rather than posterior. Why it happens: Adult CPR experience can bias the reader toward an explanation that is not typical in children.

entries.question: What timing pitfall should be avoided when the initial radiograph is negative or equivocal?
entries.answer: Trap: Treating a negative initial radiograph as excluding rib fracture in suspected abuse. Safety check: Obtain follow-up skeletal survey at about 2 weeks, not before 10 days, when suspicion persists or concerning fractures are present. Key discriminator: Acute fracture lucency is often not visible, but callus/subperiosteal new bone formation may appear after 7-10 days. Why it happens: Acute nondisplaced fractures or unfavorable fracture-plane orientation can hide the fracture line until healing makes the injury visible.

entries.question: In children younger than 1 year with rib fractures, what proportion may be due to nonaccidental trauma?
entries.answer: Fact: Up to 82% of rib fractures in children younger than 1 year are from NAT. Exam pivot: In an infant, a rib fracture should strongly raise concern for abuse unless the history and alternative diagnosis are compelling.

entries.question: How often can rib fractures be the only radiographic manifestation of nonaccidental trauma?
entries.answer: Fact: Rib fractures can be the only radiographic manifestation of NAT in up to 29% of cases. Exam pivot: A rib survey miss can mean missing the only imaging evidence of abuse.

entries.question: How commonly are rib fractures present on skeletal surveys performed for suspected abuse?
entries.answer: Fact: Rib fractures are present in 10-14% of skeletal surveys performed for suspected abuse. Exam pivot: Rib review is a routine high-yield component of every suspected-abuse skeletal survey.

entries.question: In one study of abused children, what proportion of all fractures involved the rib cage?
entries.answer: Fact: 79% of all fractures involved the rib cage. Exam pivot: Rib fractures are a dominant skeletal injury pattern in NAT and deserve deliberate search on every relevant exam.

entries.question: How often is bruising present at the site of rib fractures in suspected nonaccidental trauma?
entries.answer: Fact: Associated bruising at the fracture site is rare, about 9%. Exam pivot: Absence of bruising does not meaningfully exclude rib fractures or abuse.

entries.question: What is the core imaging workflow for suspected child abuse with possible rib fractures?
entries.answer: Initial skeletal survey: children under 2 years with suspected NAT; children under 5 years with suspicious fracture; any noncommunicative child with concern for NAT. Follow-up skeletal survey: typically 2 weeks, not before 10 days, if fractures are concerning or suspicion persists. Problem-solving: Tc-99m MDP bone scan or F-18 NaF PET can complement radiographs. CECT: use for suspected intrathoracic or intraabdominal injury. Exam pivot: initial radiographs detect morphology; follow-up and complementary imaging catch occult/healing injury.

entries.question: For abusive pediatric rib fractures, what is the best radiographic diagnostic clue and favored distribution?
entries.answer: Best clue: bulbous callus or subperiosteal new bone formation of multiple adjacent posterior ribs in an infant. Favored distribution: posterior and lateral ribs, mid rib cage ribs 5-8, left greater than right. Exam pivot: multiple healing posterior/lateral rib fractures are much more concerning than an isolated nonspecific rib finding.

entries.question: What is the radiographic appearance of acute versus healing pediatric rib fractures in suspected abuse?
entries.answer: Acute: often not visible; when seen, typically vertical/oblique linear lucency in the rib short axis. Healing: callus/subperiosteal new bone after 7-10 days, from indistinct rib broadening to sharply marginated nodular/bulbous callus. Other clues: hole-in-rib lucency with sclerosis; rib head may show mixed sclerosis/lucency without subperiosteal new bone. Exam pivot: follow-up radiographs can make occult fractures visible through healing biology.

entries.question: For pediatric rib fractures in suspected abuse, what CT role and appearance are source-supported?
entries.answer: Role: CT may be performed for suspected thoracoabdominal injury, but is not advocated solely to identify rib fractures because of radiation exposure. Performance: CT has greater sensitivity than initial skeletal survey for rib fractures. Appearance: linear lucency, often in the rib short axis; callus and subperiosteal new bone formation with time. Exam pivot: review ribs carefully on CT already obtained for injury, but do not make CT the screening tool by default.

entries.question: For pediatric rib fractures in suspected abuse, what MRI appearance and limitation are source-supported?
entries.answer: Whole-body MRI sensitivity: low, 57%, for rib fractures versus radiographs. Possible appearance: fluid signal changes in bone marrow and soft tissues, with or without elevation of periosteum, before fracture is evident on radiographs. Exam pivot: MRI can show injury-related edema but is not the primary sensitive rib-fracture test in this source.

entries.question: For pediatric rib fractures in suspected abuse, what sonographic appearance is source-supported?
entries.answer: Sonographic features: discontinuity of echogenic shadowing cortex; acoustic edge shadow at fracture margin; local hematoma with elevated periosteum. Use: may show occult rib fracture in children when skeletal survey is negative or equivocal, especially cartilaginous portion. Limitation: patient cooperation may be an issue. Exam pivot: ultrasound is a targeted problem-solving tool, not a replacement for skeletal survey.

entries.question: For pediatric rib fractures in suspected abuse, what nuclear medicine appearance is source-supported?
entries.answer: Exam/tracer: Tc-99m MDP skeletal scintigraphy or F-18 NaF PET. Appearance: focal increased radionuclide activity within 24 hours; activity normalizes within 6 months. Limitation: costochondral junction fractures are difficult to assess because of variable physiologic uptake. Exam pivot: nuclear medicine is complementary/problem-solving, especially for occult or additional fractures.

entries.question: What F-18 NaF PET versus initial skeletal survey sensitivity data are stated for fracture detection in suspected abuse?
entries.answer: All fractures: PET 85%, initial skeletal survey 72%. Thoracic fractures: PET 92%, initial skeletal survey 68%. Posterior rib fractures: PET 93%, initial skeletal survey 73%. Exam pivot: PET is more sensitive for rib/thoracic fractures but has lower sensitivity for classic metaphyseal lesions.

entries.question: What radiography and bone scan diagnostic performance data are stated for pediatric rib fractures in suspected abuse?
entries.answer: Radiography sensitivity: 73% versus follow-up radiographs in one study; 26% versus postmortem histology in one study. Tc-99m MDP bone scan vs skeletal survey: among 60 rib fractures, 63% identified on bone scan and 73% on skeletal survey. Solitary rib fracture cases: 50% identified on both modalities; remaining 50% only on bone scan. Exam pivot: skeletal survey and bone scan are complementary, not interchangeable.

entries.question: What follow-up skeletal survey timing and yield are source-supported in suspected abuse?
entries.answer: Timing: typically 2 weeks from initial evaluation; not before 10 days. Indications: concerning fractures on initial study, or normal initial study with persistent clinical/imaging suspicion. Yield: one study clarified questionable fractures or identified new fractures in 48% of cases; most additional fractures were ribs. Exam pivot: follow-up skeletal survey is a core detection step for occult/healing rib fractures.

entries.question: What clinical/reporting action is required when imaging raises concern for child abuse?
entries.answer: Concern based on imaging must be conveyed to the referring clinician as soon as possible. The final report is a legal document and must be reviewed carefully. Multidisciplinary investigation may involve physicians, social worker, Child Protective Services, and legal authorities. Exam pivot: this is an urgent safety/reporting diagnosis, not a routine incidental fracture note.

entries.question: What mortality outcome pivot is stated for child maltreatment?
entries.answer: Fact: 1,770 fatalities from child maltreatment in 2018. Highest mortality group: infants younger than 1 year, 46.6% of deaths. Exam pivot: infant abuse imaging findings carry high safety stakes and require urgent communication.

entries.question: Radiographs. Based on the images, name 4 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
