entries.question: Define stress fracture.
entries.answer: Source definition: chronic, repetitive injury that leads to incomplete or complete fracture. Boundary: related source definitions separate fatigue fracture as abnormal stress on normal bone, insufficiency fracture as normal stress on weak bone, and stress injury as edema/periosteal reaction without a fracture line that can progress to fracture. Source attribution: RadPrimer article; no unsupplied Core-only framing retained.

entries.question: Define stress injury.
entries.answer: Source definition: Bone marrow edema or long-segment periosteal reaction without a fracture line; it can progress to fracture. Boundary: It is a pre-fracture or no-line stress spectrum finding, not a visible fracture-line diagnosis. Synonyms: bone stress injury spectrum when used broadly.

entries.question: Define fatigue fracture.
entries.answer: Source definition: Fracture due to abnormal stress on normal bone. Boundary: It is the normal-bone side of the stress-fracture spectrum, not normal stress on weak bone. Synonyms: stress fracture is often used clinically as a near-synonym.

entries.question: Define insufficiency fracture.
entries.answer: Source definition: Fracture due to normal stress on weak or abnormal bone. Boundary: It is the weak-bone side of the stress-fracture spectrum, not abnormal stress on normal bone. Synonyms: none needed.

entries.question: Why can repetitive loading progress from stress injury to a visible fracture line?
entries.answer: The source defines stress injury as bone marrow edema or long-segment periosteal reaction without a fracture line and states it can progress to fracture. Mechanism framed from the source: repetitive loading first produces edema/periosteal repair response; with continued stress, the injury can organize into an incomplete or complete fracture line. Imaging consequence: early radiographs may show only focal periosteal reaction, while MRI may show marrow edema before or around a low-signal fracture line.

entries.question: Why can a healing stress fracture appear as a sclerotic band on radiographs?
entries.answer: The source states that a healing stress fracture often develops a thick sclerotic band due to callus. Mechanistically within the allowed source set, the fracture site undergoes repair: callus and sclerosis accumulate along the stressed fracture plane, so radiographs may show a sclerotic band rather than a conspicuous lucent gap. In the calcaneus, the source-described band is typically oriented perpendicular to the primary trabeculae, which explains why a subtle heel radiograph can still reveal the diagnosis when the band orientation is recognized.

entries.question: What early-radiograph pitfall can lead to a miss, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Calling the study negative because no fracture line is visible. Safety check: Actively inspect for focal periosteal reaction and compare all projections, including the lateral view for dorsal soft-tissue swelling in metatarsal cases. Key discriminator: The source states focal periosteal reaction is often the earliest radiographic sign and that dorsal soft-tissue swelling on lateral view may be the only clue to metatarsal stress fracture. Why it happens: Early stress fracture may be radiographically insensitive, so the indirect repair/inflammatory clues appear before the fracture line.

entries.question: What search-pattern pitfall can cause an early navicular case to be missed, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Missing an early navicular stress fracture because the abnormality is small and dorsal. Safety check: Search the most dorsal long-axis images through the navicular and the dorsal margin of the navicular on short-axis images. Key discriminator: RadPrimer states early navicular stress fracture is easily missed and almost always originates at the dorsal, proximal cortex. Why it happens: The early fracture begins dorsally and may be conspicuous only on the correct image plane/location, while the site is high risk for nonunion and osteonecrosis.

entries.question: What MRI pitfall occurs when edema is obvious but a line is not, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Stopping at marrow edema and failing to search for the fracture line. Safety check: Review other planes and use the correct plane/high-resolution imaging when the edema pattern is suspicious. Key discriminator: The source states the fracture line may not be visible if the correct plane and high resolution are not used, and a calcaneal case notes florid edema should prompt a search for fracture in other planes. Why it happens: The low-signal fracture line can be plane-dependent, while marrow edema is more diffuse and easier to see.

entries.question: What are the most common source-stated locations for ankle/foot stress fracture?
entries.answer: Fact: most common in the distal tibia, calcaneus, and 1st-4th metatarsals; the body and low-risk sections specify posteromedial distal tibia, while the key-facts section contains an internal anteromedial/posteromedial wording mismatch. Scope: stress fracture can occur in any bone of the foot and ankle. Exam pivot: location also drives nonunion risk and management intensity.

entries.question: Which patient groups are source-stated risk groups for ankle/foot stress fracture?
entries.answer: Fact: Athletes or military recruits who rapidly increase mileage or training intensity; osteopenic patients including postmenopausal patients and female athlete triad. Exam pivot: These groups raise the pretest probability when early radiographs are subtle or negative.

entries.question: For ankle/foot stress fracture, what radiographic findings are expected?
entries.answer: Radiographs: insensitive early. Earliest sign: focal periosteal reaction, often subtle. Metatarsal clue: dorsal soft-tissue swelling on lateral view may be the only clue. Most reliable sign: sclerotic band perpendicular to the long axis of bone. Exam pivot: Do not require a visible fracture line on early radiographs.

entries.question: For ankle/foot stress fracture, what MR appearance is expected?
entries.answer: MR: jagged, irregular low-signal fracture line, incomplete or complete. Surrounding marrow edema may be feathery, stellate, or band-like and can be extensive. In metatarsals, edema often involves the majority of the bone. Exam pivot: A missing line does not exclude fracture if the correct plane/high resolution was not used.

entries.question: For ankle/foot stress fracture, what CT appearance is expected?
entries.answer: CT: sclerotic or lucent line, incomplete or complete. Performance hierarchy stated by source: more sensitive than radiographs, less sensitive than MR. Exam pivot: CT can help when small bones such as sesamoids need separation of stress fracture, stress response, and osteoarthritis-related edema.

entries.question: For ankle/foot stress fracture, what nuclear medicine appearance is expected?
entries.answer: Bone scan: focal abnormal increased uptake in one or more bones of the foot. Morphology: may or may not be linear. Timing: uptake may take up to 48 hours after injury to manifest. Technique pivot: pinhole collimation is useful for better anatomic detail. Source attribution: RadPrimer article; unsupplied Core three-phase bone-scan language removed.

entries.question: For ankle/foot stress fracture, what is the low-risk versus high-risk site framework?
entries.answer: Low risk for nonunion: posteromedial distal tibia, calcaneus, 1st-4th MTs. High risk for nonunion: anterior distal tibial cortex, navicular, 5th MT base, medial malleolus, hallux sesamoids, talus. Exam pivot: Site determines how aggressively weightbearing restriction and surgical consideration enter the report/management discussion.

entries.question: What management pivot separates low-risk from high-risk ankle/foot stress fractures?
entries.answer: Low-risk fractures: activity modification and continued weightbearing. High-risk fractures: restricted weightbearing and possibly surgery. Exam pivot: The same diagnosis carries different management urgency depending on location.

entries.question: What imaging checklist helps avoid missing early navicular stress fracture?
entries.answer: Look on the most dorsal long-axis images through the navicular. Also check the dorsal margin of the navicular on short-axis images. Typical origin: dorsal, proximal cortex with progression distally and plantarly. Exam pivot: Navicular is a high-risk site and may progress to osteonecrosis.

entries.question: How does the source distinguish stress response from stress fracture?
entries.answer: Stress response: periosteal edema +/- bone marrow edema without fracture line. Stress fracture: fracture line is present, though it may be occult if the correct plane/high resolution is not used. Metatarsal pivot: edema in a metatarsal should be treated as stress fracture regardless of whether the fracture line is seen.

entries.question: What findings favor osteomyelitis over ankle/foot stress fracture in the source differential?
entries.answer: Osteomyelitis clues: skin ulcer and sinus tract extending to bone. Marrow edema: confluent and rounded. Soft tissues: surrounding inflammation +/- abscess. Exam pivot: Do not overcall infection from edema alone without the source-supported soft-tissue/ulcer pathway.

entries.question: What activity-specific ankle/foot stress fracture locations are source-stated?
entries.answer: Runners: posteromedial distal tibia, distal fibula, navicular. Dancers: metatarsal shafts or bases, distal anterior tibia. Jumpers: distal anterior tibia, calcaneus. Exam pivot: Activity can help target the search pattern without replacing imaging diagnosis.

entries.question: What stress-fracture locations are highlighted by this foot graphic?
entries.answer: Stress-fracture site map Highlighted sites: posterior calcaneal process, cuboid, proximal 5th metatarsal shaft, and necks of the 2nd-4th metatarsals. Other typical sites named by the caption but not shown: talar neck, navicular, and 1st toe sesamoids. Teaching pivot: the graphic broadens the search pattern beyond the common calcaneus/metatarsal cases and includes high-risk sites such as proximal 5th metatarsal and navicular.

entries.question: How does the source define pathologic fracture in the stress-fracture differential framework?
entries.answer: Pathologic fracture: fracture due to underlying tumor or infection. Use: this separates repetitive-loading stress injury from fracture driven by destructive disease. Exam pivot: if imaging suggests tumor or infection, do not force the case into fatigue/insufficiency stress-fracture language.

entries.question: What pain patterns are source-stated for ankle/foot stress fractures by location?
entries.answer: General: pain increases with activity and improves with rest. Hindfoot: vague, deep pain. Metatarsals: sharp, precisely localized, pinpoint pain. Hallux sesamoids: pain with running or dorsiflexion of the toe. Exam pivot: symptom localization should guide the search pattern, especially when radiographs are subtle or negative.

entries.question: MRI hip. Based on the image, name 3 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
entries.answer: Source-supported differentials: Osteonecrosis of femoral head Transient osteoporosis of hip Degenerative joint disease

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: Define fatigue fracture.
entries.answer: Source definition: Repetitive overuse trauma results in failure of normal bone. Boundary condition: It is abnormal/repetitive stress applied to normal bone, not normal stress applied to weakened osteoporotic bone. Synonyms: fatigue fracture, overuse fracture.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: Define insufficiency fracture.
entries.answer: Source definition: Normal activity results in failure of weakened, usually osteoporotic bone; also called fragility fracture. Boundary condition: It is normal stress applied to abnormal/weakened bone, not repetitive overuse failure of normal bone. Synonyms: insufficiency fracture, fragility fracture.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: How does repetitive loading progress from stress reaction to complete fatigue fracture?
entries.answer: Repetitive loading injures normal bone before remodeling can fully repair it. The source describes trabeculae fracturing first, which manifests as marrow edema. With continued stress, the cortex ultimately fractures incompletely and cortical healing produces callus; if activity continues before complete healing, the opposite cortex can fail and the fracture can become complete. Imaging consequence: early MR may show edema, while more advanced injury shows a low-signal fracture line and radiographic/CT sclerosis or cortical thickening.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: Why do pelvic insufficiency fractures occur in typical sites despite normal activity?
entries.answer: Insufficiency fracture occurs when normal forces are applied to abnormal, weakened bone. The source states osteoporosis is the most common weakening substrate, with other causes including rheumatoid arthritis, radiation osteitis, renal osteodystrophy, and corticosteroid use. Imaging consequence: weakened pelvic trabecular/cortical bone fails under physiologic loading, producing a low-signal fracture line with surrounding marrow edema; common pelvic sites include sacral ala, pubic ramus/body, supraacetabular ilium, and subchondral femoral head.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What is the pitfall when deciding whether a femoral head subchondral line represents fracture or osteonecrosis, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Calling a subchondral insufficiency fracture osteonecrosis because both can show femoral head marrow edema and low-signal subchondral abnormality. Safety check: Trace the line orientation. Key discriminator: Insufficiency fracture line is near and parallel to the articular surface; osteonecrosis has a serpentine contour that curves away from the articular surface and demarcates an osteonecrotic region. Why the error occurs: Both entities can involve the femoral head and produce subchondral signal abnormality, so the contour/orientation is the deciding clue.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What is the tumor-mimic pitfall in pelvic stress fracture, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking stress-fracture marrow edema for metastatic disease, myeloma, or lymphoma. Safety check: Look for a discrete fracture line and the geometry of the marrow abnormality. Key discriminator: Insufficiency fracture edema is band-like or has straight/rectilinear margins; tumor marrow replacement tends to be rounded and usually lacks a discrete fracture line. Why the error occurs: Marrow edema can be extensive, and femoral neck fatigue fracture may even have a rounded edema appearance, so CT may be useful when it shows the fracture line more distinctly than MR.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What is the pitfall when evaluating pubic symphysis-region edema, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Calling a pubic root/ramus stress fracture osteitis pubis, or missing a concomitant obturator ramus fracture in a patient with symphyseal degenerative/inflammatory changes. Safety check: Search specifically for a fracture line and determine whether the process is symmetric at the pubic symphysis. Key discriminator: Osteitis pubis shows symmetric subchondral marrow edema with erosions, osteophytes, and sclerosis at the pubic symphysis without a fracture line; stress fracture centers on a focal fracture line/edema in the pubic root, pubic ramus, or pubic body. Why the error occurs: Both can create pubic-region marrow edema and pain, and the source notes they can coexist.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What age/activity profile distinguishes fatigue fractures from pelvic insufficiency fractures?
entries.answer: Fatigue fracture: young, active adults. Insufficiency fracture: older population, greater than 55 years. Exam pivot: Use age/activity to adjust the prior, but still require the fracture-line/edema pattern on imaging.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What sex predilection is stated for pelvis stress fractures?
entries.answer: Female greater than male. Exam pivot: In an older woman with pelvic/low-back/hip pain and negative or subtle radiographs, keep insufficiency fracture high on the differential.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: For pelvis stress fractures, what is the source-supported location framework for insufficiency versus fatigue fractures?
entries.answer: Insufficiency: sacral ala; pubic ramus/body; supraacetabular ilium; subchondral femoral head. Fatigue: medial femoral neck; sacrum in long-distance runners; medial iliac crest; pubic body. Exam pivot: Location plus patient substrate helps separate fragility-type injury from overuse injury.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: For pelvis stress fractures, what MRI appearance is expected?
entries.answer: Fracture line: low signal intensity on all sequences. Marrow edema: band-like on both sides of fracture; low T1 and high on fluid-sensitive sequences. Additional findings: enhancement after gadolinium; periosteal reaction and soft-tissue edema are common. Exam pivot: A straight/band-like edema margin favors fracture over tumor.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: For pelvis stress fractures, what radiograph and CT appearance is expected?
entries.answer: Radiographs: sclerotic band with or without a lucent fracture line. Sacrum: radiographs may be occult; arcuate line disruption is useful; healing line becomes sclerotic. CT: same findings as radiographs with improved sensitivity, but still less sensitive than MR. Exam pivot: CT can make the fracture line more distinct when MR edema mimics tumor.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: For pelvic stress/insufficiency fractures, what nuclear medicine appearance and timing are source-supported?
entries.answer: 3-phase bone scan: positive on all phases. Typical uptake locations/patterns mirror MR marrow edema; sacral H-shaped uptake is the Honda sign but may be absent. Timing: positive 2-3 weeks before radiographs; may be falsely negative in first 72 hours; uptake persists for months during healing. Exam pivot: Bone scan is an MR adjunct/alternative for subtle insufficiency fractures.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What is the recommended imaging approach for suspected pelvis stress fracture?
entries.answer: Start with radiographs. If radiographs are equivocal or negative but suspicion remains, obtain MR. AP pelvis is often diagnostic; oblique views may help; inlet/outlet views can evaluate obturator rami. Exam pivot: For older adults with hip pain, include the whole pelvis to avoid missing additional sites.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What is the sacral insufficiency fracture pattern and key radiographic clue?
entries.answer: Pattern: vertical sacral ala fracture, zone 1 or 2, with possible transverse component forming an H-shaped/Honda configuration. Lateral radiograph: may show angulation/buckle at the transverse component, often at S2. Radiographic clue: disruption of arcuate lines is useful. Exam pivot: Sacral fractures may be occult due to osteopenia and bowel contents.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What source-supported femoral neck stress-fracture features matter in pelvic stress-fracture imaging?
entries.answer: Typical setting: athlete or runner with hip pain that increases with activity. Location/imaging: usually basicervical and medial femoral neck; MRI may show only a small partial low-signal fracture line with surrounding edema. Pitfall: femoral-neck fatigue fracture can be surrounded by rounded marrow edema and mimic tumor. Management pivot: high risk of progression to complete fracture, so strict activity management and possible percutaneous screw fixation matter. Source attribution: RadPrimer Pelvis Stress Fractures source package.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What progression risk makes femoral neck stress fracture high yield in athletes?
entries.answer: Femoral neck stress fractures have high risk of progression to complete fracture if activity/rest is not managed. The article specifically notes risk of progression without fixation for femoral neck stress fracture. Exam pivot: Do not dismiss subtle femoral neck edema/fracture line in an athlete as a benign marrow-edema finding.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What healing and nonunion facts are stated for pelvis stress fractures?
entries.answer: Most stress fractures heal with rest. Healing is slow: 4 weeks to 5 months. Nonunion is common in older adult patients. Exam pivot: Report healing response because stress/insufficiency fractures can develop nonunion.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What checklist item is essential after identifying a pelvic stress fracture?
entries.answer: Assess for additional sites of stress/insufficiency fracture. Always evaluate the sacrum in the setting of obturator stress fracture. Report evidence of healing response. Exam pivot: Pelvic stress fractures are often multifocal, so a single visible lesion should not end the search.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: How are complete versus incomplete fractures defined in the source?
entries.answer: Complete fracture: traverses the entire bone. Incomplete fracture: visible fracture line that does not traverse the entire bone. Exam pivot: Incomplete pelvic stress fractures may be subtle but still clinically important, especially at the femoral neck.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What clinical localization clues are source-stated for pelvic stress fractures?
entries.answer: Pubic ramus stress fracture: groin pain, point tenderness at the inferior pubic ramus, and possible standing sign. Acetabular stress fracture: anterior hip pain. Sacral insufficiency fracture: low back pain. Femoral neck stress fracture: hip pain that increases with activity. Clinical pattern: runners most often develop femoral neck stress fracture; older osteoporotic patients may present after a fall or with no clear trauma. Source attribution: RadPrimer Pelvis Stress Fractures source package.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What microscopic/healing features does the source describe for stress fractures?
entries.answer: The source describes osteoclastic resorption at the fracture site, followed by lamellated bone filling osteoclastic cavities, new periosteal and endosteal bone, and sometimes exuberant periosteal reaction. Why this matters for imaging: the healing response explains sclerosis/callus on radiographs or CT and why a healing stress fracture can look aggressive or tumor-like if the fracture line is not recognized. Source attribution: RadPrimer Pelvis Stress Fractures source package. No outside clarification used.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: What treatment and prognosis pivots are source-stated for pelvic stress fractures?
entries.answer: Most stress fractures heal with rest, but healing is slow, ranging from about 4 weeks to 5 months. Conservative care includes stopping athletic training, rest, NSAIDs, physical therapy, stretching, muscle strengthening, and medical treatment of osteoporosis when relevant. Older adults have common nonunion risk and may suffer immobility complications such as DVT and decubitus ulcers. Femoral neck stress fractures are high-risk for completion and may require percutaneous screw fixation. Sacral insufficiency fractures may be treated with sacroplasty or transiliosacral screw stabilization in selected cases. Source attribution: RadPrimer Pelvis Stress Fractures source package.

entries.deck: Corebook::MSK::Trauma::Introduction to Osseous Trauma::Pelvis Stress Fractures
entries.question: When does the source mention DEXA in pelvic stress-fracture workup?
entries.answer: DEXA is used to evaluate bone density in patients with insufficiency fractures and in young patients with atypical fractures. Exam pivot: do not stop at naming the fracture; determine whether weakened bone needs evaluation when the fracture pattern is insufficiency-type or clinically atypical. Source attribution: RadPrimer Pelvis Stress Fractures source package.

entries.clinicalContext: 36-year-old patient with abdominal pain after injury A7K2M9Q4T1XZ
entries.question: Initial CT image. Gross pathology specimen from the same patient. Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Splenic trauma with shattered spleen and active hemorrhage Caption-derived keyword findings: shattered spleen sentinel clot in the perisplenic region multiple foci of active extravasation large hemoperitoneum blood around the spleen is higher density than the blood around the liver multiple large defects and lacerations Reasoning: The CT localizes highest-density blood adjacent to the spleen and shows active bleeding with large hemoperitoneum; the same-patient gross specimen confirms extensive structural disruption requiring splenectomy. Core and STATdx both emphasize CT recognition of laceration/hematoma plus active extravasation as the key risk pivot. Differential: Splenic infarct Splenic abscess Splenic cleft

entries.clinicalContext: 29-year-old patient with abdominal pain after injury P6R8T2V4W9LA
entries.question: Initial CT image. Angiographic image from the same patient. Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Splenic trauma with parenchymal laceration and vascular injury Caption-derived keyword findings: splenic parenchymal laceration active extravasation of blood without substantial perisplenic hematoma intrasplenic active extravasation pseudoaneurysms Coil embolization occluded the bleeding vessels Reasoning: The dominant move is to identify that clinically important splenic vascular injury may be intraparenchymal even without a large perisplenic hematoma. Angiography confirms active extravasation and pseudoaneurysms, matching the source emphasis that vascular injury predicts need for intervention. Differential: Splenic cleft Splenic infarct Splenic abscess

entries.clinicalContext: 42-year-old patient with abdominal pain after blunt injury J4N7Q2L8Z5XB
entries.question: Axial CT image through the spleen. More caudal axial CT image from the same patient. Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Splenic trauma with shattered spleen and intraperitoneal active extravasation Caption-derived keyword findings: shattered spleen following blunt trauma multiple areas of active arterial extravasation poorly enhancing spleen massive arterial extravasation into the peritoneal cavity thickened small bowel loops flattened inferior vena cava (IVC) Reasoning: This is a high-grade splenic injury pattern: shattered parenchyma plus active arterial extravasation beyond the spleen and into the peritoneum. The associated thickened bowel loops and flattened IVC reinforce the shock/hypoperfusion context described in the caption. Differential: Splenic infarct Splenic abscess Splenic mass

entries.clinicalContext: 51-year-old patient with abdominal pain after injury M8C3X6P1Q9TR
entries.question: Axial CT image through the spleen. Pelvic CT image from the same patient. Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Splenic trauma with deep lacerations and delayed hemorrhage risk Caption-derived keyword findings: multiple deep splenic lacerations small amount of perisplenic blood moderate pelvic hemoperitoneum hemodynamic stability during the scan massive delayed bleeding 24 hours later requiring urgent surgery Reasoning: The teaching point is that apparently stable splenic trauma with modest perisplenic blood can still progress to life-threatening delayed hemorrhage. STATdx explicitly warns that minor-appearing injuries may lead to delayed hemorrhage, and Core notes splenic preservation but requires careful CT risk assessment. Differential: Splenic cleft Splenic infarct Splenic abscess

entries.clinicalContext: 44-year-old patient with abdominal pain after injury Q2W7E5R9T1YU
entries.question: Axial CT image through the spleen. More caudal axial CT image from the same patient. Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Splenic trauma with subcapsular hematoma and active arterial extravasation Caption-derived keyword findings: subcapsular hematoma flattening of the lateral contour of the spleen active arterial extravasation into the subcapsular hematoma more caudal level Reasoning: A crescentic subcapsular hematoma compressing the splenic contour is a source-supported hematoma pattern; the separate focus of active arterial extravasation upgrades the case from simple hematoma to vascular injury requiring urgent management consideration. Differential: Splenic infarct Splenic cyst Splenic abscess

entries.question: In splenic trauma, how common is traumatic splenic infarction and what CT pattern/risk does the source state?
entries.answer: Frequency: unusual, less than 2% of traumatic splenic injury cases. CT pattern: wedge-shaped hypoattenuation, which can be segmental or complete. Proposed cause: probably arterial thrombosis after intimal injury. Risk: delayed rupture or abscess formation. Exam pivot: traumatic infarction is rare but complication-prone; do not confuse it with the more common laceration/hematoma pattern.

entries.question: What source definition distinguishes a splenic fracture from a superficial splenic laceration?
entries.answer: Source definition: a splenic fracture is a deep laceration extending from the outer capsule through the splenic hilum. Boundary condition: it is deeper than a superficial laceration and should not be mistaken for a thin congenital cleft. Exam pivot: hilar/deep extension implies a higher-risk central injury pattern.

entries.question: Why must the spleen be evaluated for traumatic injury on portal venous phase CT?
entries.answer: In arterial phase, physiologic heterogeneous splenic enhancement can create patchy areas that either mimic low-attenuation injury or obscure a real laceration. Portal venous phase produces more homogeneous splenic parenchymal enhancement, so a true laceration stands out as a linear or branching area of decreased/nonenhancing attenuation. The imaging pivot is that arterial phase is useful for vascular injury, but portal venous phase is the safer phase for parenchymal injury detection.

entries.question: Why do delayed-phase images distinguish active extravasation from pseudoaneurysm in splenic trauma?
entries.answer: Active extravasation represents contrast leaving an injured vessel and pooling in the hematoma or peritoneal space, so the focus changes in size, shape, or attenuation on delayed imaging. A pseudoaneurysm is a contained arterial wall injury and an AV fistula is a contained artery-to-vein injury; both can appear as focal high attenuation initially, but they do not enlarge like free extravasated contrast on delayed images. The discriminator is containment versus ongoing pooling outside the vascular lumen.

entries.question: Why can a pseudoaneurysm after splenic trauma rupture if untreated?
entries.answer: Core describes pseudoaneurysm as injury to the intima and media of the arterial wall, with rupture contained only by the adventitia. Because the normal arterial wall layers are disrupted and the containment is incomplete, the lesion remains a high-risk contained vascular injury rather than a stable hematoma. The imaging pivot is that a rounded contrast collection should not be dismissed as simple clot; it may require angiographic treatment even when not actively enlarging on delayed CT.

entries.question: What CT-phase pitfall can cause missed or overcalled splenic injury, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Interpreting the spleen only on arterial phase can lead to either overcalling physiologic heterogeneous enhancement as injury or missing a true laceration hidden by heterogeneity. Safety check: Evaluate splenic parenchyma on portal venous phase, where enhancement is more homogeneous. Key discriminator: True laceration remains a linear/branching low-attenuation defect on contrast-enhanced evaluation, while physiologic arterial heterogeneity should not be used alone to diagnose injury. Why it happens: Arterial-phase splenic enhancement is normally heterogeneous and can visually mimic or mask trauma.

entries.question: What vascular-injury pitfall should trigger delayed imaging, and what discriminator resolves it?
entries.answer: Trap: Calling every focal contrast-density splenic focus active extravasation, or dismissing a rounded focus as benign, without checking delayed behavior. Safety check: Add delayed-phase images when a suspicious focus is seen on initial portal venous or arterial-phase images. Key discriminator: Active extravasation changes in size or morphology on delayed images; pseudoaneurysm/AVF remains contained and does not enlarge. Why it happens: Active extravasation and contained vascular injuries can both initially appear as focal high attenuation.

entries.question: What normal variant can mimic traumatic splenic injury, and what surrounding findings prevent the error?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking a congenital splenic cleft for a traumatic laceration. Safety check: Look for adjacent hematoma, free fluid, or stranding and assess the morphology/location of the defect. Key discriminator: A splenic cleft is a thin fissure-like low-attenuation band, most often at the upper or lower pole, without adjacent hematoma, free fluid, or stranding. Why it happens: Both cleft and laceration may appear as low-attenuation defects within splenic parenchyma.

entries.question: In blunt abdominal trauma, which solid organ is most commonly injured?
entries.answer: Fact: The spleen is the most commonly injured solid abdominal organ in blunt trauma. Exam pivot: In blunt LUQ/abdominal trauma, default search should prioritize splenic injury while still surveying for associated abdominal and left thoracic injuries.

entries.question: What proportion of patients with polytrauma have splenic injuries according to the source?
entries.answer: Fact: Splenic injuries are present in 16-24% of patients with polytrauma. Exam pivot: In polytrauma, splenic injury is common enough that subtle LUQ blood or sentinel clot should not be dismissed.

entries.question: How often are other injuries present with splenic injury according to the source?
entries.answer: Fact: Injury to other abdominal organs is present in 36.5%, and 80% of patients with splenic injury have extraabdominal injuries. Exam pivot: Once splenic trauma is identified, actively search for additional abdominal, left thoracic, pancreatic-tail, mesenteric, hepatic, and diaphragmatic injuries.

entries.question: For splenic trauma, what is the key CT phase strategy?
entries.answer: Arterial phase: more sensitive for active extravasation or pseudoaneurysm. Portal venous phase: more sensitive for parenchymal injury/laceration. Delayed phase: differentiates active extravasation from pseudoaneurysm when a suspicious focus is seen. Exam pivot: Use phase behavior to separate parenchymal injury from vascular injury.

entries.question: For splenic trauma, what CT attenuation thresholds support hemoperitoneum or perisplenic clot?
entries.answer: Hemoperitoneum: greater than 30 HU. Perisplenic clot: greater than 45 HU. Sentinel clot sign: highest-density blood localizes adjacent to the injury site. Exam pivot: Dense blood adjacent to the spleen can reveal occult splenic injury even without a visible laceration.

entries.question: For splenic trauma, what sonographic appearance and limitation are source-supported?
entries.answer: US limitation: insensitive for parenchymal injury; subtle lacerations may be missed. Lacerations: hypoechoic or isoechoic to splenic parenchyma and difficult to detect. Hemoperitoneum: intraperitoneal fluid with low-level echoes; perisplenic clot may be echogenic. Exam pivot: FAST can show fluid, but CT is needed to grade and characterize splenic injury.

entries.question: What is the 2018 AAST-OIS grading framework for splenic injury on CT?
entries.answer: Grade I: subcapsular hematoma <10% surface or capsular tear/superficial laceration <1 cm. Grade II: subcapsular hematoma 10-50%, intraparenchymal hematoma <5 cm, or laceration 1-3 cm. Grade III: subcapsular hematoma >50%/enlarging/ruptured, intraparenchymal hematoma >5 cm/expanding, or laceration >3 cm or involving trabecular vessels. Grade IV: segmental/hilar vessel laceration with >=25% devascularization or contained vascular injury/active extravasation within capsule. Grade V: shattered spleen, complete devascularization/hilar injury, or active extravasation extending beyond capsule into peritoneum. Exam pivot: Vascular injury and contained-within-capsule versus beyond-capsule intraperitoneal active bleeding drive grade escalation.

entries.question: In splenic trauma, which CT vascular findings best predict need for intervention?
entries.answer: Best predictors: active arterial extravasation or pseudoaneurysm. Exam pivot: vascular injury is more treatment-directing than laceration depth alone, so active bleeding or pseudoaneurysm should be reported clearly.

entries.question: In a hemodynamically stable splenic-trauma patient, what embolization approach is source-supported for vascular injury?
entries.answer: Distal embolization: source-supported for active extravasation, pseudoaneurysm, or hemoperitoneum in hemodynamically stable patients. Proximal splenic artery embolization: decreases splenic perfusion pressure while collateral flow preserves splenic parenchyma and improves nonoperative-management success. Exam pivot: embolization is a spleen-preserving treatment path for stable vascular injury.

entries.question: When is nonoperative management preferred in splenic trauma?
entries.answer: Preferred whenever possible in hemodynamically stable patients who do not have other injuries requiring surgery. Most typical setting: AAST grades I-III, though some higher-grade injuries may initially be treated nonoperatively if the patient is stable. Rationale: splenic preservation avoids surgery and postsplenectomy sepsis risk. Exam pivot: hemodynamic stability is the main gateway to spleen-preserving management.

entries.question: What predicts failure of nonoperative management in splenic trauma?
entries.answer: Higher-grade splenic injuries predict failure; grade V has a 75% failure rate. Other failure predictors: age greater than 55 years and associated injuries. Clinical consequence: splenectomy may be necessary with hemodynamic instability, severe injury, or failed conservative management/delayed rupture. Exam pivot: stable lower-grade injury favors observation/embolization, but grade V and patient/injury risk factors push toward failure or surgery.

entries.question: For splenic trauma, what follow-up imaging strategy is source-supported?
entries.answer: Lower-grade injuries: repeat imaging generally does not change management and is not routinely recommended. Higher-grade injuries: repeat imaging is recommended at 48-72 hours after presentation. Exam pivot: Follow-up is risk-stratified; do not reflexively reimage every low-grade injury, but do not ignore high-grade injury risk.

entries.question: Why can FAST or DPL be falsely negative in splenic trauma?
entries.answer: Source-stated limitation: 29% of all patients and 40% of children with splenic injury may not have hemoperitoneum. Exam pivot: A negative FAST/DPL does not exclude splenic injury, especially in children; CECT is the best diagnostic tool when clinical concern persists.

entries.question: What report element should be included for traumatic splenic injury?
entries.answer: Include the AAST-OIS splenic injury grade in reports detailing splenic traumatic injury. Exam pivot: The grade communicates injury severity and helps guide management, especially when vascular injury is present.

entries.question: What CT features distinguish common mimics of splenic laceration?
entries.answer: Splenic cleft: thin fissure-like polar low-attenuation band without adjacent hematoma/free fluid/stranding. Splenic infarct: wedge-shaped peripheral low attenuation, usually without surrounding free fluid or hematoma unless ruptured. Splenic abscess: rounded irregular low-attenuation collection with infection signs; gas is highly specific when present. Exam pivot: Adjacent traumatic blood and irregular branching/deep defects favor laceration/fracture.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: Define colloid cyst.
entries.answer: Source definition: Colloid cyst is a unilocular mucin-containing cyst of the 3rd ventricle, also called a paraphyseal or endodermal cyst. Refined operational definition based on the allowed source set: a benign developmental, usually nonenhancing cyst characteristically arising from the anterior roof of the 3rd ventricle/foramen of Monro. Boundary: it is an endodermal cystic lesion, not a neuroectodermal tumor; it is usually wedged at the foramen of Monro rather than broadly attached to the septum/frontal horn. Synonyms: paraphyseal cyst; endodermal cyst.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: Why can a colloid cyst cause abrupt obstructive hydrocephalus?
entries.answer: Normal CSF exits the lateral ventricles through the foramina of Monro into the 3rd ventricle. Colloid cysts are characteristically wedged into this narrow foramen/anterior-superior roof of the 3rd ventricle, where the fornices can drape around the cyst. When the cyst blocks one or both foramina of Monro, CSF outflow from the lateral ventricles is obstructed, producing rapid lateral ventricular enlargement, transependymal CSF flow/interstitial edema, herniation, coma, or death. Imaging pivot: a foramen of Monro mass plus lateral ventricular dilatation is not just a location clue; it is the mechanism of the emergency.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: What tissue/content mechanism explains the variable CT and MR appearance of colloid cysts?
entries.answer: Colloid cysts arise from embryonic endodermal elements and have a thin fibrous capsule with epithelial lining that includes goblet and scattered ciliated cells. The cyst accumulates mucinous secretions and desquamated epithelial cells, creating thick gelatinous material with variable viscosity, hydration, necrotic debris, cholesterol, and sometimes old blood. Imaging pivot: CT density correlates inversely with hydration; T1 signal correlates with cholesterol concentration; T2 signal reflects water content, while viscous/inspissated contents can appear markedly T2 hypointense or produce a black-hole effect.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: What visual pitfall can occur on this stereotactic MR image, and what safety check prevents it?
entries.answer: Trap: Mistaking enhancement along the cyst margins for true cyst-wall rim enhancement. Safety check: Trace the enhancing margins anatomically as displaced internal cerebral and septal veins when they course along the lateral cyst margins. Key discriminator: true rim enhancement surrounds the cyst wall; in this case the source states the enhancement represents displaced veins, not rim enhancement. Why it happens: venous structures displaced around a foramen of Monro cyst can visually simulate a thin enhancing cyst wall.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: What is the danger in dismissing a small or incidental colloid cyst?
entries.answer: Trap: Assuming small size or incidental discovery eliminates clinical risk. Safety check: Always assess for hydrocephalus and communicate the diagnosis, especially if ventricular obstruction is present. Key discriminator: the risk is anatomic obstruction at the foramen of Monro, not simply lesion size. Why it happens: colloid cysts may be stable or incidental, but acute foramen of Monro obstruction can cause rapid hydrocephalus, herniation, coma, or death, including with small lesions.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: What proportion of colloid cysts are asymptomatic versus associated with headache?
entries.answer: Fact: 40-50% are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally; headache occurs in about 50-60%. Exam pivot: symptoms are common but absence of symptoms does not exclude a clinically important foramen of Monro lesion.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: What percentage of primary brain tumors and intraventricular masses are colloid cysts?
entries.answer: Fact: Colloid cysts account for about 0.5-1.0% of primary brain tumors and 15-20% of intraventricular masses. Exam pivot: despite being uncommon among primary brain tumors overall, they are a major intraventricular/foramen of Monro diagnosis.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: What is the typical age distribution for colloid cyst?
entries.answer: Fact: Peak age is around 40 years; RadPrimer emphasizes the 3rd-4th decades, while STATdx broadens the adult range to the 3rd-7th decades. Pediatric cases are rare. Exam pivot: an adult foramen of Monro mass strongly favors colloid cyst; in children, SEGA is an important competing foramen of Monro diagnosis.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: For colloid cyst, what is the classic CT appearance?
entries.answer: Noncontrast CT: well-demarcated round hyperdense mass at the foramen of Monro/anterior upper 3rd ventricle. Density: about two-thirds hyperdense and one-third iso- or hypodense; density correlates inversely with hydration. Enhancement: usually absent; rare peripheral/rim enhancement can occur in complicated inflammatory/apoplexy cases. Exam pivot: hyperdense foramen of Monro mass is the best diagnostic clue.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: For colloid cyst, what location pattern is most source-supported?
entries.answer: Classic location: foramen of Monro/anterior-superior roof of the 3rd ventricle. Frequency: more than 99% are wedged into the foramen of Monro. Size: ranges from a few millimeters to several centimeters, with mean around 15 mm. Exam pivot: a well-demarcated lesion at this narrow CSF outflow point is both a diagnosis clue and an obstruction risk.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: For colloid cyst, what T1 MRI signal pattern is source-supported?
entries.answer: T1 signal correlates with cholesterol concentration. About two-thirds are T1 hyperintense and about one-third are isointense. Exam pivot: a T1-hyperintense anterior third ventricular/foramen of Monro lesion strongly supports colloid cyst, but isointense cysts still occur and may be harder to see.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: For colloid cyst, what T2 signal pattern is source-supported?
entries.answer: T2 signal is variable and generally reflects water content. Many colloid cysts are isointense to brain. About 25% show mixed hypo/hyperintensity or a black-hole/profound hypointense component from viscous or inspissated contents. Exam pivot: T2 hypointensity is not a reason to discard colloid cyst; it can be the clue to thick contents.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: For colloid cyst, what FLAIR and DWI behavior is source-supported?
entries.answer: FLAIR: colloid cyst signal does not suppress. DWI: should not show true restricted diffusion despite viscous gelatinous contents. ADC: often higher than normal brain and lower than CSF. Exam pivot: nonrestriction helps avoid mistaking a viscous colloid cyst for a diffusion-restricting intraventricular process.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: For colloid cyst, what enhancement and apoplexy caveats are source-supported?
entries.answer: Usual enhancement: absent/nonenhancing. Rare caveat: peripheral/rim enhancement can occur in complicated inflammatory or apoplexy cases. Apoplexy clue: fluid-fluid or blood-fluid levels are rare and indicate cyst apoplexy/hemorrhage. Exam pivot: do not let rare rim enhancement or hemorrhagic/apoplectic change erase the foramen of Monro diagnosis.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: What is the Colloid Cyst Risk Score framework?
entries.answer: CCRS factors: age under 65 years; headache; cyst at least 7 mm; FLAIR hyperintensity; anterior anatomic risk zone. Exam pivot: these features stratify symptomatic and hydrocephalus risk.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: Which source-supported features favor colloid cyst stability?
entries.answer: Features favoring stability: older age, small cyst size, no hydrocephalus, hyperdensity on CT, and T2 hypointensity. Natural history pivot: most cysts remain stable or stop enlarging; approximately 10% enlarge. Exam pivot: hyperdense CT + T2 hypointensity suggests inspissated/less hydrated contents and tends to favor stability in the source framework.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: Which source-supported features favor colloid cyst enlargement?
entries.answer: Features favoring enlargement: younger age, larger cyst, hydrocephalus, iso-/hypodensity on CT, and T2 hyperintensity. Exam pivot: enlargement risk is not random; integrate patient age, cyst size, hydrocephalus, CT density, and T2 signal.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: What imaging features suggest a colloid cyst may be difficult to aspirate stereotactically?
entries.answer: Hyperdensity on CT and T2 hypointensity suggest high viscosity/inspissated contents. These features can make stereotactic aspiration difficult when the cyst is extremely viscous or solid. Exam pivot: CT hyperdensity + T2 hypointensity is not just diagnostic; it predicts percutaneous therapy difficulty.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: What reporting action is emphasized when a colloid cyst is identified?
entries.answer: Notify the referring clinician immediately, especially if hydrocephalus is present. Why: acute foramen of Monro obstruction can cause rapid hydrocephalus, herniation, coma, or death, including with small lesions. Exam pivot: communication is part of the diagnosis because the dangerous feature is obstructive anatomy, not just tumor identity.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: What treatment/observation framework is source-supported for colloid cyst?
entries.answer: Usual treatment: complete surgical resection, commonly neuronavigation-guided endoscopic removal with capsule coagulation. After complete resection: recurrence is rare; short-term memory disturbance may occur after surgery and usually resolves. Observation: uncommon and generally not recommended because sudden obstruction can occur even with small cysts; serial imaging may be appropriate for asymptomatic cysts under 1 cm without hydrocephalus.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: At the foramen of Monro, how does age shift the leading diagnosis?
entries.answer: Adults: colloid cyst is the most common mass of the foramen of Monro. Children: SEGA is the key competing diagnosis. Source basis: Core evidence explicitly supports this adult-versus-child framing.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: How does subependymoma differ from colloid cyst as a foramen of Monro/anterior ventricular mimic?
entries.answer: Colloid cyst: round, well-demarcated lesion wedged at the foramen of Monro/anterior roof of the 3rd ventricle, usually nonenhancing. Subependymoma: favors frontal horn or septum pellucidum attachment and patchy/solid enhancement. Exam pivot: attachment site and enhancement pattern are the discriminator.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: How does neurocysticercosis differ from colloid cyst as an intraventricular/foramen of Monro mimic?
entries.answer: Colloid cyst: solitary foramen of Monro/anterior third ventricular lesion with classic CT hyperdensity and variable MR signal. Neurocysticercosis: usually multiple; calcification or scolex may be present, often with ependymitis or basilar meningitis. Exam pivot: multiplicity, calcification/scolex, and inflammatory meningitis/ependymitis favor neurocysticercosis.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: How can vertebrobasilar dolichoectasia or aneurysm mimic colloid cyst, and what separates it?
entries.answer: Mimic pattern: a vascular structure can simulate a hyperdense foramen of Monro mass. Discriminator: look for flow void and phase artifact on MR, or confirm with vascular imaging. Exam pivot: do not call a vascular mimic a cyst before checking vascular signal/artifact.

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
entries.question: Which additional intraventricular mimics are source-supported for colloid cyst, and what is the key caveat?
entries.answer: Craniopharyngioma: rarely involves the 3rd ventricle, is usually not wedged into the foramen of Monro, and more often calcifies or shows rim/nodular enhancement. Choroid plexus papilloma, xanthogranuloma, and choroid plexus cyst are additional intraventricular mimics. Key caveat: xanthogranuloma may be indistinguishable on imaging.

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma L7Q4N2A9X5BC
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Epidural hematoma Caption-derived keyword findings: comminuted, depressed fracture left squamous temporal bone hyperdense typical biconvex, lens-shaped configuration focal subgaleal hematoma local mass effect adjacent sulcal effacement Tight reasoning: The bone-window fracture plus hyperdense biconvex lens-shaped extraaxial collection at the impact site is the classic source-supported arterial EDH pattern. The coronal image confirms local mass effect without needing a clinical hint to solve the diagnosis. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma P8C3D6M1K9JT
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Initial NECT. Repeat NECT 3 hours later. Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Epidural hematoma (traumatic interdural variant) Caption-derived keyword findings: focus of calcium displaced to the inner margin Minimal mass effect deteriorated 3 hours later growth swirl sign actively bleeding hematoma between the periosteal and meningeal layers of the dura displaced dural calcifications Tight reasoning: The initial extraaxial collection with displaced dural calcification followed by 3-hour enlargement and swirl sign matches the source-described rare traumatic interdural/EDH variant. The interval growth and active bleeding make this a danger-pattern EDH rather than a stable small collection. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma V2H8R5K1M7QA
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Venous epidural hematoma Caption-derived keyword findings: lacerated superior sagittal sinus dura displaced away from the calvarium superior sagittal sinus displaced away from the calvarium crosses the suture line into the contralateral side major dural venous sinuses away from the skull Tight reasoning: CTA shows the dura and superior sagittal sinus displaced away from the calvarium, with the collection crossing the suture line. That crossing is a source-supported exception for venous EDH, especially when a dural sinus is displaced or compressed. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma X5M2T8Q1N4PR
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Epidural hematoma with frontal sinus fracture source Caption-derived keyword findings: swirl sign focus of air within the hematoma fractured paranasal sinus Marked mass effect copious bleeding from a branch of the ethmoidal artery nondisplaced fracture of the right frontal sinus inner wall Tight reasoning: The extraaxial hematoma has source-stated swirl sign and intralesional air, and the bone-window image shows the adjacent frontal sinus inner-wall fracture explaining the air. The combination supports EDH with an arterial/sinus-fracture source and mass-effect urgency. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Initial axial NECT. Initial coronal NECT. Initial sagittal NECT. NECT 5 weeks later. Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Epidural hematoma Caption-derived keyword findings: classic biconvex (lentiform) uniformly hyperdense right middle fossa nondisplaced skull fracture underlying the hematoma classic middle cranial fossa biconvex configuration all 3 major imaging planes decreasing in size and density Tight reasoning: The initial axial/coronal/sagittal images show a uniformly hyperdense lentiform middle-fossa collection, the classic CT appearance of acute EDH. The 5-week follow-up decreasing size and density supports expected evolution rather than a mass. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma T3W7H9Q2C5LM
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Epidural hematoma with early transtentorial herniation Caption-derived keyword findings: left temporal convexity medial displacement of the uncus early transtentorial herniation Tight reasoning: The temporal convexity extraaxial hemorrhage is accompanied by medial uncus displacement, a source-stated early transtentorial herniation clue. This converts recognition of EDH into an urgent mass-effect pattern. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma A8V2L6N5Q9KR
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Epidural hematoma Caption-derived keyword findings: crossing the falx attachment site hemorrhagic cerebral contusion Axial NECT Tight reasoning: The key source-supported discriminator is crossing the falx attachment site, which can favor EDH over SDH in this case. The accompanying hemorrhagic contusion also reinforces the trauma search pattern: EDH may coexist with other intracranial injuries. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma M5Q8D2F6J1VX
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Epidural hematoma with active bleeding and transtentorial herniation Caption-derived keyword findings: Large mixed-density rapid active bleeding transtentorial herniation left temporal uncus and hippocampus Tight reasoning: A large mixed-density collection is source-linked to rapid active bleeding, and the same image shows transtentorial herniation of the left temporal uncus and hippocampus. This is a high-risk EDH pattern rather than a simple extraaxial blood collection. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma K1P7Z4H8D2WA
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Epidural hematoma Caption-derived keyword findings: Axial T2 MR linear hypointense dura underlying brain Tight reasoning: The MR recognition move is the source-described linear hypointense dura interposed between the collection and the brain. That dural line localizes the collection external to dura and separates EDH from a subdural compartment process. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma Z6N3C9V1B8HT
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Posterior fossa venous epidural hematoma Caption-derived keyword findings: posterior fossa swirl sign focus of air right sigmoid sinus fractured mastoid air cells Marked mass effect continuous oozing from the right sigmoid sinus Tight reasoning: Posterior fossa location, air near the sigmoid sinus, and mastoid air-cell fracture identify a venous sinus injury source. The swirl sign and marked mass effect make this posterior fossa EDH surgically important despite venous oozing rather than arterial spurting. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma J4X9M2T7Q6LD
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Epidural hematoma with coexisting subdural hematoma Caption-derived keyword findings: right squamous temporal bone adjacent to the pterion small biconvex underlying the skull fracture mixed density with a less-dense center swirl sign posterior falcine subdural hematoma Tight reasoning: The pterional skull fracture plus small biconvex mixed-density collection is classic for EDH, and the less-dense center is the source-stated swirl sign. The caption also states a coexisting posterior falcine subdural hematoma, reinforcing that identifying EDH should not end the search. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma Q7L2V9P4R6MD
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Vertex venous epidural hematoma Caption-derived keyword findings: lacerated superior sagittal sinus dura displaced superior sagittal sinus displaced skull fracture barely visible mass effect vertex Tight reasoning: The MR/MRV cluster shows a vertex venous EDH with displaced dura and superior sagittal sinus, while the skull fracture is barely visible. This is the source-supported venous/vertex pattern where MR/MRV or CTV can clarify sinus displacement. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

entries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with acute head trauma C2R8N5K9V1QD
entries.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Epidural Hematoma, Classic
entries.question: Initial NECT after acute head trauma. Repeat scan 10 days later. Most likely diagnosis?
entries.answer: Epidural hematoma Caption-derived keyword findings: small right parietal mild mass effect Glasgow Coma Scale was 13 no surgery was performed unchanged in size density has decreased significantly small bifrontal subdural hygromas complete resolution Tight reasoning: This is a small right parietal acute EDH with mild mass effect in a clinically selected observation pathway. The 10-day follow-up shows unchanged size but decreased density, matching source-supported nonoperative follow-up behavior. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema

This is the key active-expansion recognition pattern. Differential: Acute subdural hematoma Extraaxial neoplasm Epidural empyema
